requirements.text: Get to know the members of your den.

activities.title: A Time to Talk – A Time to Listen
activities.description: The Cub Scout sign is a way to help Cub Scouts learn good manners and communication skills.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Be familiar with the Cub Scout sign, see Additional Resources.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts and their adult partners gather.
Demonstrate the Cub Scout sign and tell the Cub Scouts and adult partners that the Cub Scout sign represents the ears of a wolf.
Inform Cub Scouts and adult partners that when they see someone use the Cub Scout sign it means everyone stops what they are doing and listens.
Give everyone a chance to demonstrate the Cub Scout sign.
Practice using the Cub Scout sign by having Cub Scouts and adult partners talk to each other and make a lot of noise, then without saying anything, make the Cub Scout sign and wait for everyone to stop what they are doing to listen.
Remind Cub Scouts and adult partners that the Cub Scout sign gives us a way to communicate without having to talk over or yell to get everyone’s attention.
Create pairs made up of two Cub Scouts and their adult partners. Have them get to know each other by sharing what they like to do as a family, what their favorite food is, and what their favorite color is.
When it looks like everyone is done, use the Cub Scout sign to get everyone’s attention to move on to the next activity.
Tip – When using the Cub Scout sign, patience is key. Do not talk over or yell to get the attention of Cub Scouts. Use the Cub Scout sign and wait for everyone to place their sign up and stop what they are doing and listen. Avoid calling out “signs up” or any other verbal command.

activities.title: Den Doodle Tiger
activities.description: The den doodle is a craft project that can be used to track attendance, reward good behavior, and completion of requirements.
supply_list: 4 – 12 inch 2” x 1” boards for the base
1 – 4 ft. 2” x 1” board for the pole
1-foot-long cord that is 3/16” or less than ¼” thick– one for each Cub Scout
Power drill with a 1/4 drill bit
Blue plastic pony beads (enough to present each Cub Scout with one for every den meeting)
Yellow plastic pony beads (enough to present each Cub Scout with one for every den meeting)
Orange plastic pony beads (enough to present each Cub Scout when they earn an elective Adventure)
White plastic pony beads (enough to present to each Cub Scout when they earn a required Adventure)
Add more colors of beads if you want to track or recognize other items such as wearing the uniform, bringing your handbook, good behavior, or helping others.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Sand the edges of each board and the plywood to remove any rough edges.
Paint the 3’ x 1’ ¼” plywood with the orange spray paint and let it dry.
Paint the 4 boards that are 12-inch 1” x 2” with blue spray paint and let it dry.
Paint the 4ft. 1” x 2” board with the yellow spray paint and let it dry.
Attach the one 12-inch 1” x 2” , using wood screws, to each side of the bottom of the 4ft 1” x 2” so that the 12-inch 1” x 2” are vertical. See illustration in additional resources.
With a pencil space out the names of each Cub Scout on the bottom of the 3’ x 1’ ¼” plywood. Names may need to be placed at an angle or vertically to fit everyone. You may consider leaving one space open just in case a new Cub Scout joins the den later. Leave space to drill a hole below each name. See illustration in additional resources.
Once names are properly placed and penciled in, paint the names using black latex paint and a fine paintbrush.
Decorate the rest of the ¼” plywood with the pack number, Tiger rank stickers or patches, etc., and let dry.
Drill a hole under each name and attach a 1’ long cord under each name.
Center the ¼” plywood to the top of the 4 ft. 1” x 2” board and attach with wood screws.
During the meeting:
Introduce the den doodle to the den by letting the Cub Scouts know how they can earn a bead and what each color bead means.
Blue is for attending the den meeting, pack meeting, and other Cub Scout activities
Yellow is for wearing their Cub Scout uniform to the den meeting
White is for when they earn a required Adventure, in addition to their Adventure loop.
Orange is for when they earn an elective Adventure, in addition to their Adventure loop.
At the end of each Den meeting award the beads to each Cub Scout and attach them to the cord on the den doodle below their name. Attach the beads by looping the bead(s) through the cord, push the beads to the top, and tie an overhand knot just below the last bead.
Use the den doodle to reward positive behavior. Do not take beads away once they are earned.
After the meeting:
After each meeting look at the den doodle and look for Cub Scouts who may be lagging behind. Reach out to the Adult Partner to address any concerns about participation.
Tip: Den doodles can be made from different materials and there are several different designs. This is one example of a den doodle that can be made.

activities.title: Den Flag Tiger
activities.description: A den flag is a craft that can bring your den together by getting to know everyone’s name and having a symbol that everyone has a part in making.
supply_list: 60” long 1 1/8” diameter wooden staff or dowel
2’ x 3’ orange felt – this is the flag, and it will be displayed vertically
30” piece of twine or thin rope
7” x 7” black felt squares (one for each adult partner)
7” x 7” orange felt squares (one for each Cub Scout)
(If the Den Leader is not an adult partner of one of the Cub Scouts in the den add another black felt square)
Thick black Sharpie marker to write on orange felt squares
Scissors – one for each Cub Scout or enough to share

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Wrap the bottom of the wooden staff with tin foil as high as the paint bucket is tall.
Follow the directions for the concrete mix to fill the 2-gallon paint bucket ¾ of the way full.
While the concrete is wet place the wooden staff, the end with the tin foil, into the bucket and hold it in place until the concrete is dry.
Once the concrete is dry, remove the wood staff, the tin foil will allow the pole to come out. This is the base for your den flag.
Sand the ends of the wooden dowels and staff to remove sharp edges
Lay the flag on a table so that it is vertical with the 2’ section as the bottom and top.
Place the ½” dowel across the top and fold the top of the flag over by 1 inch to cover the wood dowel and glue the folded section to the flag to the back section of the flag with the wood dowel inside.
Use the 1 ½’ x 1’ black felt to cut out letters and numbers to spell the word “Pack” and the pack numbers. If your pack uses den numbers include the word “Den” and the den number. Letters and numbers should be 6” tall.
Attach the letters and numbers using fabric glue to the top of the flag. Place the Pack and the number above the Den and number.
Attach the teacup hook to the top of the flagpole.
Attache the 30” twine or rope to each end of the dowel.
During the meeting:
Give each Cub Scout a 7” x 7” orange felt square and each adult partner a 7” x 7” black felt square
Have adult partners help their Cub Scout trace their hand (either left or right) onto the orange felt using the chalk and then help them cut out the shape of their hand.
Have adult partners trace their hand (the same side as their Cub Scouts) onto the black felt using the chalk and cut out the shape of their hand.
Have Cub Scouts write their name on the cut out of their hand.
Have each Cub Scout and their adult partner glue the Cub Scout’s orange hand on top of the adult partner’s black hand, making sure the Cub Scout’s name is visible.
Have each Cub Scout and adult partner glue their cut-out hands on the flag one by one. As they glue their cut-out hands onto the flag have them share what their favorite outdoor activity is and what their favorite food is.
When all the hands are on the flag, attach the flag to the flagpole by hanging it by the twin or rope onto the teacup hook.
Tip: Den flags can be made from different materials and there are several different designs. This is one example of a den flag that can be made.

activities.title: Me Too Name Game
activities.description: Learn how much everyone in the den has in common.
supply_list: At least two Cub Scouts and adult partners

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare a space for Cub Scout to be able to move freely about.
Read them during the meeting to understand the game.
During the meeting:
Include adult partners in this game
Have everyone sit on the floor in an open space.
Choose a Cub Scout to start by having them stand up and move 5 feet from the group.
Have the Cub Scout say what their favorite food is.
Anyone else who also has that as a favorite food shouts, “Me Too!” and walks over to the Cub Scout to stand next to them.
Pick an adult partner next who is still sitting and have them do the same, move 5 feet away from the group and away from the other group that is standing and say what their favorite food is.
Anyone else who is sitting and has that as a favorite food shouts, “Me Too!” and walks over to form a new group.
Continue until no one is sitting.
Move on to the next thing by keeping everyone standing and picking someone who has not had a chance to share yet. This time have them step away from all groups to form a new group. This time have them share what their favorite color is.
Anyone else who also has that as a favorite color shouts, “Me Too!” and walks over to stand next to them.
Continue until you have everyone in new groups based on their favorite color.
Continue this until every Cub Scout and adult partner has had a chance to form a group based on what they like. Additional categories to use; flavor of ice-cream, genre (type) of music, genre (type) of movie, or video game console

activities.title: Spider Web
activities.description: Members of the den learn about each other as they build a spider web of yarn.
supply_list: 30 ft. of blue yarn rolled in a ball
30 ft. of yellow yarn rolled in a ball
30 ft. of orange yarn rolled in a ball
Large name tags for each player

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare a space for Cub Scouts and Adult Partners to sit in a circle with about a foot between each player.
Prepare the balls of yarn.
Prepare a name tag for Cub Scouts and Adult Partners with just their first name, make sure to find out what name people prefer to go by. For example, Joshua or Josh / Elizabeth or Liz.
Review the game below.
During the meeting:
Have everyone sit on the floor in a circle in an open space.
The den leader takes the ball of blue yarn and says, “My name is (den leader’s name) and I am adding (one of the players) to our web” and then gently throws the ball of yarn to that person. That person then catches it and holds on to a piece of the yarn and remains holding onto it for the rest of the activity. This is where the name tags come into play so people can read the name of the person. The only rule is that the yarn must be tossed to someone new each time, and no one should get the yarn more than once, so everyone is added to the web.
The den leader then takes the ball of yellow yarn and says, “When I get home from school or work I like to….(the den leader then says what they like to do) and then tosses the ball to someone else who states “When I get home from school/work I like to……” this is repeated until each player is given a chance to share. As before players continue to hold on to a piece of the blue yarn and now a piece of the yellow yarn before they toss the yarn to someone else.
The den leader then takes the ball of orange yarn and says, “My favorite food is…” and repeats the same as the blue and yellow yarn.
At the end when everyone has shared the den leader says “Look how beautiful our web is. Although we are going to pick up the yarn I hope you remember that each of us is connected in some way. One way that we are all connected is that we have chosen to be Cub Scouts and to always Do Our Best and to live by the Scout Oath and Scout Law.”

requirements.text: Recite the Scout Oath with your den, including your Tiger adult partner.

activities.title: Cub Scout Land
activities.description: This activity is designed to cover requirements 1-5. Cub Scouts play Cub Scout Land to learn about each other, the Scout Oath, the Scout Law, and other fundamentals of the Cub Scout program.
supply_list: Cub Scout Land cards; 44 cards total (found in Additional Resources)
Cub Scout Land game board (found in Additional Resources)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print out the Cub Scout Land game board and tape the four pages together to make the large game board.
Print and cut out the Cub Scout Land cards and game pieces.
Separate the action cards (the cards with the colorful squares and point of the Scout Law or the Cub Scout ranks) from the game pieces (the cards with items like a flashlight, a campfire, a school bus, etc.).
Place the shuffled action cards face down, creating a draw pile.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and ask them each to pick out a game piece for playing Cub Scout Land. The object of the game is for the Cub Scouts to advance along the Cub Scout trail, from Lion through all the Cub Scout ranks to Arrow of Light, and ending in the yellow “You Made It” circle, symbolizing joining a Scouts BSA Troop. Along the trail, Cub Scouts will learn about each other, the Scout Oath, the Scout Law, and other fundamentals of the Cub Scout program.
Explain the rules of the game.
To start the game, all Cub Scouts and adult partners will say the Scout Oath together.
Next, Cub Scouts will share their birthdays (month and day). The Cub Scout whose birthday is next, goes first. Play continues clockwise.
On their turn, Cub Scouts will draw a card from the draw pile.
If the card has one colored square, their adult partner will read the point of the Scout Law printed on that card. The Cub Scout who drew the card shares a time they showed that trait. Then, the Cub Scout moves their game piece to the next space of that color.
If the card has two colored squares, their adult partner will read the point of the Scout Law printed on that card. The Cub Scout who drew the card shares a time they showed that trait. Then, the Cub Scout moves their game piece to the second matching color space.
If a rank card is drawn, the Cub Scout moves their game piece to the matching rank space on the game board. Every time a player lands on or passes a Cub Scout rank space, everyone must do the following:
Lion rank space: one at a time, Cub Scouts say their name and favorite color.
Tiger rank space: one at a time, Cub Scouts say their favorite food and favorite animal.
Wolf rank space: together, everyone demonstrates the Cub Scout sign.
Bear rank space: together, everyone demonstrates the Cub Scout salute.
Webelos rank space: with their adult partner, Cub Scouts demonstrate the Cub Scout handshake.
Arrow of Light rank space: together, everyone says the Cub Scout motto.
If a Cub Scout ends on a space touching the river, they can take a shortcut up the river, toward the end of the game board.
Once the first Cub Scout reaches the yellow “You Made It!” circle, one at a time, everyone shares a time when they have demonstrated the Cub Scout motto “Do Your Best.” The first Cub Scout to reach the yellow circle wins the game. Encourage all Cub Scouts to demonstrate good sportsmanship by congratulating the winning Cub Scout. Cub Scouts can choose to either continue playing the game until everyone has reached the yellow circle, or they can start the game over.

activities.title: Tiger Chatterbox
activities.description: Fold a piece of paper into a chatterbox/fortune teller to introduce the Scout Oath to your Cub Scout.
supply_list: Each Cub Scout will need their Tiger handbook

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare meeting space for Cub Scouts and adult partners to make a craft.
Use the Tiger handbook on page 5.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts open their Tiger handbook to page 5
With help from their adult partner have Cub Scouts make a chatter box of the Scout Oath
Cut out the chatterbox on page five.
Start with the print side down.
Crease a square piece of paper diagonally from each corner. Fold the top right corner to touch the bottom left corner. Crease the fold with your finger and then unfold it so your sheet is flat again. Then take the top left corner and fold it over to the bottom right corner.
Fold the paper in half from each side. Bring the top edge of the paper to the bottom edge and crease the fold.
Unfold the paper so it’s flat again and rotate it 90 degrees. Fold the new top edge of the paper to the bottom to crease it and then flatten it out again. Your paper will have four lines intersecting in the middle.
Bring the corners to the center of the paper. Start with one of the bottom corners and fold it to the middle of the paper where the creases intersect.
Press down on the fold with a fingernail so it stays in place.
Turn paper 90 degrees and fold the other bottom corner toward the center. Keep rotating and folding paper until you’ve made a smaller square containing four triangles.
Flip the paper over and fold each corner to the center again.
Have Cub Scouts and adult partners take turns picking colors and numbers to become familiar with the Scout Oath. Have them continue until they have completed the Scout Oath.

activities.title: Tiger Oath and Law Puzzle
activities.description: Introduce the Scout Oath to Cub Scouts by making a puzzle out of popsicle sticks.
supply_list: 9 popsicle sticks for each Cub Scout in the den
Small tip or thin markers, enough to share

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up space for Cub Scouts and adult partners to sit down to make a craft
During the meeting:
Give each Cub Scout 9 popsicle sticks and a marker
Have the adult partner write on each popsicle stick a part of the Scout Oath broken up in the following way:
On my honor
I will do my best
To do my duty
To God and my country
And to obey the Scout Law
To help other people at all times
To keep myself physically strong
Mentally awake
And morally straight
Have Cub Scouts gather their sticks in one hand and raise their hand above a table about 1 foot and then let go of the sticks. The idea is for the sticks to fall on the table in a small group together.
Each Cub Scout then tries to pick up a stick without disturbing the other sticks and then places the stick with the word side up next to the pile.
The adult partner then tries to pick up a stick without disturbing the other sticks and then places the stick with the word side up and together the Cub Scout and adult partner decide if the stick should go before or after the first stick.
Cub Scout and adult partner then share what that part of the Scout Oath means to them.
Cub Scout and adult partner continue to take turns until all the sticks are picked up and they have placed them in the proper order to make out the Scout Oath.

requirements.text: Have your Tiger adult partner or den leader read the Scout Law to you. Demonstrate your understanding of being trustworthy, helpful, or friendly.

activities.title: Don’t Wake the Dragon
activities.description: In this game, Cub Scouts have to work together and demonstrate being trustworthy, helpful, and friendly.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare meeting space to remove obstacles so Cub Scout and adult partners can move around.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and adult partners to explain the rules.
Explain that in this game the Den Leader is a sleeping dragon. To get past the sleeping dragon the den has to perform different tasks.
To keep from waking the dragon the den cannot talk while they are performing the tasks.
The leader, the sleeping dragon, moves 10 ft away from the den and will give a task for the den to do.
Once they have completed the task the den walks past the dragon.
If they were quiet during the task and did the task correctly the dragon stays “asleep”.
If they were not quiet during the task or did it incorrectly when the den walks past the dragon the dragon shouts “boo!”
The first task is that the den must line up in order from shortest to tallest.
The second task is that the den must line up in order from oldest to youngest

activities.title: Tiger Maze
activities.description: Cub Scouts help their adult partner navigate a maze.
supply_list: 3 rolls of painter’s tape (1.88 In. x 60 Yds.)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare a meeting space that is large around 12’ x 12’ and free of obstacles. Make sure the floor won’t be damaged by placing the painter’s tape down and picking it back up.
Use the painter’s tape to make a simple maze on the floor making the halls of the maze at least 2 ft. wide.
During the meeting:
Recite the Scout Law as a den.
Explain that in this activity Cub Scouts will need to demonstrate being trustworthy, helpful, and friendly by leading their adult partner through a maze.
Choose a Cub Scout and their adult partner to go first.
Have the adult partner place their blindfold on at the entrance to the maze.
The Cub Scout may not touch the adult partner when the adult partner is in the maze.
Using only verbal communication, the Cub Scout is to help the adult partner get through the maze.
Give every Cub Scout and adult partner team a chance to complete the maze.
Have Cub Scouts and adult partners talk about why being trustworthy, helpful, and friendly is important to this activity and where else could Cub Scouts demonstrate these values of the Scout Law.

activities.title: Tiger Scout Law Bingo
activities.description: Use a bingo card to act out values of the Scout Law.
supply_list: Scout Law Bingo Card found in Additional Resources
Pencils or markers, enough for 1 per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print out a Scout Law Bingo Card for each Cub Scout in the den.
During the meeting:
Give each Cub Scout a Scout Law Bingo Card.
Have Cub Scouts complete the bingo card with their adult partner.

requirements.text: Demonstrate the Cub Scout sign, Cub Scout salute and Cub Scout handshake. Show how each are used.

activities.title: If You Are Happy Show the Cub Scout Sign
activities.description: Sing the interactive song “If you are happy and you know it” using the Cub Scout sign, handshake, and salute as the actions.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare the meeting space to allow Cub Scouts and adult partners to move around.
During the meeting:
Demonstrate the Cub Scout sign, salute, and handshake found on page 7 of the Tiger handbook.
Explain that the Cub Scout sign is used to get everyone’s attention. When you see someone use the Cub Scout sign that means to stop what you are doing and listen.
Explain that the Cub Scout salute is used to show respect to the US flag during flag ceremonies. We do not use the Cub Scout salute to salute people.
Explain that the Cub Scout handshake is a special way to say fellow to fellow Cub Scouts.
Have Cub Scouts and adult partners space apart by arm’s length.
Explain how the song “If you are happy and you know it” is sung and the actions that go with it.
Everyone signs and then demonstrates an action when it is called out.
If you’re happy and you know it give the Cub Scout sign
If you’re happy and you know it and you really want to show it
If you’re happy and you know it give the salute
If you’re happy and you know it shake hands and say do your best ()
If you’re happy and you know it shake hands and say hello (hello!)
If you’re happy and you know it do all three
(hello!)
(Hello!)
If time allows you can have Cub Scout color Page 7 of the Tiger handbook that demonstrates the Cub Scout sign, salute, and handshake.

activities.title: Sign, Salute, and Handshake Relay
activities.description: Use a relay race to get Cub Scouts moving and learning the Cub Scout sign, salute, and handshake.
supply_list: Best played with at least four Cub Scouts and four adult partners for a total of eight or more people.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare meeting to remove obstacles and provide a clear path for the relay race.
During the meeting:
Demonstrate the Cub Scout sign, salute, and handshake found on page 7 of the Tiger handbook.
Explain that the Cub Scout sign is used to get everyone’s attention. When you see someone use the Cub Scout sign that means to stop what you are doing and listen.
Explain that the Cub Scout salute is used to show respect to the US flag during flag ceremonies. We do not use the Cub Scout salute to salute people.
Explain that the Cub Scout handshake is a special way to say fellow to fellow Cub Scouts.
Divide the den into two teams and line the teams up next to each other.
The den leader and assistant den leader stand about 25 yards away. One team will run to the den leader and the other team will run to the assistant den leader.
On their signal the first person in line runs to their assigned leader and the leader will ask them to give either the Cub Scout sign, salute, or handshake. If they do it properly, they run back and tag the next person in line and that person runs to the assigned leader. If they do not do it properly or give the wrong action they must run back to the line and run back to the leader for another try. They keep trying until they get it correct and the next person in line goes.
The first team to have everyone complete the relay wins.
If time allows you can have Cub Scout color page 7 of the Tiger handbook that demonstrates the Cub Scout sign, salute, and handshake.

activities.title: Tiger Simon Says
activities.description: Play a game of Simon Says using the actions of the Cub Scout sign, salute, and handshake.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare the meeting space to allow Cub Scouts and adult partners to move around.
During the meeting:
Demonstrate the Cub Scout sign, salute, and handshake found on page 7 of the Tiger handbook.
Explain that the Cub Scout sign is used to get everyone’s attention. When you see someone use the Cub Scout sign that means to stop what you are doing and listen.
Explain that the Cub Scout salute is used to show respect to the US flag during flag ceremonies. We do not use the Cub Scout salute to salute people.
Explain that the Cub Scout handshake is a special way to say fellow to fellow Cub Scouts.
Have Cub Scouts and adult partners space apart by arm’s length.
Explain the rules to Simon Says. To play the game the den leader will call out an action by saying “Simon says.” For example, “Simon says, give the Cub Scout sign.” Everyone is to do that action.
If the den leader calls out an action without saying “Simon says” anyone who did that action has to sit down.
The den leader calls out the different actions of Cub Scout sign, Cub Scout salute, and Cub Scout handshake. To do the handshake the person will just put their hand out, they don’t have to shake hands with anyone.
The last person standing wins.
If time allows you can have Cub Scout color Page 7 of the Tiger handbook that demonstrates the Cub Scout sign, salute, and handshake.

requirements.text: Share with your Tiger adult partner, at a den meeting or at home, a time when you have demonstrated the Cub Scout motto “Do Your Best.”

activities.title: Do Your Best Handbook Activity
activities.description: This activity is in the Tiger handbook where Cub Scouts will identify actions that demonstrate the Cub Scout motto “Do Your Best”
supply_list: Crayons or markers, enough to share

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare meeting space for Cub Scouts and adult partners to complete activity in the Tiger handbook.
During the meeting:
Explain that a motto is a rule for living. The Cub Scout motto is “Do Your Best.” That means trying your hardest, not just a little bit. Cub Scouts do their best all the time.
Have Cub Scouts with help from their adult partner color and circle the Scouts that are doing their best on page 8 of the Tiger handbook and then have them color page 9.
When everyone is done, have each Cub Scout share with den their “Do Your Best” coloring on page 9 and talk about a time that they did their best.

activities.title: Do Your Best Handbook Sharing
activities.description: Cub Scouts share with their adult partner a time when they did their best.
supply_list: Crayons or markers, enough to share

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare meeting space for Cub Scouts and adult partners to complete activity in the Tiger handbook.
During the meeting:
Explain that a motto is a rule for living. The Cub Scout motto is “Do Your Best” and that means trying your hardest, not just a little bit. Cub Scouts do their best all the time.
Have Cub Scouts with help from their adult partner color page 9.
When everyone is done have each Cub Scout share with the den their “Do Your Best” coloring on page 9 and talk about a time that they did their best.

requirements.text: At home, with your parent or legal guardian do the activities in the booklet “ How to Protect Your Children from Child Abuse: A Parent’s Guide .”

activities.title: Child Abuse Protection Review Tiger
activities.description: Review the activities in the booklet “How to Protect Your Children from Child Abuse: A Parent’s Guide.”
supply_list: “How to Protect Your Children from Child Abuse: A Parent’s Guide” booklet found in the Tiger Adult Partner Guide.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
At home:
Parents or legal guardians must read the “How to Protect Your Children from Child Abuse: A Parent’s Guide” booklet and complete the exercises with their Cub Scout.

requirements.text: Identify the 5 different food groups.

activities.title: Food Group Tiger Relay
activities.description: Relay race to identify food items and the food group they belong to.
supply_list: 3 plastic or toy foods that are vegetables
3 plastic or toy foods that are fruits
3 plastic or toy foods that are proteins
3 plastic or toy foods that are grains
3 plastic or toy foods that are dairy

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Using the
USDA MyPlate
, become familiar with the types of food that are in the five different food groups.
Set up an area clear of obstacles to conduct a relay race.
Label one box for each food group; vegetables, fruits, proteins, grains, and dairy.
Line up the five boxes in a row.
Place all the plastic or toy foods into a pillowcase.
During the meeting:
Introduce the five different food groups and what types of food are in each group.
Divide the den, Cub Scouts, and adult partners, into two teams.
Have each team form a line 5 yards away from the five boxes.
Explain the rules of the relay
The first person on each team reaches into the pillowcase and picks one item and then runs to the food group boxes and places the item in the correct box. If the item is placed in the correct box, they return to the line and the next person on the team goes. If the item is placed in the wrong box, the person takes it out of the box they placed it in and places it in the correct box, they repeat until the item is in the right box.
The first team to have all members of the team place an item correctly and return to the line wins.

activities.title: My Favorite Foods
activities.description: Cub Scouts draw their favorite food for each of the five good groups.
supply_list: Images of foods that are in the five different food groups

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Using the
USDA MyPlate
, become familiar with the types of food that are in the five different food groups.
Set up the meeting space for Cub Scouts and adult partners to complete the activity in the handbook.
During the meeting:
Introduce the five different food groups and what types of food are in each group.
Have adult partners work with their Cub Scout to identify a food that they like for each of the food groups and draw it in their handbook.

activities.title: My Favorite Snack
activities.description: Cub Scouts bring and share their favorite food from one of the five food groups.
supply_list: My Favorite Snack adult partner guide found in Additional Resources
Images of foods that are in the five different food groups.
Cub Scouts bring their favorite food from one of the five food groups.
Instructions for adult partners to prepare for the meeting
Cleaning supplies to wipe down eating areas before and after the meeting.
Tables and chairs for Cub Scouts and adult partners to eat at

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Using the
USDA MyPlate
, become familiar with the types of food that are in the five different food groups.
Review the “My Favorite Snack” adult partner guide. Make any necessary edits based on your den and send to all parents and adult partners in the den at least two weeks before the den meeting. You may need to adjust how many different types of food you ask each Cub Scout to bring based on the size of your den.
Send a reminder to adult partners a week prior to the meeting.
Send a reminder to adult partners a day prior to the meeting.
Confirm that at least one food item from each of the five food groups will be available.
Prepare the meeting space to have food samples and a place for everyone to eat.
Clean surfaces where food will be.
Use the 3”x5” index cards to make labels for the five different food groups.
Space the index cards on the table to label where Cub Scouts and adult partners are to place their food.
During the meeting:
As Cub Scouts and adult partners bring in the food have them place it on the table in the appropriate food group the item belongs to.
Have each Cub Scout and adult partner talk about their food item and what food group it belongs to.

requirements.text: Practice hand washing. Point out when you should wash your hands.

activities.title: Scout Oath and Law Hand Washing
activities.description: Proper handwashing and learning how long it takes to do a good job.
supply_list: Scout Oath and Scout Law printed on back of Tiger handbook
Print out of 11”x17” Wash Your Hands poster from the CDC
Print out of 11”x17” Know When to Wash Your Hands at School poster from the CDC

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Confirm a meeting location that has a sink for Cub Scouts to wash their hands.
Review content about
washing hands
from the CDC Handwashing in Communities: Clean Hands Save Lives website.
Set up a handwashing station with soap and paper towels.
Print out the “Wash Your Hands” poster and place it at the handwashing station.
Print out the “Know When to Wash Your Hands at School” poster and place it at the handwashing station.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and adult partners and ask when you should wash your hands. Give everyone who wants to share a chance to answer. Review any item that wasn’t mentioned.
After you go to the bathroom
After you play with a dog, a cat, or other animal
After you blow your nose, sneeze, or cough
After you touch garbage
Before and after you help to prepare food
Before you handle plates, utensils, or cups
Before you eat
When your hands have dirt on them
When your hands have been touching a lot of things that others have touched
Bring Cub Scouts over to the handwashing station to demonstrate how to wash your hands.
Put your hands under clean, running water. Put soap on your hands. Turn off the water.
Rub your hands together palm to palm. They should get sudsy.
With your left palm facing down, place your right hand on top of your left and interlock your finger. Scrub vigorously to clean the space between your fingers. Switch hands and repeat.
With your right hand, grab your left thumb and rotate your hand around it. Switch hands and repeat.
Take the tips of your fingers and press them into your opposite palm, rotating them around the palm in a circular motion. Switch hands and repeat.
Rinse the soap from your hands, grab a towel or paper towel and then use it to turn the faucet off.
After you have demonstrated the steps to washing hands inform Cub Scouts and adult partners that the time it takes to do all these steps should be the time it takes for you to say the Scout Oath and Scout Law.
Have each Cub Scout take a turn washing their hands following the steps as they recite the Scout Oath and Scout Law.

activities.title: Super Clean Hands! Worksheet
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about when and how they should wash their hands using a worksheet.
supply_list: Printed Super Clean Hands! Worksheet for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting:
Print a copy of the Super Clean Hands! Worksheet for each Cub Scout.
Review the worksheet so that you are prepared to lead this activity.
During the Meeting
Discuss the importance of washing hands with Cub Scouts.
Ask Cub Scouts to work with the adult partner to complete the worksheet.

activities.title: When Should I Wash My Hands Game
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about when they should wash their hands in this active game.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the Meeting
Line Cub Scouts up next to each other.
Explain that you will call out different situations. They should decide if they need to wash their hands or not.
If they should wash their hands, they should jump. If they should not wash their hands, they should freeze.
Call out situations such as:
Talking to a friend.
Before eating.
After using the bathroom.
After reading a book.
After playing outside.
After completing your homework.
At the end of the game, gather Cub Scouts.
Discuss the proper way to wash hands using the information in Additional Resources.

requirements.text: Be active for 30 minutes.

activities.title: Tiger Obstacle Course
activities.description: Obstacle Course.
supply_list: 5 – 10ft. long 1” PVC pipes cut into the following lengths 9 – 3ft. long 1” PVC pipes 6 – 2ft. long 1” PVC pipes 10 – 1ft. long 1” PVC pipes
10 – 1” PVC Schedule 40 S x S x S Tee

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Construct 3 low hurdles for Cub Scouts to jump over.
Connect a 90-degree elbow connector to each end of a 3ft. long pipe
Connect 2ft. long pipes to each end of the 90-degree elbow connector of the 3ft. long pipe, forming three sides of a rectangle.
Connect PVC schedule 40 S x S x S Tee to the bottom of the 2ft. long pipes
Insert the 1ft. long pipes into the PVC schedule 40 S x S x S Tee to create a hurdle.
Construct 2 high bars for Cub Scouts to duck under.
Connect 3ft. long pipes to each end of the 90-degree elbow connector of the 3ft. long pipe, forming three sides of a rectangle.
Layout the obstacle course.
Find a location that is level and free of tripping hazards to lay out obstacles.
The layout of the course may be in a single line, or you may add turns to accommodate the space available.
From the starting line place a low hurdle 10 ft. away, next place a high bar 10 ft. away, next place a low hurdle 10 ft. away, next place a high bar 10 ft. away, next place a low hurdle 10 ft. away.
Place one of the 2”x4” on the ground 10 ft. away from the last low hurdle.
Place the 6 Hula Hoops™ in a straight-line end to end 10 ft. away from the 2”x4”.
Place the other 2”x4” on the ground 10 ft. away from the Hula Hoops™.
Create a finish line 10ft. away from the 2”x4”.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts gather at the obstacle course.
Demonstrate how to run the course. Jump over the low hurdle, duck under the high bar, jump over the low hurdle, duck under the high bar, jump over the low hurdle, walk across the 2”x4”, go through the Hula Hoops™ by jumping from one to the next, walk across the 2”x4”, then to the finish line.
Give each Cub Scout a turn to run the obstacle course and record how fast they did it.
Allow each Cub Scout to run the course at least twice to see if they can improve their time.

activities.title: Tiger Red Light Green Light
activities.description: Play Red Light / Green Light.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare the meeting location for a place to play red light / green light free of obstacles.
Become familiar with how to play red light / green light.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts and adult partners form a line side by side about 2 ft. apart from each other.
Explain the rules of how to play red light / green light.
Stand 20 feet away from the Cub Scouts and adult partners with your back turned to them.
When you shout, “green light” Cub Scouts and adult partners move towards you.
When you shout “red light” turn around and anyone who is still moving must go back to the beginning.
The game is won by the person who reaches you first.
The winner of the game gets to be the one who calls for the next game.

activities.title: Tiger Soccer
activities.description: Play Soccer with the Den.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Keep the rules of this soccer game simple. Some youth may play on a team and want to play by other rules. The purpose of this activity is for the Cub Scouts and adult partners to be active and play the game following the values of the Scout Oath and Scout Law.
Before the meeting:
Prepare the soccer field that is free of obstacles and place four orange sports cones to make a rectangle that is 45ft. by 75ft. or 75ft. by 105ft.
Place two cones, one on each end of the field, to designate the middle of the field.
Place two cones on each end that are 6ft. wide apart to form the goals.
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and adult partners to explain the rules of soccer and discuss good sportsmanship.
Ask the Cub Scouts and adult partners what parts of the Scout Law are important to keep in mind when playing a game.
The objective is to get the ball in the opposing teams goal.
You may not touch the ball with your hands. There will be no goalie in this game. Someone may defend the goal, but they may not use their hands.
If the ball goes out of bounds the team that did not touch it last gets to throw the ball back into play.
When a goal is scored the ball will be placed in the middle of the field and the team that did not score the goal gets to kick off.
Tripping, kicking, or pushing other players is not allowed.
Divide the den into two teams including adult partners.
Play soccer, during the game look for opportunities to recognize good sportsmanship.

requirements.text: Practice methods that help you sleep.

activities.title: Sleep Like a Star! Worksheet
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about how to get the best rest using a worksheet.
supply_list: Printed Sleep Like a Star! Worksheet for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting:
Print a copy of the Sleep Like a Star! Worksheet for each Cub Scout.

requirements.text: With your Tiger adult partner, demonstrate how to access emergency services.

activities.title: Emergency Services 911 Relay Race
activities.description: Emergency Services 911 Safety Relay

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Inform adult partners to come with the names and phone numbers of five trusted adults. These trusted adults should have been identified in the Bobcat requirement for the exercises in the pamphlet “How to Protect Your Child from Child Abuse: A Parent’s Guide”.
Set up the meeting space to allow Cub Scouts and adult partners to work on the activity on page 23 of the Tiger Handbook.
Set up an area free of obstacles to conduct a relay race.
Secure additional adult leadership to assist with relay race.
Make two sets of cards for the relay race. On a 3”x5” index card writes one scenario below. On the front write the scenario on the back write the answer.
If you see someone breaking into a car? (yes)
If your brother or sister breaks your toy? (no)
If you are with a friend and they fall and are bleeding a lot? (yes)
If you fall down and scrap your elbow? (no)
If you see a building on fire? (yes)
If you can’t find your homework? (no)
If you see a car get into an accident? (yes)
If a stranger approaches you and asks you to get in their car? (yes)
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts open their handbook to page 23.
Ask Cub Scouts if they know how to contact emergency services using a smartphone.
Ask adult partners to pull out their smartphones and show their Cub Scout how to access emergency services using their phones. If an adult partner does not have a smart phone have them demonstrate how to dial 911 on the activity sheet.
Discuss when it is appropriate to call emergency services, 911, and what to expect when they call.
Police officers, firefighters, and EMTs are busy helping people with real emergencies, it is important never to call 911 except in a real emergency.
If you need to call 911, remember:
Always know where you are.
Do not hang up!
Answer all the dispatcher’s questions. The dispatcher is the person who answers the phone.
Never be afraid to call if you have a real emergency. They can help you at any time of the day or night.
Divide the den into two teams, including adult partners. The teams each create a single file line. 20 feet away the den leader and one other adult stand with a deck of scenarios cards. On the signal, the first person for each team will run to their assigned adult who has a deck of scenario cards. The adult will show the scenario (and read it for Cub Scouts) and the person has to say yes or no if they should call 911. If they get it correct, they run back to their team and sit down. If they get it wrong, they run back to their team and they must go again, they repeat until they get it right. The first team to have everyone sitting wins.
After the relay race, ask adult partners to then discuss the five trusted adults with their Cub Scout and write their phone numbers on the activity sheet.

activities.title: Emergency Whistle Testing
activities.description: Cub Scouts will blow whistles and demonstrate how to use the whistle if they get lost.
supply_list: Cub Scouts bring their whistle which is part of their Cub Scout Six Essentials
Cub Scouts will need their Tiger handbook, page 24
Pencils or pens, one for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Remind Cub Scouts and adult partners to bring a whistle. If you have already completed the Tigers In the Wild Adventure, have them bring their whistle which is part of their Cub Scout Six Essentials. If you have not completed the Tigers in the Wild Adventure, inform Cub Scouts and adult partners that having a whistle will be part of other Adventures and something they bring with them whenever participating in outdoor activities.
Ensure the location for this activity is in a place where the blowing of whistles will not be a problem.
Prepare a space for Cub Scouts and adult partners to work on the activity in their Tiger handbook.
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and adult partners and check to make sure everyone has their whistle.
Ask Cub Scouts why they think it is important to have a whistle with them.
Inform Cub Scouts and adult partners that at times a person may get separated from the group they are with when they are outside.
Inform Cub Scouts and adult partners that if they ever get separated from the group they are with or get lost, there are three things they can do to increase the chances that they will get found.
Stay – Do not go looking or wandering around. When you get lost or separated your group or parents are likely to start looking for you in the last place, they saw you or at places you have been. If you stay where you are, chances are they will come back to that place to look for you.
Answer – When you hear your name being called, answer back.
Whistle – Use your whistle. Blow your whistle with three short blasts. Do this repeatedly until you are found.
Ask Cub Scouts, how do you know if your whistle works? Allow for answers.
Now is the time to test your whistle, I want you to blow your whistle with three short blasts and then stop.
Allow Cub Scouts to blow their whistles.
Gather Cub Scouts and adult partners and have them complete the activity on page 24 of the Tiger handbook.

activities.title: Hide and Seek
activities.description: A twist on hide and seek where after 5 minutes Cub Scouts use methods learned to be found.
supply_list: Cub Scouts bring their whistle which is part of their Cub Scout Six Essentials
Cub Scouts will need their Tiger handbook, page 24
Pencils or pens, one for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Identify a large area outside that has places to hide and is free of obstacles.
Remind Cub Scouts and adult partners to bring a whistle. If you have already completed the Tigers In the Wild Adventure, have them bring their whistle which is part of their Cub Scout Six Essentials. If you have not completed the Tigers in the Wild Adventure, inform Cub Scouts and adult partners that having a whistle will be part of other Adventures and something they bring with them whenever participating in outdoor activities.
During the meeting:
Inform Cub Scouts and adult partners that if they ever get separated from the group they are with or get lost, there are three things they can do to increase the chances that they will get found.
Stay – Do not go looking or wandering around. When you get lost or separated your group or parents are likely to start looking for you in the last place, they saw you or at places you have been. If you stay where you are, chances are they will come back to that place to look for you.
Answer – When you hear your name being called, answer back.
Whistle – Use your whistle. Blow your whistle with three short blasts. Do this repeatedly until you are found.
Explain the rules of hide, seek, and found
This game is like hide and seek but after 5 minutes the team that is hiding follows the stay, answer, and whistle. S.A.W.
A Cub Scout and their adult partner will be the first to hide. They will be given 30 seconds to find a place to hide. After 30 seconds the rest of the den will look for them. Cub Scouts and adult partners stick together as they search.
If they are found the Cub Scout and adult partner who found them get to hide next.
If the Cub Scout and adult partner who are hiding cannot be found after 3 minutes, the den leader blows a whistle once. Now the Cub Scout and adult partner who are hiding have to stay, answer, and whistle.
The team that finds them first gets to hide next.
After playing the game ask the Cub Scouts was it easier to find someone when they were following stay, answer, and whistle.
Gather Cub Scouts and adult partners and have them complete the activity on page 24 of the Tiger handbook.

activities.description: Cub Scouts create a Pinewood Derby® driver’s license that doubles as an ID card.
supply_list: Self-sealing laminating pouches that will fit 3.5” x 2” card stock
Pinewood Derby® Driver’s License, found in Additional Resources
Black magic markers, one for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Make a Pinewood Derby® Driver’s License:
Use the project board and decorate it like a driver’s license for your state.
Keep an 11” x 8.5” horizontal space empty, this is where the Cub Scout ID form for each Cub Scout will be placed.
Cut out the space where the photo would be.
Confirm the meeting location has a place for the printer and laptop to be plugged in.
Create a space with good lighting to take photos and set up camera and driver’s license cut out.
Print Pinewood Derby® Driver’s License, one for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Inform Cub Scouts and adult partners that at times a person may get separated from the group they are with when they are outside.
Inform Cub Scouts and adult partners that if they ever get separated from the group they are with or get lost, there are three things they can do to increase the chances that they will get found.
Stay – Do not go looking or wandering around. When you get lost or separated your group or parents are likely to start looking for you in the last place, they saw you or at places you have been. If you stay where you are, chances are they will come back to that place to look for you.
Answer – When you hear your name being called, answer back.
Whistle – Use your whistle. Blow your whistle with three short blasts. Do this repeatedly until you are found.
Sometimes we may get separated and we may not be able to remember important information like our parent’s phone number or our address.
Inform Cub Scouts that today you are making special IDs. These IDs will have important information on them in case they get lost, but it will also serve as their license for the upcoming Pinewood Derby®.
Have Cub Scouts with their adult partners complete the Cub Scout ID form, using the black magic marker. Make sure they write big and clear.
Once a Cub Scout has their form completed have them step over to the photo area with their Cub Scout ID form.
Place sticky putty on the back side of the Cub Scout ID form on the four corners and place it on the Driver’s License.
Have the adult partner hold the driver’s license up and have the Cub Scout place their head in the cut-out area.
Take a picture of the driver’s license with the Cub Scout in it. Repeat this for each Cub Scout.
Upload photos to the laptop and size them to 3.5” x 2” horizontal. Place 8 different photos onto an 8.5” x 11” sheet of paper.
Print the photos onto card stock paper. Cut out individual driver’s licenses and laminate.

activities.title: Tigers Play Cornhole
activities.description: Play a game of cornhole.
supply_list: Cornhole boards – one set for every four members of the den, including adult partners

4 48-inch 2x4s 4 21-inch 2x4s 2 24×48-inch sheets of ½-inch plywood 4 11 ½-inch 2x4s Deck screws Carriage bolts, washers, and wing nuts 120-grit sandpaper Water-based polyurethane Tape Measure Table saw Scribe tool Power drill 6-inch hole saw (bit) Jigsaw Clamps Paintbrush Paint roller Foam brushes

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Visit the
American Cornhole Association website
and become familiar with the rules of cornhole.
Keep the rules simple and adjust the distance of the cornhole boards to bring them closer so Cub Scouts can compete.
Contact the families in the den to identify a parent or adult partner that has cornhole boards that can be used for the meeting or someone who is willing to build cornhole boards.
Gather cornhole boards or build them, see additional resources for instructions on how to build cornhole boards.
Set up a cornhole course for every four people in the den, including adult partners in an area that is free of hazards.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and adult partners and divide them into groups of four, keeping adult partners together with their Cub Scouts. If necessary, you can have a group of two to create even teams. Cornhole is played with either two players or teams of two vs. another team of two.
Ask Cub Scouts why following rules in a game is important. Ask Cub Scouts which points of the Scout Law they should follow when they are playing a game and why.
Review the rules to cornhole and how to score.
Cornhole is played with two teams, each consisting of one player (singles) or two players (doubles).
Players throw their bags, in an underhand motion from next to each side of the board.
Players alternate turns to throw their cornhole bags toward the opposite board.
After each team has thrown four bags, players take the score and resume throwing to the opposite board.
The team who scored points in the previous round goes first in the next round. If it was tied, the team who went first in the last round gets to go first again.
The objective is to be the first team to score 21 points.
A cornhole bag that goes through the hole is worth 3 points.
A cornhole bag that lands on the board and stays there is worth 1 point.
A cornhole bag that lands on the ground or bounces onto the board is worth 0 points.
Have Cub Scouts and adult partners play at least one round of cornhole together.

activities.title: Tigers Play Kickball
activities.description: Play a game of kickball.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Visit the
World Kickball Association website
and become familiar with the rules of kickball.
Keep the rules simple and adjust the distance of the kickball field so Cub Scouts can compete.
Identify a space clear of obstacles and hazards to lay out the kickball field.
Layout the kickball field using baseball bases.
If the kickball field you are using is not at your regular meeting location, send a reminder to all parents, legal guardians, and adult partners in the den about the date, time, and location of the den meeting.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and adult partners and divide them into two teams, keeping adult partners together with their Cub Scouts.
Ask Cub Scouts why following rules in a game is important. Ask Cub Scouts which points of the Scout Law they should follow when they are playing a game and why.
Review the rules to kickball and how to score, rules are like baseball.
To begin, one team will be in the outfield and the other will be the kicking team.
A member of the outfield team is the pitcher and begins the game by rolling the ball to the first kicker on the kicking team.
Once the kicker kicks the ball, they run around the bases in order.
If the ball lands in the foul zone, the kicker must try again, and the foul will count as a strike.
If the ball is caught without touching the ground the kicker is out.
When running bases, a kicker can be out if they are touched with the ball while it is in the hands of an opposing team member when they are off the base.
You may not throw the kickball at someone to get them out.
A team gets three outs before the team switches to the outfield.
The team with the most points

activities.title: Tiger Flag Ceremony
activities.description: Participate in a flag-raising ceremony for your school.
supply_list: Cub Scouts will need to be in their full uniform

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Become familiar with
United States flag etiquette
.
Contact a local school to identify an opportunity for the den to conduct a flag-raising ceremony.
Ask that after the ceremony that the principal meet with the Cub Scouts to thank them.
Become familiar with how to raise the United States flag. There are several variations to conducting a flag ceremony. Keep the ceremony simple and give plenty of time for Cub Scouts to practice raising the flag before doing so in front of an audience.
The United States flag is to be flown in a position of honor. If flown with other flags on the same pole, the United States flag is displayed on top. If it is flown with other flags that are on separate poles near the United States flag flies on the tallest pole.
It takes at least three people to raise the United States flag to form the color guard. Two unfold the flag and hold it while the third person attaches the flag and raises the flag. As the flag is being raised the two holding the flag ensure that the flag does not touch the ground and that the lines the flag is attached to remain untangled.
If you have more Cub Scouts participating, they may join the color guard and simply walk with them to and from the flagpole, this counts as meeting the requirement.
When the United States flag is being raised it is to be done quickly. When it is coming down it is to be done slowly.
Those who are near the flagpole are asked to stop and stand.
The adult leader calls out “Attention!”
Then they call out “Color guard advance.” The Cub Scouts who are raising the flag move to the flagpole with any other Cub Scouts following.
The adult leader calls out “Color guard, raise the colors.” The Cub Scouts then attach the United States flag and wait.
Once the flag is attached the adult leader calls out “Scouts salute.” All Cub Scouts, except the three who are raising the flag, give the Cub Scout salute. The three Cub Scouts raise the flag. Once the flag reaches the top, the Cub Scouts tie off the line, and then salute the flag.
Once everyone is saluting the leader then calls out “Two.” All Cub Scouts then stop giving the salute.
The adult leader calls out “Color guard, dismissed.” All Cub Scouts then return to where they started.
At prior den meetings give time for Cub Scouts to practice raising the flag.
Send a meeting reminder to all parents, legal guardians, and adult partners to remind them of the date, time, and location of the flag ceremony.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and adult partners at least 30 minutes prior to the ceremony.
Conduct a walk-through of the ceremony.
Conduct the flag ceremony.
Have the principal thank the Cub Scouts.
After the meeting:
Send a thank you note to the school principal.

Set up a table for advancements
Unlock bathrooms
Write a list of things that need to be done to clean up the room on one sheet of paper. For example:

Lock bathrooms
Sweep the floor
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and adult partners at least 30 minutes prior to the pack meeting.
Review the list of things that need to be done to set up and what to do to clean up.
Make assignments of Cub Scouts and adult partners on what they will do.
Set up the room for the pack meeting.
After pack meeting clean up.

requirements.text: Play a game that requires at least 2 teams with your den, or two other family members. Afterwards discuss what it means to be part of a team and what makes a good team member.

activities.title: Tiger Charades
activities.description: Play a game of charades with your den.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Become familiar with how to play charades.
Write down items that will be used for charades on the index cards.
A Lion
A Tiger
A Wolf
A Bear
A Scout
Going on a camping trip
Going on a hike
Starting a fire
Being friendly
Being brave
Being clean
Mix cards up and place in basket
During the meeting:
Divide the den into two teams, including adult partners.
Review how to play charades.
Keep the rules simple.
The first team picks someone to go first. That Cub Scout picks a card from the cards in the basket and looks at what is on it without showing it to anyone.
Set the timer for 2 minutes.
The Cub Scout does their best to act out what is on the card. Their team tries to guess what it is before the timer dings. If they guess correctly in time, they get a point. If they do not guess, the card goes back into the basket.
The second team then selects a card from the basket.
Continue going back and forth until all the cards have been selected.

activities.title: Tiger Volleyball

supply_list: Backyard volleyball net set to 5 ft. in height

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Visit the
USA Volleyball website
and become familiar with the simplified youth rules of volleyball.
Modify the size of the court to fit the number of Cub Scouts and adult partners in your den.
Set up the volleyball net and court in an area that is free of hazards. Use the orange sports cone to mark the corners of the court.
During the meeting:
Divide the den into two teams, including adult partners.
Ask Cub Scouts why following rules in a game is important. Ask Cub Scouts which points of the Scout Law they should follow when they are playing a game and why.
Discuss what it means to be part of a team and ask Cub Scouts what they will do to be good members of their team.
Review how to play Tiger volleyball.
Keep the rules simple.
The objective is to score a point by the beach ball landing on the opponent’s side of the court.
A team cannot hit the ball more than four times and a player cannot hit it more than once at a time, if they do the other team gets a point.
If the ball goes out of bounds the team that didn’t touch the ball last gets a point.
Cub Scouts and adult partners play Tiger volleyball.
Look for opportunities to recognize good sportsmanship.

activities.title: Tiger Wiffle Ball

Wiffle Ball website

One team plays the outfield and the other is at bat.
The rules are similar to baseball but there are no bases to run. Bases are earned based on the distance the ball lands if it is not caught.
Track the bases and points on a piece of paper.

requirements.text: Participate in a service project.

activities.title: 10,000 for the Troops – Tiger
activities.description: Cub Scouts participate in a special nation-wide project to create holiday cards for military personnel. Please have letters mailed to the Scouting America National Service Center by November 6, 2026 .
supply_list: 8 ½” x 11” construction paper – various colors
Smart device to email photos to Scouting America

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting:
Become familiar with the instructions on how to write and sign holiday cards on the Holiday Cards Challenge website:
https://militaryholidaycardchallenge.com/how-to-send/
Gather supplies and make a sample holiday card.
During the Meeting:
Share with the Cub Scouts that for their service project for this Adventure, they are going to make holiday cards for people in the military. Explain that sometimes people who serve in the military are not able to come home for the holidays and that we want to let them know that we are thinking of them during this special time of year.
Review the steps to making a letter.
Address their card to “Dear Warrior”.
Write a holiday/gratitude greeting, keeping in mind that our Troops are diverse in their holiday practices and beliefs.
Write a personal note. For example: How do you celebrate the holidays? What are your family memories of holidays? According to our Warriors, this is known to be the favorite part of receiving your cards!
Sign your first name ONLY and the town and state where you live, and your Cub Scout Pack Number.
Keep the size to no larger than an 8 x 11 size paper folded in half.
Allow Cub Scouts to make and decorate as many cards as you have time for in the meeting.
After the Meeting:
Please have letters mailed to the Scouting America National Service Center by November 6, 2026
. Gather all the cards and send them in one package to the Scouting America National Service Center at:
10,000 for the Troops
Scouting America
1325 West Walnut Hill Lane
Irving, TX 75015-2079

activities.description: Collect game boards for a community center.

11” x 17” pieces of paper, one for each Cub Scout

sections.content:
This activity will take one den meeting and two pack meetings. The den meeting for Cub Scouts to decorate boxes and flyers for the game board drive. The pack meetings to distribute the flyers and one pack meeting to collect the board games.

Inform Cub Scouts that they will be conducting a board game drive and the name receiving organization. Include who the organization serves and the need for board games.
Explain that today the den will decorate donation boxes and make promotional flyers to hand out at the next pack meeting.
Explain that the collection boxes and flyers should include the date of the next pack meeting when the board games will be collected, and the organization that will receive the board games.
At the next pack meeting:
Cub Scouts greet fellow Cub Scouts and collect board games placing them in the collection boxes.

requirements.text: Identify the Cub Scout Six Essentials. Show what you do with each item.

activities.title: Grab the Six Essentials
activities.description: Relay race for Cub Scouts to identify the Cub Scout Six Essentials.
supply_list: Tiger handbook for each Cub Scout
Cub Scout Six Essentials (Recommend using small – youth-sized items) Filled Water Bottle Small first aid kit Whistle Flashlight Sun Protection Trail Mix

Miscellaneous Items (Recommend using small – youth-sized items. Make the items obvious that they are not part of the Cub Scout six essentials.) Suggested list, keep to six items: Sponge Duct Tape Spoon Toilet Paper Washcloth Tennis Ball
An open cardboard box to place the Cub Scout Six Essentials and miscellaneous items in

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Watch the four-minute video on the
Cub Scout Six Essentials
.
Take notes on the Cub Scout Six Essentials so you can explain the items to the den.
Gather Cub Scout Six essentials and miscellaneous items.
Place Cub Scout Six Essentials and miscellaneous items in an open cardboard box.
Prepare the meeting space to create an area free of obstacles for the relay race.
Place the box of items about 10 yards from a designated starting point.
Prepare a place for Cub Scouts and adult partners to complete the activity on page 15 of the Tiger handbook.
During the meeting:
Explain how the relay race will work with the Cub Scouts and adult partners
If you have a small den run the relay race as individuals. If you have a larger den, create teams.
The first Cub Scout runs from the starting point to the box and picks an item they think is important to have when they are doing an outdoor activity and runs back to the starting point. The den leader stands at the starting point and tells the Cub Scout whether or not the item is part of the Cub Scout Six Essentials. If the item is one of the Cub Scout Six Essentials, the next Cub Scout in line runs to the box.
If the item is not part of the Cub Scout Six Essentials, the Cub Scout runs back to the box with the item they picked, place it back in the box, and choose another item they think is part of the Cub Scout Six Essentials.
Repeat until all items that are part of the Cub Scout Six Essentials have been retrieved from the box.
Gather the den together and pick up each of the Cub Scout Six Essentials one at a time and tell the den why that item is important.
Have Cub Scouts, with help from their adult partners complete the activity on page 15 of the Tiger handbook.

Cub Scout Six Essentials

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print out and prepare outdoor code flash cards.
Become familiar with the
Outdoor Code
Be Clean in my outdoor manners
.
A Cub Scout takes care of the outdoors and keeps the outdoors clean. A Cub Scout knows that putting marks on buildings, trees, or natural objects causes permanent damage.
Be Careful with ﬁre.
A Cub Scout may enjoy a campﬁre only with adult leaders. A Cub Scout knows not to play with matches and lighters.
Be Considerate in the outdoors.
A Cub Scout shares our outdoor places and treats everything on the land and in the water with respect.
Be Conservation-minded.
During the meeting:
Give each adult partner a set of flash cards.
Have adult partners work with their Cub Scout to become familiar with the Outdoor Code using the flashcards.

requirements.text: With your den leader or Tiger adult partner, learn about the Outdoor Code.

activities.title: Outdoor Code Puzzle
activities.description: Cub Scouts use their Tiger handbook to create an Outdoor Code puzzle.
supply_list: Tiger handbook for each Cub Scout
Scissors one for each Cub Scout or enough to share

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare the meeting space for Cub Scouts and adult partners to color and cut out the Outdoor Code puzzle in the Tiger handbook.
During the meeting:
With help from their adult partner have the Cub Scouts color and then cut out the Outdoor Code puzzle on page 15 in the Tiger handbook.
Review the Outdoor code as they are making their puzzle.
There are four C’s in the outdoor code, review each one.
Clean – Be Clean in my outdoor manners. Ask Cub Scouts and adult partners how they can be clean in their outdoor manners. Then share the following:
Treat the outdoors as a heritage.
Take care of it for myself and others.
Keep trash and garbage out of lakes, streams, fields, woods, and roadways.
Careful – Be Careful with fire. Ask Cub Scouts and adult partners how they can be careful with fire when in the outdoors. Then share the following:
Prevent wildfires.
Build fires only when and where they are permitted and appropriate.
When finished using a fire, make sure it is cold out.
Leave a clean fire ring or remove all evidence of my fire.
Considerate – Be considerate in the outdoors. Ask Cub Scouts and adult partners how they can be considerate in the outdoors. Then share the following:
Treat the land and other land users with respect.
Follow the principles of outdoor ethics for all outdoor activities.
Conservation – Be conservation-minded. Ask Cub Scouts and adult partners what it means to be conservation minded. Then share the following:
Learn about and practice good conservation of soil, waters, forests, minerals, grasslands, wildlife, and energy.
Urge others to do the same.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare the room by removing tripping hazards.
Place the rope on the ground to divide the space into two areas.
During the meeting:
Cub Scouts take turns naming an animal they have seen without repeating an animal.Cub Scouts should make the sound of the animal identified.
On the count of 3, while they are making the animal sound, Cub Scouts move to the wild or domestic side of the room.
Discuss why each Cub Scout identified wild or domestic and allow Cub Scouts to change sides after the discussion.
Repeat this game until Cub Scouts can’t identify more animals.

activities.title: My Favorite Animals

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare the meeting space for Cub Scouts to draw animals.
Gather photos or images of domesticated and wild animals.
During the meeting:
Discuss the difference between wild and domesticated animals. Ask Cub Scouts and adult partners what they think makes an animal wild and to give examples of wild animals.
Ask Cub Scouts and adult partners what they think makes an animal domesticated and to give examples of domesticated animals.
Wild animals are animals that live outdoors and do not rely on humans and are considered wild animals. Most wild animals avoid humans, so you may not see them. Wild animals usually have better sight, hearing, and smell than humans, which helps them stay out of our sight. You should observe wild animals but never approach them.
Domesticated animals are animals that live with humans and rely on us for things like food and shelter are called domesticated. Some animals have become domesticated as a source of food or to help humans with work, and others have become pets. Just because an animal is domesticated does not mean the animal is safe.
Never approach an animal that you do not know. You cannot tell whether an animal is domesticated or wild just by looking at it. For example, most dogs you may see are domesticated, but some dogs are wild and do not rely on humans. Wild dogs should not be approached.
Have Cub Scouts draw their favorite wild animal on one sheet of paper and their favorite domesticated animal on another sheet of paper.

8 stuffed animals that are domesticated animals

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:

Place four stuffed wild animals and four domesticated stuffed animals in each basket.
During the meeting:

Ask Cub Scouts and adult partners what they think makes an animal domesticated and to give examples of domesticated animals.

Wild animals usually have better sight, hearing, and smell than humans, which helps them stay out of our sight. You should observe wild animals but never approach them.
Domesticated animals are animals that live with humans and rely on us for things like food and shelter are called domesticated. Some animals have become domesticated as a source of food or to help humans with work, and others have become pets. Just because an animal is domesticated does not mean the animal is safe.
Never approach an animal that you do not know. You cannot tell if an animal is domesticated or wild just by looking at it. For example, most dogs you may see are domesticated, but some dogs are wild and do not rely on humans. Wild dogs should not be approached.
Divide the den into two teams, including adult partners.
In this relay race the den leader will call out either “wild” or “domesticated” and the first person on each team runs to their assigned basket and picks a stuffed animal that matches what was called then runs back to the line. If the animal they picked was not correct they go again. If the animal they picked was correct they go to the back of their team and sit down. The winning team is the one who has all its team members sitting first.
After each turn, the animals that were picked up are replaced in the basket. A team may not pick the same animal more than two times.

activities.title: Wild or Domestic Sorting Game
activities.description: Cub Scouts will sort animal cards into a Venn diagram, distinguishing between wild, domestic, or both. Then, they will draw their favorite animal.
supply_list: 1 set of Wild or Domestic Sorting Cards (found in additional resources)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print and cut out the Wild or Domestic Sorting Cards.
Draw a Venn diagram on the poster board with the permanent marker by drawing 2 overlapping circles. Label the left circle “Wild” and the right circle “Domestic”. Label the overlapping space “Both”.
During the meeting:
Discuss the difference between wild and domesticated animals.
Ask Cub Scouts and adult partners what they think makes an animal wild and to give examples of wild animals.
Ask Cub Scouts and adult partners what they think makes an animal domesticated and to give examples of domesticated animals.
Explain that wild animals are animals that live outdoors and do not rely on humans and are considered wild animals. Most wild animals avoid humans, so you may not see them. Wild animals usually have better sight, hearing, and smell than humans, which helps them stay out of our sight. You should observe wild animals but never approach them.
Explain that domesticated animals are animals that live with humans and rely on us for things like food and shelter are called domesticated. Some animals have become domesticated as a source of food or to help humans with work, and others have become pets. Just because an animal is domesticated does not mean the animal is safe.
Explain that you should never approach an animal that you do not know. You cannot tell whether an animal is domesticated or wild just by looking at it. For example, most dogs you may see are domesticated, but some dogs are wild and do not rely on humans. Wild dogs should not be approached.
Explain that Cub Scouts are going to use the animal picture cards to sort out wild and domestic animals. Show Cub Scouts the poster board and explain that domestic animal cards go in the right circle, while wild animal cards go in the left circle. Explain that some animals can be both wild and domestic, so those animals go in the overlapping space between the two circles.
Go through the animals from the Wild or Domestic Sorting Cards. With each animal, ask the Cub Scouts if it is wild, domestic, or both. Ask why they think so. If there is disagreement, discuss until a consensus is reached. Encourage Cub Scouts to take turns answering and placing the card in the corresponding circle.
After Cub Scouts have sorted all of the animals, ask them to identify their favorite animal and draw a picture of that animal on the poster.
