requirements.text: With your den create a den Code of Conduct.

activities.title: Code of Conduct Collage
activities.description: Cub Scouts will create their den code of conduct.
supply_list: 1 printed Code of Conduct choice sheet (found in Additional Resources)
Blue, yellow and red paper (2 sheets of each color)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print rules on the appropriate colored paper and cut out all rules.
Gather glue sticks, poster board and markers.
During the meeting:
Explain that Cub Scouts will be making a code of conduct for their den. They will choose which rules they will want to follow during their den meetings. Allow them to choose 5-7 rules as a group.
Place all the printed out rules onto a table and allow Cub Scouts to go through them and decide as a group which rules they want to attach to their poster board.
Once 5-7 rules have been decided upon, Cub Scouts will work together to glue the rules onto the poster board then, decorate it using the markers and stickers. Each Cub Scout and Den Leader should write their name on the newly created code of conduct.
Explain to Cub Scouts that by writing your name on the board after the rules have been glued on, that they agree to follow the rules.
After the meeting:
Bring the code of conduct to each meeting and hang it up.

activities.title: Code of Conduct Wolf
activities.description: Cub Scouts will be invested in their own conduct when they help create their den code of conduct.
supply_list: Optional den Code of Conduct poster from Scout Shop found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Read the following to understand the den code of conduct:
Positive behavior can be achieved by using many of the tools provided by Cub Scouting, such as
Having clear expectations of good behavior expressed to the Scouts and their families.
Developing a code of conduct with the Scouts in the den.
Using two-deep leadership, especially on trips and outings.
Having trained den chiefs assist with den activities.
Following the suggested Cub Scout den meeting structure outlined in Scouting America resources.
Using positive recognition of reinforcement aids such as conduct candles, marble jars, and stickers.
USING DEN RULES: The den leader and the Scouts in the den should develop a den code of conduct. The subject of a den code of conduct, a set of group rules, can be introduced in an open discussion of how friends act toward one another. They will often contribute proposals that relate to safety, to respect for property, and to relationships with others.
Put-downs and physical aggression should not be tolerated. The leader can make suggestions along these lines if the Scouts don’t bring them up. A few rules are enough for a start, but the Scouts might need to add others from time to time. They also might want to write out their den rules and sign on a line at the end of the list. This is a way of sharing with parents and guardians the expectations of their children.
Although groups of Scouts of this age will have their good days and bad days, they are most likely to try to live up to rules that they helped set up for themselves. Scouts need to learn to judge their behavior in terms of more than conformity to rules. They need to learn about caring, too. Just as they can make up rules, they can decide on some of the caring values that they want to represent their den.
During the meeting:
Using the den code of conduct information above, help the Cub Scouts create their own code of conduct.
Have Cub Scouts write the den code of conduct on a posterboard.

requirements.text: Demonstrate the Cub Scout sign, Cub Scout salute and Cub Scout handshake. Show how each is used.

activities.title: Bobcat Relay Wolf
activities.description: In this Cub Scout relay game, teams show the Cub Scout sign, salute, and handshake.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Divide the den into two teams and have them line up at one end of the room. At the other end, station an adult or den chief for each team.
Have the first Cub Scout on each team run to the adult/den chief for their team. The adult or den chief asks the Cub Scout to demonstrate one of the following:
Cub Scout Sign
Cub Scout Handshake
Cub Scout Salute
If the Cub Scout can demonstrate properly, they run back to tag the next Cub Scout in line on their team.
If the Cub Scout can’t demonstrate properly, they run back to their team to get help then they return and demonstrate again.

activities.title: Scout Sign Sound of Silence
activities.description: Practice the Cub Scout sign by playing the Scout Sign Sound of Silence game.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Tell the Cub Scouts to be as loud as they can, but when they see you show the Cub Scout sign, they should immediately stop making noise. Ask one of the other adults or den chief to time them to see how long it takes them to be quiet.
Then tell the Cub Scouts that you know they can beat that time, so you want them to be loud again. Repeat the process of showing the Cub Scout sign while having an adult time how long it takes for them to be quiet.
You can repeat this several times.
Tip: When giving the Cub Scout sign, do it in silence.

activities.title: Simon Says Wolf
activities.description: Play Simon Says to learn the Cub Scout sign, handshake, and salute.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
The leader demonstrates the Cub Scout handshake, salute, and sign.
Cub Scouts will demonstrate when the command is prefaced by “Simon Says.”
To make this activity more fun, include other options like:
Jump like a rabbit
Put your hand on your head
Twirl in a circle
Touch your toes
Stick out your tongue

requirements.text: Share with your den, or family, a time when you demonstrated the Cub Scout motto “Do Your Best.”

Cut out shields.
Make an example for Cub Scouts to reference.

Give each Cub Scout a blank
shield.
Ask them to draw a picture of a time they Did Their Best (school, home, sports, helping others, etc.). Example: a baseball game, finishing homework, helping siblings, trying something
new.
Add the Cub Scout motto “Do Your Best” across the top or bottom of the
Once finished, have Cub Scouts sit in a

Have Cub Scouts take turns holding up their shield and briefly sharing the story behind their

activities.title: Do Your Best Showcase
activities.description: Cub Scouts share a time when they did their best.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Explain to the Cub Scouts that you’ll be asking each of them to share about a time when they did their best. Share some examples with them such as:
I did my best when my mom was teaching me how to fold clothes
I did my best on my last spelling test
I did my best when I was learning how to ride my bike
The leader should start by sharing a time when they did their best.
Go around to each Cub Scout that would like to share.

activities.title: Do Your Best Talking Neckerchief
activities.description: Cub Scouts share a time when they did their best.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and ask them to sit in
a
circle.
Explain that they are going to be asked to share a time when they did their best. They can only share when they are holding the talking neckerchief.
Pass the talking neckerchief Encourage each Cub Scout, while holding the neckerchief to briefly share the details of when they did their best. If a Cub Scout is shy, they can say “pass” and share later when ready.
After each story, invite the group to raise their hand if they’ve had a similar experience (e.g., “I also did my best at soccer,” “I also tried hard on a test”).

Best
.

requirements.text: Sample 3 different foods that are naturally 3 different colors . The food must be a protein, vegetable, fruit, dairy, or a grain .

activities.title: Trail Mix
activities.description: Cub Scouts will create a trail mix using three different foods that are naturally different in colors. These foods will consist of protein, vegetables, fruit, dairy, and a grain.

During the Meeting
Gather Cub Scouts and explain that you are making a trail mix that includes at least three foods that are naturally the color that they see.
Ask Cub Scouts which foods do they think are naturally the color that they see.
Provide each Cub Scout with a zip-top bag.
Ask Cub Scouts to write their name on their bag.
Direct each Cub Scout to scoop 1/2 cup of Cheerios into their bag.
Next have each Cub Scout Scoop ½ cup of Root Vegetable Chips into their bag.
Instruct Cub Scouts to scoop ¼ cup of yogurt covered raisins and dried cranberries into their bag.
Finally, have Cub Scouts put 1 tablespoon of sunflower seeds into their bags.
After making their trail mix, have Cub Scouts eat the trail mix so they can try items that are naturally three different colors.

Clean up the meeting space.

activities.description: Cub Scouts will share their favorite foods of different colors with each other.

sections.heading: Directions

Explain they are to choose a food that is naturally colored and to prepare the snacks into individual servings for each Cub Scout and store properly until the meeting begins. Be sure to include any information on food allergies in your den.

During the meeting:
Have each Cub Scout wash or clean their hands using hand sanitizer (if soap and water are not available).
Give Cub Scouts a plate and a napkin.
Allow each Cub Scout to share what food they brought, what color it is, and what they like about it.
Hand out pieces of what each Cub Scout brought and encourage them to try at least 3 differently colored snacks.
Allow each Cub Scout to try the foods.
Ask Cub Scouts which food they liked and which they did not.
After the meeting:
Congratulate everyone on a successful potluck and clean the space.

requirements.text: Discuss “safe touch” as seen in the Protect Yourself Rules video.

activities.title: I Know What to Say
activities.description: Cub Scouts will practice recognizing uncomfortable situations and using their voice to say “no,” get away, and tell a trusted adult .
supply_list: 1 copy of I Know What to Say Scenarios found in additional resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Inform parents and guardians that you will be talking about safe touch during the meeting and ask them to watch the
Protect Yourself Video Wolf
with their child before the meeting.
Print 1 copy of I Know What to Say Scenarios found in additional resources.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and Say “Today we’re going to practice using our strong voices to keep our bodies safe!” Ask:
“What’s a strong voice?” (Let them demonstrate—make it fun!)
“When might you use a strong voice?”
Show me a silly voice, now show me a strong voice. Remember that we need to use a strong voice to keep ourselves safe.
Introduce the simple steps: Say if you feel unsafe you should use a strong voice and say
“No – Go – Tell”
Have Cub Scouts repeat it like a chant:
“Say NO!”
“GO away!”
“TELL a grown-up you trust!”
Practice together with motions:
Hand out (stop sign) = NO
Turn/run in place = GO
Hand to mouth (calling) = TELL
Tell Cub Scouts, “We’re going talk about silly situations and practice what to do.” Keep tone playful, not scary.
Have Cub Scouts stand up and practice together:
You call out:
“What do we say?” → Kids:
“NO!”
“What do we do?” → Kids:
“GO!”
“Then what?” → Kids:
“TELL!”
Repeat a few times, faster each round for fun.
Ask Cub Scouts:
“Who are some trusted adults you can tell?”
“What if the first person doesn’t listen?”
Reinforce: “Keep
telling until someone helps you.”
Tips for Success
Keep everything
light and empowering
, not scary
Never force a child to act—let them volunteer
Praise effort: “That was a strong voice!”
Normalize boundaries: “It’s always okay to say no to touch”

activities.title: Safe Touch Poster

activities.title: Shout Run and Tell Relay
activities.description: In this relay, Cub Scouts will practice what they would say to a stranger who is making them feel uncomfortable.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Have the Wolf Scouts line up single file with each youth about ten yards away from the adult/den chief.
When the adult/den chief signals “Go,” the first Wolf in line will yell something like “No!” or “Stay away from me!” or anything else they would say if someone did something that made them feel uncomfortable.
The first Wolf will then run to that adult/den chief. When this is done, the next Wolf gets a turn.
Repeat until all the Wolves have had a chance to practice how they would Shout, Run, and Tell.
During this activity, allow each Wolf to decide what they want to shout.

requirements.text: Learn about the buddy system and demonstrate how it works.

activities.title: Buddy Check Game
activities.description: Learn about the buddy system by playing a buddy check game.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Line up your den.
Provide a number for each Cub Scout. For example, if you have a den of six, you will number 1-2-3 (for your first three Cub Scouts) and start again 1-2-3 for the next three Cub Scouts.
Have all Cub Scouts with the same number stand together and inform them they are buddies for this game.
Tell Cub Scouts that when they hear “Buddy Check!” they must find their buddy as quickly as possible.
Have Cub Scouts move away from their buddy by skipping, hopping, or walking.
After a short amount of time, call out “Buddy Check!”.
Call out each number. If BOTH buddies are together, they can say “Here!” If they are not together, they need to find their buddy and then yell “Here!”.
The game is done when all buddy groups have said “Here!”.

activities.title: Buddy Games
activities.description: Play catch with a buddy .
supply_list: Small ball for each pair of Cub Scouts

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Collect as many balls as needed for your den, one per pair.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts line up alphabetically by last name.
Count off to create buddy pairs.
Have each pair move away from each other and instruct them to gently toss the ball back and forth.

activities.title: Buddy-legged Race
activities.description: Using a buddy , participate in a race .

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Identify a good starting point and finish line for the race.
Ask another adult/den chief to stand at the finish line.
During the meeting:
Pair Cub Scouts off so each has a buddy and ask them to remember their buddy.
Give one Cub Scout of each buddy pair a neckerchief.
Ask Cub Scouts to skip and hop around the meeting space to separate from their buddy.
Have an adult/den chief stand at the finish line.
Explain the directions of the game. When Cub Scouts hear “Go!” they find their buddy, run to the starting line, tie their neckerchief around their ankles, and run/walk to the finish line.
Stand at the start line.
Yell “Go!”
Tip: Help Cub Scouts that may have a challenge tying their neckerchief around their ankles.

requirements.text: Review common safety rules and demonstrate the proper use of playground equipment.

activities.title: Heads Down, Thumbs Up
activities.description: Cub Scouts will play a game and share answers about playground safety.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print out the trivia questions.
During the meeting:
Explain the rules of the game.
Read each question out loud, give time for Cub Scouts to think of their answer, then say loudly “Heads down, Thumbs Up”
Cub Scouts will put their heads down, and thumbs up. During the first round the Leader will walk around and choose 3 Cub Scouts and once they have been chosen, the Leader will say loudly, “Heads Up, Thumbs Down”. Cub Scouts who were chosen to go to the front to share their answers.
Reveal the correct answer and briefly explain why.
In the following rounds, any Cub Scout who got the answer correct will get to choose the next players.
Continue to play until all questions have been answered.
Use the following questions:
What should you do before going down a slide?
Where should you sit on a swing?
What is the safest way to climb playground equipment?
What should you do if someone falls and gets hurt?
How many people should go down the slide at one time?
What should you do before running on the playground?
What kind of shoes are best for the playground?
If playground equipment is broken, what should you do?
Is it safe to walk in front of someone who is swinging?
What should you keep to yourself on the playground?
Is it safe to slide down feet first?
What should you throw on the playground?
There is a playground that is away from where your guardian is and you really want to play on it, what do you do?

activities.title: Holiday Mosaic
activities.description: Make a construction paper mosaic using your family’s favorite holiday tradition symbol.
supply_list: Holiday symbol image for reference, simple symbols would do best for this project

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to find an image of their family’s favorite holiday symbol to help draw their design and bring it to the meeting.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts choose a solid color paper for the background of their mosaic.
Ask Cub Scouts to draw their favorite holiday symbol as large as they can onto the background paper. Simple symbols would do best for this project.
Have Cub Scouts cut or tear small pieces of desired colored paper, no smaller than ½ inch, to create the mosaic pieces. Irregular shapes are encouraged.
After Cub Scouts have finished creating their small pieces, they may glue the individual pieces onto the drawn shape. They can choose to overlap pieces or choose for them to be close, but not touch. Both create a creative image.
Encourage Cub Scouts to fill up the entire symbol with cut pieces of colored paper.
After the glue is dry, have the Cub Scouts display their mosaic.

activities.title: Sun Catcher
activities.description: Make a sun catcher of a holiday symbol that can be hung in your home.
supply_list: Colored tissue paper, cut to torn into small pieces or strips

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting:
Have Cub Scouts find a simple silhouette of a holiday symbol and bring it to the meeting.
During the Meeting:
Have Cub Scouts trace their holiday symbol onto black paper.
About 1” in from the first line, Cub Scouts should draw a second silhouette of their symbol.
Cut out both silhouettes to create a black border of their symbol.
Leaders cut a piece of contact paper a little bit bigger than the Cub Scout’s symbol border and carefully peel away the protective layer, to reveal the sticky side of the contact paper.
Cub Scouts place the black symbol border onto the sticky side of the contact paper.
Note
Cub Scouts get one chance to do this, otherwise they would have to start over.
Once Cub Scouts are happy with their border, they can start placing tissue paper pieces in whatever color pattern they desire onto the sticky part inside their black border.
After all the sticky has been covered, Cub Scouts can cut away the left-over contact paper from the outside of the symbol.
The symbol can be hung up on a window using tape or adding a piece of string at the top.

requirements.text: Learn how to properly care for and fold the United States flag. With your den or pack, participate in a flag ceremony.

activities.title: Fold the Flag
activities.description: Learn how to properly fold the United States flag.
supply_list: Scout Life “ How to Display and Fold the American Flag ”

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Have the Cub Scouts buddy up.
Taking turns, each pair of Cub Scouts hold the flag at waist level between themselves.
Ask the Cub Scouts to fold the flag in half lengthwise, then fold it in half lengthwise again, always keeping the blue field on the outside.
While one Cub Scout holds the flag by the blue field, the other should make triangular folds from the opposite end until only the blue field is available.
Ask the Cub Scouts to continue folding in a triangular pattern until they reach the end of the flag.
Have the Cub Scouts tuck any excess fabric into the final fold to ensure a neat triangle.
The final folded flag should resemble a neatly folded triangle with only the blue field showing.

activities.title: Building My Home with Cardboard
activities.description: Use household items to build a model of your home.
supply_list: Photos of the Cub Scout’s home for reference

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Ask the Cub Scouts to bring photos of their home to the next den meeting. This can be a physical photo or on a phone or pad.
During the meeting:
Explain to the Cub Scouts that they’ll make a model of their homes using cardboard or shoeboxes.
Have the Cub Scouts look at the photos of their homes or think about them and talk about the parts of their house they want in the model.
Ask the Cub Scouts to draw a simple plan on paper to show how their model will look.
If using a shoebox, have the Cub Scouts take off the lid and use the box as the base.
Instruct the Cub Scouts to cut cardboard pieces for walls, roof, and other parts if using cardboard sheets.
Have the Cub Scouts attach walls to the base with glue to create the shape of their home.
Ask the Cub Scouts to cut outdoors, windows, and any special parts of their home from cardboard.
Have the Cub Scouts decorate their model using the markers, colored pencils, or crayons.
Tip: Requirements 3, 4, and 5 can be done at the same meeting. The models built for requirements 3 and 4 will be used for requirement 5.

activities.title: Building My Home with Toys
activities.description: Use Lego® bricks, Lincoln Logs®, Tinker Toys® sets, or other building toys to build a model of your home.
supply_list: Assorted building toys such as Lego®, Lincoln Logs®, or Tinker Toys®
Photos of the Cub Scouts’ homes for reference

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to bring photos of their home to the next den meeting. This can be a physical photo or on a phone or pad.
During the meeting:
Explain to the Cub Scouts that they will be using building toys to create a model of their own homes.
Have Cub Scouts look at the photos of their homes or think about their home and talk briefly about the different parts of their houses they’d like to include in their models.
Cub Scouts can sketch their model on a piece of paper to plan it out if needed.
Distribute the building toys.
Encourage the Cub Scouts to start building by selecting blocks and pieces that resemble the different parts of their homes. For example, rectangular pieces for walls, flat pieces for roofs, and smaller pieces for details like windows and doors.
Cub Scouts can begin by building the main structure of their homes. For example, if Cub Scouts live in a two-story house, they can start by creating the lower floor before adding the upper floor.
Remind the Cub Scouts to be creative and use their imagination to adapt the building toys to match the unique features of their homes.
Once the basic structure is in place, the Cub Scouts can start adding details like windows, doors, chimneys, and any other distinctive features of their homes.
Tip: Requirements 3, 4, and 5 can be done at the same meeting. The models built for requirements 3 and 4 will be used for requirement 5.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:

If using a shoebox:
Have Cub Scouts take off the lid and use the box as the base.
Instruct Cub Scouts to cut cardboard pieces for walls, roof, and other parts if using cardboard sheets.
Have Cub Scouts attach walls to the base with glue to create the shape of their home.
Ask Cub Scouts to cut out doors, windows, and any special parts of the building from cardboard.
If using toys:
Encourage Cub Scouts to start building by selecting blocks and pieces that resemble the different parts of their homes. For example, rectangular pieces for walls, flat pieces for roofs, and smaller pieces for details like windows and doors.
Cub Scouts can begin by building the main structure of their homes. For example, if Cub Scouts live in a two-story house, they can start by creating the lower floor before adding the upper floor.
Remind Cub Scouts to be creative and use their imagination to adapt the building toys to match the unique features of their homes.
Once the basic structure is in place, Cub Scouts can start adding details like windows, doors, chimneys, and any other distinctive features of their homes.
Tip: Requirements 3, 4, and 5 can be done at the same meeting. The models built for requirements 3 and 4 will be used for requirement 5.
Tip: Ask each Cub Scout to build a different community building.

activities.title: 10,000 for the Troops – Wolf
activities.description: Cub Scouts participate in a special nation-wide project to create holiday cards for military personnel. Thank you for a great 2025, Cub Scout submitted over 35,000 letters . We look forward to doing this again in 2026.
supply_list: 8 ½” x 11” construction paper – various colors
Smart device to email photos to Scouting America

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting:
Become familiar with the instructions on how to write and sign holiday cards on the Holiday Cards Challenge website:
https://militaryholidaycardchallenge.com/how-to-send/
Gather supplies and make a sample holiday card.
During the Meeting:
Share with the Cub Scouts that for their service project for this Adventure, they are going to make holiday cards for people in the military. Explain that sometimes people who serve in the military are not able to come home for the holidays and that we want to let them know that we are thinking of them during this special time of year.
Review the steps to making a letter.
Address their card to “Dear Warrior”.
Write a holiday/gratitude greeting, keeping in mind that our Troops are diverse in their holiday practices and beliefs.
Write a personal note. For example: How do you celebrate the holidays? What are your family memories of holidays? According to our Warriors, this is known to be the favorite part of receiving your cards!
Sign your first name ONLY and the town and state where you live, and your Cub Scout Pack Number.
Keep the size to no larger than an 8 x 11 size paper folded in half.
Allow Cub Scouts to make and decorate as many cards as you have time for in the meeting.
After the Meeting:
Please have letters mailed to the Scouting America National Service Center by November 6, 2026
. Gather all the cards and send them in one package to the Scouting America National Service Center at:
10,000 for the Troops
Scouting America
1325 West Walnut Hill Lane
Irving, TX 75015-2079

requirements.text: Learn about the buddy system and how it works in the outdoors. Pick a buddy for your walk.

activities.title: 1-2 Buddies
activities.description: ​ ​ Arrange Cub Scouts in alphabetical order and give them numbers 1-2 in sequence to quickly select buddies. ​ ​ ​ ​ ​

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Arrange Cub Scouts in a line using their first names in alphabetical order.
Starting at the front of the line, count off – 1-2.
Pair Cub Scouts with numbers one and two together to form buddies.

activities.title: Buddy Circle Game
activities.description: Cub Scouts find their buddy in this enjoyable circle game.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Cub Scouts come together to form a circle, with one Cub Scout placed at the center.
Cub Scout in the middle closes their eyes and twirls around before coming to a stop.
The Cub Scout they’re facing after the spin becomes their buddy.
Paired Cub Scouts step out of the circle.
The game proceeds until all Cub Scouts have found their buddies.

activities.title: Popsicle Stick Buddies
activities.description: Popsicle sticks are used to pair buddies.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting:
Gather your supplies.
During the Meeting:
Cub Scouts personalize a popsicle stick with their name.
Place popsicle sticks in a bag.
Draw two popsicle sticks at a time from the bag.
The two Cub Scouts whose names are chosen are paired as buddies.

activities.description: Play a relay game to identify the right clothes and shoes to wear on a walk during different seasons.
supply_list: Two to three items of ​ appropriate outdoor ​ clothing for each season (fall, winter, spring, and summer)
Two to three pairs of walking shoes for each season
Two to three accessories for each season

Collect

clothing

Ask parents

activities.title: Sketchy Weather Wardrobe
activities.description: Cub Scouts draw picture ​ s ​ of clothes they would wear when it: rains, snows, sunny or windy.

Print Sketchy Weather Wardrobe, one for each Cub Scout.

ask them to draw a picture
of clothing that
is

requirements.text: With your den, pack, or family, take a walk outside for at least 30 minutes to explore nature in your surroundings. Describe four different animals, domestic or wild, that you could see on your walk.

activities.title: Outdoor Scavenger Hunt
activities.description: Take a 30 minute​ or more​ walk. Describe four animals that you might see on your walk.
supply_list: If the walk will be at a location that is not your regular meeting location you will need a Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record on each participant (youth and adult)
​​​Outdoor Scavenger Hunt​ card found in Additional Resources ​

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
​​Determine where the outdoor walk will take place. This can be in an urban, suburban, or rural setting. This can be where your den typically meets.​
​​Remind Cub Scouts to bring their ​Cub Scout Six Essentials​ ​ ​​​​
​​Remind Cub Scouts to dress appropriately.​
Print ​Outdoor​ Scavenger Hunt card, one for each Cub Scout.
If the walk is away from your regular meeting location:
Gather copies of the
Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record
on each participant (youth and adult)
Review Annual Health and Medical Records for any restrictions that may impact participation
During the meeting:
If the walk is away from your regular meeting location bring copies of the
Remind Cub Scouts of the Outdoor Code and Leave No Trace​ Principles for Kids​ they’ve learned. Cub Scouts will get to apply these principles while exploring nature.
​​Have ​Cub Scouts ​write down​ at least four different animals they might encounter during the walk on the reverse side of their sheet—whether wild or domestic.
Take Cub Scouts on a walk in a previously​ determined outdoor area.​​​​​
​​During the walk, Cub Scouts stay with their buddy and follow the leader.​​​
​​During the walk, Cub Scouts work on their scavenger hunt.​
​​At the end of the walk, ask ​ each Cub Scout ​to ​share about the four different animals they ​saw or could have seen ​during the walk.

activities.title: Sketch Animals
activities.description: Cub Scouts will observe animals while on a hike and then sketch 1 wild and 1 domestic animal they saw on their hike.
supply_list: 1 wild and domestic worksheet per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print one copy of the wild and domestic worksheet for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts together and tell that that they are going to be looking for wild and domestic animals on a hike.
Ask Cub Scouts if they know the difference between wild and domestic animals.
What a wild animal is (an animal that is found in nature)
What a domestic animal is (an animal that is kept as a pet)
As you are walking ask Cub Scouts to point out different animals they see and ask them to draw them in the wild or domestic area of the paper.
After the hike, ask Cub Scouts to tell you about the wild animals they found, then ask about the domestic animals they found.

activities.title: Wild or Domestic Collage
activities.description: Cub Scouts will make a collage of wild and domestic animals.
supply_list: Magazines with animals in them 1 per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Review for your knowledge wild and domestic animals
Draw a line down the middle of the poster board and label one side Wild Animals and the other Domestic Animals.
Gather Cub Scouts together and tell them that they are going to be looking for wild and domestic animals in magazines.
Ask Cub Scouts if they know the difference between wild and domestic animals.
What a wild animal is (an animal that is found in nature)
What a domestic animal is (an animal that is kept as a pet)
Tell Cub Scouts to look through the magazine and cut out animals.
Ask Cub Scouts to glue the animals they cut out onto the correct side of the poster board.
When they finish, ask Cub Scouts if they think all of the animals have been glued to the correct side. If someone disagrees, ask them to explain why.

requirements.text: Identify the type of water you will be fishing in and what type of fish live in the water.

activities.title: Fish Name Game
activities.description: Play a game and learn about the diverse local fish species within your state.
supply_list: Printed pictures of native/local fish; these can be found by going to your state’s fish and wildlife department website
Small flat magnets (one for each fish)
½” diameter 2’ length dowel rods (one for every 2 or 3 Cub Scouts)
String or yarn for fishing line
Tarp to serve as the “pond” or string or tape to mark off an area for the “pond”

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Cut out the fish and write facts about them on the backs of the pictures.
Glue a magnet to each picture.
Make “fishing rods” by tying or taping a length of string to each dowel rod. Tie a paper clip to the other end of the string.
Place the fish in an area that you designate as the pond. Put paper, pencils, pens, and crayons on a table close to the pond.
During the meeting :
Explain to Cub Scouts that they’re going to learn about the fish that live in their area.
Tell Cub Scouts that after they catch a fish, they are to take it to the table and draw it on a piece of paper adding the name of the fish and one or two facts about it.
Give each Cub Scout a fishing rod and have them line up by the pond.
Instruct Cub Scouts to catch a fish using their magnetic fishing rod. After they finish their drawing of the fish, tell them to release the fish back into the pond.
You can set a time limit for the game or let Cub Scouts play until they’ve caught and learned about all the fish pictures.
Tip: You can laminate the fish for durability.
Tip: With slight modifications, you can use the same fishing poles for the Fish Names Game, Cast & Learn, Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge, Crazy Casting Spin-Off, and Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge.

sections.content:
