Ask whether the visit will be a guided tour led by fishery staff or a self-guided tour where your group will explore independently.
If it’s a self-guided tour, request informational materials and guidelines from the fishery or hatchery staff. This will help you prepare for the tour.
Inform Cub Scouts’ parent or legal guardian about the visit.
Gather copies of the
Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record
on each participant (youth and adult).
Review Annual Health and Medical Records for any restrictions that may impact participation.
During the meeting:
Bring copies of the
on each participant (youth and adult)
Gather Cub Scouts outside the meeting space.
Encourage Cub Scouts to ask questions.
If it is a guided tour, thank the person who guided the tour.
After the meeting:
Write a thank you note to the fishery or fish hatchery and send.

activities.title: Who’s That Fish?
activities.description: A game of Who’s that Fish? Where Cub Scouts guess what fish is pictured and if it is native .
supply_list: Printed pictures of native/local fish; these can be on your state’s fish and wildlife department website; a minimum of 1 per Cub Scout
Printed pictures of fish that are not native to your area; a minimum of 1 per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print pictures of fish that are native to your area.
Print pictures of fish that are not native to your area. You can use the pictures found in Wolf A Wolf Goes Fishing 1 Who’s That Fish.pdf or you can find your own.
On the back of each fish, write down two facts.
During the meeting:
Stand at the front of the room with a second adult.
Have the second adult turn their back to Cub Scouts and tape one of the fish pictures to their chest.
Ask the adult to turn around showing the fish picture to Cub Scouts. Read a couple of the facts about that fish to Cub Scouts.
Ask Cub Scouts to raise their hands if they think the fish is native to their area. Then ask them to raise their hands if they think it is not native to their area.
Start again with the leader taping a different fish picture to their chest.
Continue until you’ve talked about all of the fish.

requirements.text: Learn about the different types of bait used to attract fish.

activities.title: Bait-ology Bonanza
activities.description: Learn about fishing bait s with a memory game .
supply_list: Artificial lures such as plastic worms, spinnerbaits, roundhead jigs, dropshots
Live bait such as worms, crickets, and minnows
Household items that can be used as bait: corn, hot dogs, sandwich meat, bread
Something to cover the bait such as newspaper, a piece of fabric, a plastic tablecloth, etc.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Collect different types of fishing bait, including both live and artificial. Gather more examples than the number of Cub Scouts in your den.
Immediately before the meeting begins, arrange the bait on a table so Cub Scouts can examine it.
During the meeting:
Tell Cub Scouts that there are several factors that go into choosing the type of bait you’ll use. These include the type of fish you want to catch and your fishing location.
Explain to Cub Scouts that they’re going to learn about different types of fishing bait
Show Cub Scouts each type of bait and the name of the bait.
After you’ve given Cub Scouts all the names, tell them that you’re going to allow them to gather around the table for two or three minutes. At the end of that time, you’ll cover up the bait so that they can’t see it.
Ask Cub Scouts to name one of the types of bait that they saw by calling on them one at a time.
After each Cub Scout has had an opportunity to name an example, uncover the bait and count how many they got right.

activities.title: Meat Stick Bait
activities.description: Cub Scouts will learn about bait and how to make bait out of a meat stick.
supply_list: 1 Slim Jim for every 2 Cub Scouts
1 Pair of Scissors per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Watch the video about how to make a fishing lure out of a meat stick in Additional Resources.
Make one fishing lure to share as an example for your den.
Learn about different kinds of bait for fishing.
Write each Cub Scout’s name on a baggie.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and tell them that today we are learning about different kinds of bait used for Fishing.
The first kind of bait we are going to talk about are Live Bait some examples of live bait include:
Worms:
Excellent all-around bait for panfish, trout, and bottom feeders in both lakes and rivers.
Minnows:
Effective for active predators like crappie, bass, and pike; great in early spring or fall.
Crickets/Grasshoppers:
Best for trout in streams or panfish in lakes.
Leeches:
Durable, ideal for walleye in rocky, deep areas.
Frozen/Dead Bait (Shrimp, Squid):
Best for muddy water or deep sea, as scent carries well.
Salmon Eggs:
Ideal for trout and steelhead in tributary streams, particularly near spawning areas.
Another kind of bait is artificial bait and this includes:
Spinnerbaits
:
Ideal for fishing in heavy, submerged vegetation or cover. Use gold blades for cloudy water and silver for clear water.
Jigs/Soft Plastics
Best for cold water (slow metabolism) or targeting bottom-dwelling fish like perch and walleye.
Topwater Lures (Frogs, Poppers)
Most effective in low-light conditions (dawn/dusk) or warm water when fish are aggressive, especially near surface vegetation.
Crankbaits/Spoons
Ideal for covering open water, attracting active fish with vibration and flash.
Another thing to think about with picking your bait would be the water conditions where you are going fishing:
Clear Water:
Use natural, realistic colors (greens, browns, silver).
Murky/Muddy Water:
Use bright colors (chartreuse, white) or high-scent baits (cut bait).
Cold Water:
Slow, small, and subtle (live bait, jigs).
Warm Water:
Fast, flashy, and aggressive (topwater, crankbaits)
Explain to Cub Scouts that today you are going to be making bait for your fishing trip.
Show Cub Scouts the
Meat stick bait video
.
Give each Cub Scout a paper plate, their baggie, a pair of Scissors, and ½ of a Slim Jim.
Ask Cub Scouts to cut the Slim Jim into ¼ inch slices.
After slicing the Slim Jim into slices, have Cub Scouts place the slices into their baggie.
Have Cub Scouts use their meat stick bait when they go fishing.

activities.title: Visit a Bait Shop
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about bait by visiting a bait shop.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Call a local bait shop and ask if your Cub Scouts can visit the store to learn about different kinds of bait.
Schedule the visit to the store.
Provide Cub Scouts and their families with the date, time, and address of the bait shop visit.
During the meeting:
Meet the Cub Scouts at the bait shop, and explain that they are there to learn about different kinds of bait and when to use them.
Introduce the host at the store to Cub Scouts.
Have host show different kinds of bait and why you would use each bait type with Cub Scouts.
Ask Cub Scouts if they have any questions about bait.
After the meeting
Have Cub Scouts sign the thank you card for the bait shop.
Mail the thank you card.

requirements.text: Demonstrate a proper cast for the pole or rod you are using.

activities.title: Cast & Learn
activities.description: Learn how to cast a fishing pole with accuracy by trying to hit a target.
supply_list: ½” flat washers – one for each fishing pole
Cast & Learn scoresheet found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Spread out frisbees in the casting area to serve as targets. Decide how many points Cub Scouts can earn for landing in each frisbee. The further the frisbee the more points they are worth.
Print Cast & Learn scoresheet, one for the den.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that they’ll be practicing casting their fishing pole and that the goal is to hit the center of the target.
Remove any hooks from the fishing poles and replace them with flat washers
Demonstrate how to cast the pole toward the target. Cast the pole five times and add up your points for the five casts.
Have Cub Scouts line up and practice. When they are ready allow them to go to cast for a score.
Take turns casting five times. After their five turns, tell them to add up their points and record their score on the den scoresheet.
Tip: With slight modifications, you can use the same fishing poles for the Fish Names Game, Cast & Learn, Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge, Crazy Casting Spin-Off, and Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge.

activities.title: Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge
activities.description: Cub Scouts practice casting their pole or rod to catch a paper fish.
supply_list: ½” flat washers – one for each fishing pole
Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge pattern found in Additional Resources
½” flat washers that magnets will attach to. (Iron, steel, or nickel)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Designate an area as a pond using blue painter’s tape on the floor. Make the area at least 25 feet long to allow for long casting.
Block off the area to prevent anyone from walking near or around where Cub Scouts will be casting.
Make several fish using the Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge pattern and card stock. You’ll need at least one for every two Cub Scouts in your den.
Print out the fish pattern on card stock.
Cut out the fish and match them up so that the blue color shows on each side.
Using tape, tape a magnet to the back (white) side of one of the fish.
Put the other fish on top of the fish with the magnet, and tape (with the regular tape) or glue them together.
Test to make sure that the flat washers will attach to the magnets and hold the fish.
During the meeting:
Designate an area in your meeting room as your “pond,” and spread the fish out in the pond.
Remove any hooks from the fishing poles and tie on flat washers.
Mark lines that are 6 feet apart on the casting end of the “pond” for Cub Scouts to cast from.
Demonstrate the proper way to cast.
Allow Cub Scouts to practice.
Divide Cub Scouts into two teams and have each team line up 6 feet behind one of the casting areas.
Explain the rules of the game.
The first Cub Scout in line will step up to the casting area and cast until they catch a fish.
Once they catch a fish they go to the back of their team’s line.
The team that has each team member catch a fish wins.
Tip: With slight modifications, you can use the same fishing poles for the Fish Names Game, Cast & Learn, Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge, Crazy Casting Spin-Off, and Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge.

activities.title: Crazy Casting Spin-Off
activities.description: Cub Scouts practice their casting skills by distance and accuracy .
supply_list: ½” flat washers – one for each fishing pole
Crazy Casting Spin-Off spinner pattern found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print the spinner on card stock, cut it out, and assemble it with the brad fastener.
Mark off a safe area that is at least 40 feet long to allow for long casting.
Mark off three spots that are 6-feet apart that will serve as casting areas for Cub Scouts.
Place the hoops 20-feet from each of the three casting areas.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts gather in an open area outside free of obstacles.
Demonstrate the proper way to cast, make sure to cover the methods that are on the Crazy Casting Spin-Off spinner.
​
Give Cub Scouts time to practice casting.
Have Cub Scouts line up 6 feet behind one of the casting areas.
Have the first Cub Scout in line, spin the spinner, and attempt the cast the spinner lands on. A successful cast is one that lands in a hula hoop.
Continue until every Cub Scout has at least one chance at the challenge.
Tip: Some of the casts are silly like “do three bunny hops then cast.” This is to make the activity more exciting.
Tip: If you have a large den, you may want to divide Cub Scouts into two or three groups and make two or three spinners and two or three fishing poles.
Tip: With slight modifications, you can use the same fishing poles for the Fish Names Game, Cast & Learn, Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge, Crazy Casting Spin-Off, and Cast-A-Thon Relay Challenge.

requirements.text: Learn the rules of fishing safely.

activities.title: Bait and Switch Safety Rules Game
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn the fishing safety rules in this flashcard game.
supply_list: Bait & Switch Safety Rules Game found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Bait & Switch Safety Rules Game on cardstock.
Cut out each flashcard.
During the meeting:
Place the flashcards face down in a pile.
Have Cub Scouts read the fishing safety rules in their Wolf handbook.
Have Cub Scouts pick a buddy.
Explain the game to Cub Scouts. Each pair of Cub Scouts will turn a card over, read it, and shout out “rule” or “not rule.”
Continue the game with the next pair of Cub Scouts until you’ve gone through all the cards.
Tip: Instead of Cub Scouts saying “rule” or “not rule,” they could say “bait” when it is a rule and “switch” when it isn’t.
Tip: Laminating the flashcards will make them more durable.

activities.title: Hook, Line, and Safety Poster
activities.description: Cub Scouts make a poster about fishing safety.
supply_list: Poster board, 1 for every two Cub Scouts

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Divide Cub Scouts into teams of two to three.
Explain that Cub Scouts will be working together to make a poster to show the rules they should follow to safely fish.
Using the fishing rules found in the Wolf handbooks, have Cub Scouts write the rules somewhere on their poster. Fishing rules:
Fish with proper adult supervision.
Get permission to fish where you plan to fish.
Check the weather before you go. Do not fish in a thunderstorm or inclement weather.
Use the buddy system. You must be able to see them.
Give plenty of room to others who are fishing nearby.
Never fish where people are swimming.
Encourage Cub Scouts to draw pictures representing the fishing safety rules.
Encourage Cub Scouts to decorate their poster using crayons, markers, or stickers.

activities.title: Tacklebox Trivia
activities.description: A fun and interactive way to learn the rules of fishing safely through a jeopardy-type game.
supply_list: Poster board or a large sheet of cardboard
Tacklebox Trivia cards found in Additional Resources
Access to Tacklebox Trivia Clues and Answers found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Lay out your poster board horizontally or vertically, depending on your preference. Use a ruler to create a large table with six rows and four columns for your categories and point values.
Write the names of the categories in the top row: Fishing Safety, Fishing Equipment, Types of Bait, and Cub Scout Six Essentials.
Print the clues from Tacklebox Trivia and cut them out.
Tape or glue each clue into one of the boxes in the correct category.
Write the point values (100, 200, 300, 400, and 500) onto individual Post-it notes. You’ll need four sets, one for each category.
Place the Post-it notes over the clues.
During the meeting:
Divide Cub Scouts into two or three groups.
Before beginning the game, ask an adult to determine which team raises their hand first and to keep score.
Explain the game rules to Cub Scouts. After a clue is read, the first team to raise one of their hands is called on to try to answer the clue. If they answer correctly, they are awarded the value of the points. Their answer must be in the form of a question (who is, what is, etc.).
Ask one of the teams to select a category and point value.
Remove the Post-it note from the selected clue, and read it to the teams.
Call on the first team that raises their hand.
If the team gives the correct answer in the correct format, they are awarded the points. If they answer incorrectly, the points are deducted from their score, and another team is allowed to answer.
The team that gives the correct answer selects the next category and point value.
Continue playing until all the categories and points have been answered.

requirements.text: With your den, pack, or family, go fishing.

activities.title: Go Fish
activities.description: Cub Scouts go on a fishing expedition with their den.
supply_list: Fishing poles, one per Cub Scout
Bait or tackle based on the fish you will be fishing for
Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record on each participant (youth and adult)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Research local fishing spots that are family-friendly and have easy access. Get permission, if needed, to fish there.
Ensure you are aware of any fishing regulations and licensing requirements in your area. Purchase a fishing license if necessary. Youth may not need a fishing license but adults who are fishing are likely to need one.
Inform parents and guardians of the date/time/location of the fishing activity.
Secure additional adult supervision.
Gather copies of the
Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record
on each participant (youth and adult)
Review Annual Health and Medical Records for any restrictions that may impact participation
A week prior to the activity visit the site to become familiar with facilities such as access to drinking water, bathrooms, and parking. Inform parents and guardians of any details about the facilities that are important such as where to park and where the den will meet up.
Confirm with parents and guardians that every Cub Scout has a fishing pole and develop a plan to provide fishing poles for those who do not have one.
During the meeting:
Bring copies of the
Meet at the designated area of the fishing spot.
Collect Activity Consent Forms.
Review the fishing safety rules and any local rules or regulations with Cub Scouts.
Discuss what type of fish you will be fishing for and what type of bait or lure to use.
Have adults help Cub Scouts with attaching bait or lures.
Ensure that Cub Scouts are spaced a safe distance apart from each other and away from obstacles.
As Cub Scouts are fishing have adults give positive coaching and encouragement.
If a fish is caught practice catch and release.
Assist Cub Scouts who catch a fish to release it.
Before leaving the fishing area, have Cub Scouts and adults pick up any trash that may be found.

requirements.text: Identify different parts of a coin.

activities.title: Coin Designer Challenge
activities.description: Cub Scouts will design their own coin.
supply_list: Coin Designer Challenge found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Coin Designer Challenge worksheets, one for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that they are going to design their own coin. Pass out the worksheet.
Ask Cub Scouts to choose a theme for the coin. It could be related to a favorite hobby, a historical event, a fictional story, or something else of personal significance.
Have Cub Scouts think about what they’ll put on the obverse (front). Give them some ideas such as:
Portrait: Consider including a portrait, either of a fictional character or someone important to the theme.
Date: Add a year or date that holds meaning for the theme.
Symbolism: Incorporate symbols that represent the theme or story. For example, if it’s about space exploration, include stars, planets, or rockets.
Denomination: Clearly label the coin’s value if it’s part of a play or educational activity.
Have Cub Scouts think about what they’ll put on the reverse (back) such as:
Design Continuation: Ensure that the reverse complements the theme on the obverse.
Motto or Slogan: Add a motto, slogan, or catchphrase that relates to the theme or story.
Country or Origin: Include a fictional country or origin for the coin. Kids can get creative with this aspect.
Edge: Design the edge of the coin, considering unique patterns, lettering, or features.
After Cub Scouts have finished their designs, have them take turns sharing it with the rest of the den.

activities.title: Coin Hunter’s Odyssey
activities.description: Learn about coins in a coin scavenger hunt.
supply_list: Coin Hunter’s Odyssey worksheet found in Additional Resources
Pencils, enough for each Cub Scouts

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Coin Hunter’s Odyssey worksheets, one for each Cub Scout.
Gather coins of different denominations. Make sure that you have coins that match each of the items on the scavenger hunt list.
Hide the coins around the meeting location.
During the meeting:
Give each Cub Scout a copy of the Coin Scavenger Hunt.
Explain to Cub Scouts that they’re going on a scavenger hunt to find coins that have the characteristics listed on their paper. Tell them the boundaries of their hunt (coins are all inside the room, coins aren’t in any cabinets or drawers, etc.)
Have Cub Scouts walk around the room looking for the coins. Give them a set amount of time for the activity. Ten minutes will be sufficient.
Once the time is up, gather around and ask Cub Scouts to share their sheets.

activities.title: Coin Quest Adventure
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about the characteristics and values of different coins.
supply_list: One penny, one nickel, one dime, and one quarter for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Collect the coins you’ll need.
During the meeting:
Place all the coins in a pile on a table, and ask Cub Scouts to each take one penny, one nickel, one dime, and one quarter.
Have Cub Scouts work with a buddy.
Ask Cub Scouts to work with their buddy to examine their coins. Have them identify the following:
The bust
is a picture of a person’s head.
The legend
is the main writing.
The field
is the background of the coin.
The relief
is all the raised parts of the coin.
The inscription
is the writing on the coin.
The mint mark
is a letter telling where the coin was made.
The edge
is the outer surface of the coin. It could have lettering, designs, or ridges on it.
The rim
is a raised area near the edge around the coin on both sides. It helps the coin keep from wearing out too quickly.
Have each Cub Scout pick a coin.
Tell Cub Scouts that you’re going to ask some questions about their coin. They should take turns answering them with their buddy.
What is this coin called?
What can you tell me about it?
Whose face is on the coin? What do you know about this person?
Does the coin have writing on it? What does it say?
What is the value of the coin?
Does the coin have a mint mark? What is the mint mark?
Have Cub Scouts select a different coin and answer the questions for the new coin.

requirements.text: Find the mint mark on a coin and identify the mint facility where it was made and the year it was made.

activities.title: Mint City Showdown
activities.description: In this activity, Cub Scouts will count coins from each mint.
supply_list: Magnifying glasses, one for every two Cub Scouts
Five coins for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Draw a line down the middle of the whiteboard and make two columns. Label the columns Philadelphia and Denver.
Learn about mint marks on coins and the different locations where coins are made.
P = Philadelphia
S = San Francisco
D = Denver
W = West Point
During the meeting:
Distribute coins to Cub Scouts.
Gather Cub Scouts and inform them that in the United States coins are made in four different places called mints.
Show them what a mint mark looks like on a coin.
Let each Cub Scout examine the different mint marks in the coins using a magnifying lens.
Ask Cub Scouts to separate their coins by mint mark and count the number they have of each.
Have each Cub Scout write the number of coins they have from each mint in the appropriate column on the poster board or whiteboard.
Add up the totals in each column to determine how many Cub Scouts have from each mint.
Ask Cub Scouts why they think there is more from one mint than the other. For example, if you live on the east side of the country, you may have more quarters from the Philadelphia mint.
Tip: Coin Anatomy Expedition, Mint Mark Masterclass, and Mint City Showdown could all be completed at the same den meeting

activities.title: Mint Mark Masterclass
activities.description: Cub Scouts will learn about coin mint marks.
supply_list: Magnifying glasses, one for every two Cub Scouts
Five coins for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Learn about mint marks on coins and the different locations where coins are made.
P = Philadelphia
S = San Francisco
D = Denver
W = West Point
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and inform them that in the United States coins are made in four different places called mints.
Show them what a mint mark looks like on a coin.
Ask Cub Scouts to use the magnifying glass to find the mint mark for their coins.
Have Cub Scouts share what mints made their coins.
Tip: Coin Anatomy Expedition, Mint Mark Masterclass, and Mint City Showdown could all be completed at the same den meeting.

activities.title: Pile of Pennies
activities.description: Learning to find the mint mark and date on pennies. Submitted by: Jenny Dunn Council Name: NCAC
supply_list: Print out of the face of a penny

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Gather $5-10 in pennies.
Place the pennies in a jar.
Learn about mint marks on coins and the different locations where coins are made.
P = Philadelphia
S = San Francisco
D = Denver
W = West Point
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and inform them that in the United States coins are made in four different places called mints.
Use the large image to show them what a mint mark looks like on a coin.
Ask each Cub Scout to find the mint mark on a penny.
Dump the pennies into a pile where all Cub Scouts can reach the pile. Tell them they have 5 minutes to find the oldest penny from each mint. Start the 5-minute timer.
After the 5 minutes are up, have Cub Scouts share the oldest penny they found and ask what mint it is from. See who found the oldest penny from each mint.
After the meeting
Put all the pennies back into the jar,

requirements.text: Play a coin game.

activities.title: Coin Basketball
activities.description: Cub Scouts will play basketball with coins.
supply_list: One quarter for each Cub Scout
One cup or bowl for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that they’re going to play coin basketball where they’ll try to toss a quarter into the cup or bowl.
Have Cub Scouts sit at a table and place their cup two or three feet in front of them.
Instruct Cub Scouts to hold the coin upright on its rim between one finger and thumb.
Tell Cub Scouts to try tossing the coin into the cup a couple of times for practice. If they make it into the cup or bowl, they earn two points.
After the practice time is up, tell Cub Scouts that they’ll have two minutes to toss the coin in the cup or bowl as many times as possible. Have them keep up with the number of points they earn.

activities.title: Coin Bingo
activities.description: Play Coin Bingo.
supply_list: Coin Bingo card found in Additional Resources
One of each for the caller: penny, nickel, dime, quarter, and dollar coin
One pencil or pen for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Coin Bingo Card, one for each Cub Scout.
Collect coins.
During the game:
Ask an adult or a denner to assist with this activity by keeping track of how many times a coin is called.
Give each Cub Scout their bingo card and the coins.
Explain that you’ll hold up a coin. Cub Scouts will identify the value of the coin and if they have that value on their bingo card, they’ll mark off the square on their card. They can only mark one square per turn. When they get four in a row, they should shout out, “Bingo!”
Continue holding up coins until someone gets four in a row.
When Cub Scout shouts, “Bingo,” ask the adult or denner to verify their results.
The first Cub Scout who gets four coins in a row wins the game.

activities.title: Coin Wars Game
activities.description: The coin wars game will help teach Cub Scouts to add up the value of coins.
supply_list: Coin Wars Game cards found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print enough copies of the Coin Wars Game cards for each Cub Scout to have seven cards.
Cut the pages into cards.
During the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to buddy up. Give each set of buddies a stack of fourteen cards.
Have one Cub Scout deal the cards to themselves and to their buddy.
Each player turns over one of their cards and adds up the value of the coins on the card.
The player who has the highest value gets all the cards for that hand.
Continue playing until all the cards have been played.

activities.title: Eggstravaganza Coin Quest
activities.description: Cub Scouts will practice their coin-counting skills with this fun coin game using plastic Easter eggs.
supply_list: Plastic craft eggs, three for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Using the marker, write different amounts on each of the plastic eggs. For example, 84¢, 21¢, 38¢.
After the amounts are written on the eggs, add the amounts up to ensure that you have the correct amount in coins.
Set up an area free of obstacles to conduct a relay race.
Make the relay course 30 feet long.
Divide the eggs evenly into two baskets. Set up the table at the end of the opposite end of the starting line. Place the two baskets on opposite ends of the table.
Divide the change into two equal portions onto the two paper plates. Place a plate next to each basket.
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and divide the den into two teams.
Explain the rules of the relay.
The first person on the team will run to the table to their team’s basket. Pull out an egg and read the amount on the egg.
The person then places the correct amount of change to equal the amount that is on the egg, opens the egg and places the change into the egg, and then runs back.
The team will get 1 point for each egg that has the correct change in it.
The team that collects all the eggs first gets 1 point.
The point system is set up so accuracy counts more than speed so the team that makes sure the amount in each egg is correct will more than likely win the race.
Run the relay race, look for opportunities to celebrate those who demonstrate the Scout Oath and Law as they play.

requirements.text: Choose a coin that interests you and make a coin rubbing. List information next to the coin detailing the pictures on it, the year it was made, and the mint where it was made.

activities.title: Coin Rubbings
activities.description: Making a coin rubbing to learn more about your favorite coin.
supply_list: Wolf handbook or Coin Rubbings worksheet found in Additional Resources
Assortment of coins, at least three for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Either ask that Cub Scouts bring their Wolf handbook to the meeting or print the Coin Rubbings worksheet, enough for 1 for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Place the coins on a table. Ask Cub Scouts to gather around the table.
Have Cub Scouts pick out 3 coins of various sizes and denominations.
Have Cub Scouts place the coin on a smooth surface. Using the page in the handbook or the worksheet, place the paper on top of a coin. Hold the paper firmly to keep the coin steady.
Tell Cub Scouts to use the side of the pencil lead, rub back and forth across the paper over the coin. Have them continue rubbing until the entire side of the coin is copied on the paper.
Explain that when Cub Scouts are done with that side, they should repeat for the other side of the coin.
On their coin rubbing paper, Cub Scouts write down:
Type of coin
Pictures
Year
Mint

requirements.text: Make a paper airplane and fly it five times. Record the flight distance and time.

activities.title: Make a Paper Airplane
activities.description: Cub Scouts make and fly a paper airplane.
supply_list: 8 ½” x 11” inch paper (several pages for each Cub Scout)
​​F​olding instructions sheets for each Cub Scout, see Make a Paper Airplane found in Additional Resources
Flight distance and time sheet for each Cub Scout, see Make a Paper Airplane tracker in Additional Resources
Stopwatch or phone with stopwatch app

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting:
Print copies of folding instructions, and flight distance and time sheet.
Ask two adults to assist. One to be the timekeeper and one to measure distance.
During the Meeting:
Pass out handouts and paper to make the airplanes to each Cub Scout.
Tell Cub Scouts that they’re going to make and fly paper airplanes. Let Cub Scouts know that they can use any design they want, but they have the folding instructions sheet as a reference.
While Cub Scouts are making their planes, mark a start line. Cub Scouts will stand behind this line when they fly their planes.
After all Cub Scouts have finished folding their airplanes, explain that they’re going to fly them five times and record how far they travel and how long they stay in the air.
Ask Cub Scouts to line up behind the start line. One at a time, have Cub Scouts fly their paper airplane.
Have the time and distance keepers announce the results and remind Cub Scouts to record their numbers on their sheet.
Have the next Cub Scout in line fly their paper airplane. Repeat step 6.
Continue steps 5, 6, and 7 until all Cub Scouts have flown their airplanes five times.
Ask Cub Scouts what features the paper airplanes that flew the furthest have in common.
Tip: This activity can be done with the paper airplane comparison activity for requirement 2.

requirements.text: Make a paper airplane of a different design and fly it five times. Record the flight distance and time.

activities.title: Paper Airplane Comparison
activities.description: Cub Scouts will make a different paper airplane design and fly it five times.
supply_list: 8 ½” x 11” inch paper, several pages for each Cub Scout
​​Folding instructions sheets for each Cub Scout, Paper Airplane Comparison​ in Additional Resources
Flight distance and time sheet for each Cub Scout, Paper Airplane Comparison tracker in Additional Resources
Stopwatch or phone with stopwatch app

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print one copy of the folding instructions sheet and one copy of the flight distance and time sheet for each Cub Scout.
Ask two adults to assist. One to be the timekeeper and one to measure distance.
During the meeting:
Pass out handouts and paper to make the airplanes to each Cub Scout.
Tell Cub Scouts that they’re going to make and fly a different paper airplane design. Let Cub Scouts know that they can use any design they want, but they have the folding instructions sheet as a reference.
While Cub Scouts are making their planes, mark a start line. Cub Scouts will stand behind this line when they fly their planes.
After all of Cub Scouts have finished folding their airplanes, explain that they’re going to fly them five times and record how far they travel and how long they stay in the air.
Ask Cub Scouts to line up behind the start line. One at a time, have Cub Scouts fly their paper airplane.
Have the time and distance keepers announce the results and remind Cub Scout to record their numbers on their sheet.
Have the next Cub Scout in line fly their paper airplane. Repeat step 6.
Continue steps 5, 6, and 7 until all Cub Scouts have flown their airplanes five times.
Ask Cub Scouts what features the paper airplanes that flew the furthest have in common.
Tip: This activity can be done with the make a paper airplane activity for requirement 1.

requirements.text: Compare and contrast the two paper airplanes by distance and flight times.

activities.title: Paper Airplane Derby
activities.description: Cub Scouts participate in a paper airplane derby.
supply_list: 8 ½” x 11” paper, at least 6 or 7 pieces per Cub Scout
Stopwatch or phone with stopwatch app
Paper Airplane Derby scoresheet found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Paper Airplane Derby scoresheet, 4 scoresheets per page, enough for 1 scoresheet for each Cub Scout.
Just before the meeting, set up each of the four rounds. Ask adults to help and assign one or two of them to each round.
Depending on how many Cub Scouts you have, you might want to have them rotate through the rounds instead of everyone competing at one station before moving to the next one
For the Bullseye Bonanza Target Round: Find a suitable target, such as a pole, tree, or marked spot on the ground. Find a throwing spot, ensuring it’s about 10 steps away from the target.
For the Hang-Time Heroes Hang Time Round: Find an open area without obstructions where Cub Scouts can fly their planes. Mark the throwing spot.
For the Pathfinder Precision Accuracy Round: Find a suitable straight path along which Cub Scouts can fly their planes such as a sidewalk, hallway, or marked area. Mark the throwing spot.
For the Sky’s the Limit Distance Round: Find an open area without obstructions where Cub Scouts can fly their planes. Mark the throwing spot.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that there are four rounds of the Paper Airplane Derby.
Bullseye Bonanza – Land the airplane as close as possible to the target.
Hang-Time Heroes – Keep the airplane in the air as long as possible.
Pathfinder Precision – Fly the airplane in a straight path, landing it as close as possible to the middle.
Sky’s the Limit – Fly the airplane as far as possible.
Instruct Cub Scouts to make at least four airplanes, one for each round. They may also want to make some extra planes to practice with. Have them write their names on each of their planes. They may also decorate their planes by drawing pictures or designs on them.
Give Cub Scouts time to practice flying their planes. When the practice time is up, have them choose which planes they’ll fly for each round.
For the Bullseye Bonanza Target Round:
Have Cub Scouts line up behind the throwing spot. Ask one or two parents to stand near the target with a measuring tape.
Each Cub Scout will take a turn throwing their airplane at the target, aiming to land it as close to the target as possible. The parents will measure how far away from the target the plane is. Each Cub Scout will record how far away they are from the target.
For the Hang-Time Heroes Hang Time Round:
Have Cub Scouts line up behind the throwing spot. Ask one parent to watch the plane and another parent to work the stopwatch.
Each Cub Scout will take a turn throwing their airplane, aiming to keep it in the air as long as possible. When the plane lands, the parent watching it will tell the other parent to stop the stopwatch. Each Cub Scout will record how long their plane stayed in the air.
For the Pathfinder Precision Accuracy Round:
Have Cub Scouts line up behind the throwing spot. Ask one or two parents to stand by the path with measuring tape.
Each Cub Scout will take a turn throwing their airplane, aiming to land it as close to the middle of the path as possible. When the plane lands, the parents will measure how close to the middle of the path it is. Each Cub Scout will record how far away they are from the middle of the path.
Tip: You might want to set an acceptable minimum distance for throws to count.
For the Sky’s the Limit Distance Round:
Have Cub Scouts line up behind the throwing spot. Ask one or two parents to stand near the throwing spot with a long measuring tape.
Each Cub Scout will take a turn throwing their airplane, aiming to fly as far as possible. When the plane lands, the parents will measure how far the plane flew from the throwing spot. Each Cub Scout will record how far their plane flew.
Have Cub Scouts compare their results. You can award small prizes to the winners of each round if you would like.
Ask Cub Scouts what features the paper airplanes that did the best in each challenge have in common.
Tip: If you have a large den, you may not have time to do all four rounds. If you don’t, pick two to do.

activities.title: Paper Airplane Golf
activities.description: Cub Scouts will play paper airplane golf.
supply_list: 8 ½” x 11” paper, at least 2 or 3 pieces per Cub Scout
Markers and colored pencils to decorate the airplanes
Items to create “hole” such hula hoops, laundry baskets, or buckets
Paper Airplane Golf scorecard found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print a Paper Airplane Golf scorecard for each Cub Scout.
Find an open outdoor area with enough room for each hole.
For each hole, place a hula hoop, laundry basket, bucket, etc. on the ground and mark a starting point a few steps away.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts make paper airplanes.
Starting at hole 1, each Cub Scout flies their plane, trying to land it inside the “hole” with the fewest throws.
After their turn, each Cub Scout records their score on the scorecard.
When all Cub Scouts have had a turn at hole 1, they move to hole 2 and so on, until Cub Scouts complete all the holes.
Ask Cub Scouts what features the paper airplanes that did the best have in common.

activities.title: Paper Airplane Obstacle Course
activities.description: Cub Scouts participate in a paper airplane obstacle course.
supply_list: 8 ½” x 11” paper, 2 or 3 pieces per Cub Scout
Markers and colored pencils to decorate the airplanes
Supplies for obstacles, items such as pool noodles, cardboard boxes, paper, wire hangers, etc.
Print one Den Obstacle Course Time Sheet, see Paper Airplane Obstacle Course in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Design your obstacle course by brainstorming the obstacles you want to include in your course. Some ideas include hoops, tunnels, targets, and rings.
Determine the layout of your course, keeping in mind the available space and the order of the obstacles.
Create the obstacles. For each obstacle, you’ll need to create a target or a structure. Here are a few ideas:
Hoops: Create large hoops using wire hangers or pool noodles. Shape them into circles and secure the ends with tape or string.
Tunnels: Use large cardboard boxes or sheets to create tunnels.
Targets: Draw or print out targets on sheets of paper. These can be circles, squares, or any shape you like.
Rings: Create rings using pool noodles or flexible plastic tubing. Shape them into circles and secure the ends.
Immediately before the meeting, set up your obstacles.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts how the obstacle course will work.
Have Cub Scouts make their paper airplanes and write their names on them. They may decorate them with markers or colored pencils.
Each Cub Scout takes turns flying their paper airplane through the obstacle course, attempting to complete it as quickly and accurately as possible.
Time each Cub Scout’s run and have them record it on the den time sheet.
Ask Cub Scouts what features the paper airplanes that did the best have in common.

requirements.text: Build a flying object that is not a paper airplane.

activities.title: Balsawood Airplanes
activities.description: Cub Scouts build and fly balsawood airplanes.
supply_list: Balsawood airplane kits, one per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Put together one of the balsa wood airplanes using the instructions found in the package so that you can demonstrate this to Cub Scouts.
Identify a place to fly planes that is free of obstacles.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts put together their balsa wood airplanes according to the instructions found in the package.
Have Cub Scouts fly their balsa wood airplanes.

activities.title: Paper Cup Rockets
activities.description: Cub Scouts will build a flying object that is not a paper airplane.
supply_list: 1 bottle of liquid glue per 2 Cub Scouts
1 pair of scissors per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Collect materials
Print 1 paper cup rocket template per Cub Scout
Make one of the paper cup rockets to show Cub Scouts. Watch the video linked in additional resources for instructions.
During the meeting:
Give each Cub Scout two paper cups and a Have them set one of the cups aside for now.
Instruct Cub Scout to poke a hole in the cup near the Then have Cub Scouts poke 3 more holes evenly spaced around the cup. The holes should be in a 3:00, 6:00, 9:00, and 12:00 pattern.
Cut out the circle with the wolf shape and attach it to the middle of the side of the cup.
Have each Cub Scout cut out the 5-inch circle and two right triangles.
Have each Cub Scout cut out a right triangle from their circle.
Ask Cub Scouts to apply glue to one side of the newly cut edge on the circle. Then ask them to make a cone shape by pulling the other edge on top of the glued edge. Attach the clothespin to the cone while it
dries.
Direct Cub Scouts to break the two toothpicks in half
Instruct Cub Scouts to push the rubber band through one hole and fasten in with the toothpick and then do the same with the other end.
Repeat with the other rubber band forming an x in the cup.
Fold a small 1/8-inch part of the right triangle, add glue, and attach to the side of the cup. Repeat with the second triangle.
Put glue around the top of the cup and attach the cone.
Once the glue has dried, have Cub Scouts place the cup on top of the second cup, push down, then let go and watch it fly.

activities.title: Paper Kites
activities.description: Cub Scouts make and fly a paper kite.
supply_list: 8 ½” x 11″ piece of paper for each Cub Scout, colored paper makes the best kites
Bamboo skewer for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Break off the pointed end of each skewer.
Prepare meeting space to allow for making kites.
Identify an area free of obstacles to fly kites.
During the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to fold their piece of paper “hamburger” style so that the paper is 8 ½” by 5 ½”.
Have Cub Scouts fold one side of the paper on an angle. Then have them turn the paper over and fold the other side at an angle.
Have Cub Scouts unfold one side. Leave the folded side facing up.
Ask Cub Scouts to tape down the folded edge.
Have Cub Scouts tape the skewer to the wider end of the paper, across the fold.
Ask Cub Scouts to pick up the paper and hold the kite by the folded part under the skewer.
Ask Cub Scouts to punch a hole through the double pages right below the skewer.
Have Cub Scouts run a length of string through the hole and tie it to the kit.
If they want, Cub Scouts can tape streamers to the narrow end of their kites.
Take Cub Scouts outside to fly their kites.
Tip: This YouTube video,
How to Make a Simple Kite
, from Inner Child Run Media, LLC, shows exactly how to make a simple kite.

activities.title: Wolf-Copters
activities.description: Cub Scouts make and fly Wolf-Copters.
supply_list: Wolf-Copter template found in Additional Resources
Paper clip for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print a Wolf-Copter template for each Cub Scout.
Set up meeting area for Cub Scouts to make Wolf-Copters.
Identify a space free of obstacles to fly Wolf-Copters.
During the meeting:
Pass out the Wolf-Copter templates and paper clips to Cub Scouts.

activities.title: The Great Scatter Relay
activities.description: Cub Scouts sort renewable and non-renewable items in a relay game.
supply_list: 6 Items made from wood – renewable natural resources: Pencil Chopsticks Paper Cardboard box Book Toothpick
6 Items made from cotton or wool – renewable natural resources: Sock T-shirt Towel Sweater Canvas bag Pillowcase
6 Items made from glass or aluminum – non-renewable natural resources: Soda can Glass jar Tin foil Can of beans Aluminum roasting pan Glass soda bottle
6 items made from stone – non-renewable natural resources: Brick Ceramic coffee mug Floor tile Costume jewelry Ceramic bowl Marble

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting:
Gather items for the relay.
Label bins, one “renewable” and the second “nonrenewable”.
Scatter the different items around the meeting area and place the bins close to the front of the room.
During the Meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and discuss what makes a natural resource renewable. A renewable natural resource is something that can be used over and over again and cannot be used up or it can be renewed in the same time frame or shorter than it is used. For example, wind and solar power can be used repeatedly. Things like cotton or bamboo are things that can regrow at a faster rate than we use it.
Cub Scouts form a line.
One at a time, Cub Scouts run to any item. They decide if the item they’ve chosen is made from a renewable or renewable resource. Once they have made their choice, they place the item into the appropriate bin.
Once Cub Scout places their item into a bin, they run back to the line and tag the next person to go.
After all the items have been placed into the bins, check to see which items were sorted correctly.
If the item is placed in the wrong bin, have a discussion with the Cub Scouts about the choice and place in the correct bin.

requirements.text: Learn about the 3 R’s: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle.

activities.title: Compost Jar
activities.description: Make a composting jar and how using compost connects to the 3 Rs.
supply_list: 24 oz. glass jar with lid (washed spaghetti glass jar with lid)
2” penny nails, one for each Cub Scout
1 page of newspaper, one for each Cub Scout
1 cup of dirt for each Cub Scout, use dirt from outside, not potting soil
Compost materials, 6 ounces for each Cub Scout, enough to fill the jar a ¼ of the way full Banana peel Eggshells Grass clippings Vegetable scraps
2 ounces of dead leaves for each Cub Scout
One paper plate for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting:
Gather 24 oz. spaghetti glass jars and wash them.
Gather compost materials, enough for each scout.
Gather dirt, shredded newspaper, and dead leaves.
Fill a spray bottle with clean water.
Collect the nails and paper plates.
During the Meeting:
Share with the Cub Scouts that a Scout is Thrifty. Ask them what being thrifty means to them and allow them to use their handbooks for a definition.
A Scout is THRIFTY. Work to pay your own way. Don‘t be wasteful. Use time, property, and natural resources wisely.
Inform the Cub Scouts that since we want to be thirty and not waste, one way we can reduce or eliminate waste is by the 3 R’s of recycling – reduce, reuse, recycle.
Inform the Cub Scouts that we can reduce the amount of something we use. We can reuse things a second time either for the same purpose they were designed for or to use them in a different way. We can recycle things by breaking them down into their raw materials and making something new from them.
Inform Cub Scouts that today we are going to use reuse spaghetti jars and we are going to reduce our waste by creating a composting jar.
A composting jar is a way to take some types of trash and instead of putting it into the garbage we can break it down to create soil that can be used for planting or fertilizing plants.
With the help of a parent or legal guardian, tell Cub Scouts to use the nail to punch eight to ten holes in the top of their lid.
Ask Cub Scouts to place their glass jar onto their paper plate.
Tell Cub Scouts to layer the following into their jar, in this order:
Dirt
Shredded newspaper
Dead leaves
Spray the paper and dirt until moist.
Add compost materials.
Spray the compost materials until moist.
Cub Scouts will now put the lid onto their coffee can and place it in a sunny spot in their home. In about a month they will start to see the breakdown of the materials as what trash was before it turns into compost.
Remind Cub Scout to turn the jar around once a week and add a small amount of water each day, this will help the materials break down faster.
Tip: Make sure Cub Scouts understand that the more compost materials they add at home, the longer the project will take to complete.
Tip: Remind Cub Scouts and adults, that they will see fluffy mold growing through this process, so always keep it covered when they’re not working with the compost and always wash hands when they’re finished.
After the Meeting:
Cub Scouts will spray water into their compost jar every day.
Cub Scouts can continue to add compost materials to their jar.
Every 3-4 days Cub Scouts will shake their compost jar to mix the compost materials.
Once the compost materials have completely broken down, the Cub Scouts can use it to plant seeds to grow a plant.

requirements.text: Create a secret code. Send a message to a member of your den or family. Have that person send a message back to you using the same secret code.

activities.title: Code Stick
activities.description: Create and decipher a code stick coded message.
supply_list: Paper strips cut into ¼” to ½” wide by 11” long for each Cub Scout
Tape, one dispenser for every group of 4 Cub Scouts

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Cut the paper into long thin strips of about ¼ to ½ inch wide.
Make a sample code stick.
Set up meeting space so there is room for Cub Scouts to make decoder sticks.
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and ask them if they have ever sent or received an email. Explain to them:
To protect the information in the email a computer may scramble the message so if someone who wasn’t supposed to receive the email gets it, they can’t read it. This is called encryption.
Encrypting messages has been going on way before computers. When all messages were written the message would use a code and to understand the code you needed a key.
Today we will create a secret code using a method that was used before computers.
Give each Cub Scout a strip of paper and 2 pencils.
Tape the piece of paper to the top of the pencil. Wrap it tightly around the length of the pencil so the edges of the strip are exactly side by side.
Tape the paper strip to the other end of the pencil so the paper strip stays in place when you write on it.
Ask Cub Scouts to write a secret message down one side of the pencil. Remind them to add a few extra letters on the other sides.
Unwrap the strip of paper from the pencil. The letters will be mixed up and seem random.
Ask Cub Scouts to pass their secret code with another Cub Scout.
Each Cub Scout wraps the paper strip around a pencil to decode it. The letters will now form the secret message.

activities.title: Decoder Wheel
activities.description: Send a secret message using a decoder wheel.
supply_list: Decoder Wheel worksheet found in Additional Resources
1 pair of scissors for each Cub Scout
Round brads, one for each Cub Scout
Paper, one for each Cub Scout
Pencil, one for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print a copy of the Decoder Wheel, one for each Cub Scout.
Make a sample decoder wheel. Become familiar with how the decoder wheel works. The decoder wheel can be used only if you have the key. The key is the position at which the decoder wheel starts.
Set up meeting space so there is room for Cub Scouts to make decoder wheels.
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and ask them if they have ever sent or received an email. Explain to them:
To protect the information in the email a computer may scramble the message so if someone who wasn’t supposed to receive the email gets it, they can’t read it. This is called encryption.
Encrypting messages has been going on way before computers. When all messages were written the message would use a code and to understand the code you needed a key.
Today we will create a secret code using a method that was used before computers.
​​​Give each Cub Scout a decoder wheel sheet, a pair of scissors, and a round brad.
Ask Cub Scouts to cut out the three circles and stack in order from number one wheel on the bottom, then number two and finally wheel three on the top.
Have Cub Scouts attach the three circles by carefully poking the brad through the middle of the three wheels.
Select a letter on the outer wheel and a number in the inner circle – this will be the key (ex. T10). Turn the inner wheel so that the number (10 in the example) lines up with the outer wheel letter (T in example). On the wheel 10 also corresponds with G in the shaded section. Don’t move the wheels now, keep them in place.
Each Cub Scout writes a secret message as letters on their paper (no numbers and no punctuation).
For each letter of the message, Cub Scouts find that character on the outer wheel, and then write down the letter that is exactly beneath it on the inner wheel until the message is complete.
Give the secret message to a buddy to decode.
To read the encrypted message, Cub Scouts will use the key from the message sender and align the wheel. For each letter of the message, find that character on the inner wheel, and write down the letter that is exactly above it on the outer wheel.

activities.title: Pigpen Code
activities.description: Send and decode a message using Pigpen Code.
supply_list: Strips of paper, one piece per Cub Scout
Pencils, one piece per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Review the Pigpen Code
In the pig pen code, the alphabet is copied into grids. Then, each part of the “pig pen” is substituted for the letter in that part. For the second grid of each type, dots are added.
Draw two tic-tac-toe type grids and two large “X”.
Start in the top left corner of the first tick-tac-toe grid and write the letter A. Then moving left to right, top to bottom, fill in the first grid with the remaining letters B through I.
In the second grid add a dot in each grid, then in the same manner as the first grid fill in the letters J through R.
In the first large X place the letters S, T, U, and V.
In the second large X place dots in each section and add the letters W, X, Y, and Z.
To create a letter, draw the section of the grid without the letter. For example, the letter A is written by drawing the top corner of the grid with one line horizontally meeting another line vertically at a 90-degree angle at the lower right corner.
Set up room to allow space for Cub Scouts to make pig pen codes.
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and ask them if they have ever sent or received an email. Explain to them:
To protect the information in the email a computer may scramble the message so if someone who wasn’t supposed to receive the email gets it, they can’t read it. This is called encryption.
Encrypting messages has been going on way before computers. When all messages were written the message would use a code and to understand the code you needed a key.
Today we will create a secret code using a method that was used before computers.
Give each Cub Scout a piece of paper and a pencil.
Ask Cub Scouts to open their Wolf handbook to the Pigpen Code.
Ask Cub Scouts to create a message using Pigpen Code.
Ask Cub Scouts to exchange their codes and decode the message they got from their buddy.

sections.heading: Directions

activities.title: Essentials Quest

One pencil for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Essentials Quest worksheet, one for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to place their three essentials on their “My Essentials” Quest grid by drawing rectangles on it. Essentials can be oriented either vertically or horizontally, but they cannot overlap or touch. Leave some space between the essentials for clarity.
Flashlight = 3 squares
First Aid Kit = 2 squares
Trail Food = 1 square
Tell Cub Scouts that on their turn, they pick a spot on their partner’s grid, like “A3” or “B7” and tell their partner their guess. The partner will say “Found” if the spot has one of the essentials or “Miss” if it doesn’t.
Instruct Cub Scouts to mark their My Guesses grid with “X” for finds and “O” for misses.
Tell Cub Scouts to keep track of their opponent’s finds and misses by marking their own grid with “X” for finds and “O” for misses.
Cub Scouts continue taking turns, targeting each other’s grids until one player has successfully found all of their opponent’s essentials. An essential is considered found when every square it occupies has been found.

activities.title: Wolf and Fox Game
activities.description: Use logic to break your opponent’s code.
supply_list: Wolf and Fox Game found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print two copies of the Wolf and Fox game.
Become familiar with how to play Wolf and Fox by reading the directions below.
During the meeting:
Split the den into two teams.
Provide a Wolf and Fox game card and a pencil for each team.
Have each team select a ​​three-digit number, write it down, keeping it a secret from the other team. All the digits must be different.
Team 1 guesses team 2’s number by writing their guess on their paper under the guesses using all different numbers.
If the matching digits are in their right positions, they are “wolves”, if it’s a correct number but in a different position, they are “foxes”.
Example: Team 1’s Secret number: 427
Team 2’s try: 124
Answer: 1 Wolf and 1 Fox. (The wolf is “2”, the fox is “4” but sssh .. don’t tell the other team which numbers are wolves or foxes.)
Team 1 marks the response on their score sheet next to the guessed number.
If the number isn’t guessed, team 2 guesses team 1’s number.
Team 2 writes down their guessed number on their sheet.
Team 1 provides the number of Wolves and Foxes for the guessed number.
Team 2 marks the number of Wolves and Foxes on their sheet next to the guessed number.
Play continues until a team guesses the number correctly.
The first team to reveal the other’s secret number wins the game.

activities.title: Shapes in Nature
