sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Select a place for your den’s nature walk.
Remind Cub Scouts to bring their Cub Scout Six Essentials.
Print Shapes in Nature Observation worksheet, one for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Before you start on the walk, ask Cub Scouts to name all the shapes they can think of.
Provide Shapes in Nature Observation Sheet and pencil to each Cub Scout
Go on a walk with Cub Scouts to see how many different shapes can be found in leaves, flowers, trees, rocks, clouds, and grass.
Ask Cub Scouts prompting questions as you walk such as what shape are dandelion flowers? Point out that some patterns in nature repeat such as fern leaves. What shape are bird’s nests? Can you find a leaf that is heart-shaped?

requirements.text: Using a package that contains a number of different colored items, discover the most common color.

activities.title: Tasty Predictions
activities.description: Predict which color of candy is most common.
supply_list: Large bag of multi-colored candy such as M&Ms, Skittles, Starbursts, etc. (If there are food sensitivity or allergy issues, substitute a non-food item such as colored paper clips)
Small container – one for each Cub Scout (approximately ½ cup)
Tasty Predictions worksheet found in Additional Resources
One pencil or pen for each Cub Scout
Piece of paper and pen or pencil to record predictions and numbers

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print the Tasty Predictions worksheet, one for each Cub Scout.
Prepare the candy by placing it into smaller containers.
Prepare the meeting space ensuring that it is clean enough for serving food.
During the meeting:
Hand out the small containers of candy, the Tasty Predictions worksheet, and the pencils to each Cub Scout.
Tell Cub Scouts not to eat it until the activity is over.
Ask Cub Scouts to write the names of each color item on the line within the circle. Then ask them to sort and count their items and to write the number they have of each in the square.
Give them time to sort and count.
Ask each Cub Scout to guess which color has the most items based on what they’ve counted. Record their predictions on a piece of paper.
Ask each Cub Scout how many of each color items they have.
After all Cub Scouts have given their prediction and number of items, add up the total number of each color item to determine which color was the most plentiful.
Announce the most plentiful and which Cub Scouts predicted that color.
Allow Cub Scouts to enjoy the tasty treats or take home for later.

requirements.text: Discover the basic components of a computer.

activities.title: Computer Components Fidget Spinner
activities.description: Learn about computer components with a fidget spinner.
supply_list: Fidget Spinner Game found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print 1 copy of the Fidget Spinner Game onto cardstock. Cut out the fidget spinner game card.
Attach fidget spinner to game card.
Familiarize yourself with the internal components of the computer(s) you will be taking apart and their function. Identify the following parts:
Keyboard
Mouse
Monitor
Central processing unit (CPU)
Hard drive
Motherboard
Power supply
Random-access memory chip (RAM)
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts into a circle.
Cub Scouts take turns spinning the fidget spinner and guess the name of the computer component they landed on.

activities.title: Computer Matching Game
activities.description: Play a computer matching game.
supply_list: Matching Game Cards found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Matching Game Cards, one set for every two Cub Scouts.
Cut out the sets of cards.
Familiarize yourself with the internal components of the computer(s) you will be taking apart and their function.
Identify the following parts:
Keyboard
mouse
Monitor
Central processing unit (CPU)
Hard drive
Motherboard
Power supply
Random-access memory chip (RAM)
During the meeting:
Divide the den into groups of two to three Cub Scouts.
Hand out a deck of cards to each group.
Ask Cub Scouts to shuffle the cards and place them face-down on the floor or table in front of them.
The goal of the game is to find the word that matches the computer component picture. The first Cub Scout selects two cards and flips them over. If the picture on the card matches the name of the computer part, the Cub Scout keeps the pair of cards.
If the two cards do not match, the cards are returned to their starting place and flipped face-down.
Players take turns until all the cards have been matched and removed.
The game ends when all the cards are matched.
The player who matches the most pairs of cards wins the game.

activities.title: Inside a Computer
activities.description: Take apart a computer.
supply_list: Computer that is ready for disposal – unplugged and battery removed. One for each Cub Scout is ideal
Two small bowls to hold screws and small miscellaneous pieces
Safety glasses for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Familiarize yourself with the internal components of the computer(s) you will be taking apart and their function. Identify the following parts:
Keyboard
Mouse
Monitor
Central processing unit (CPU)
Hard drive
Motherboard
Power supply
Random-access memory chip (RAM)
Lay out the computer, tools, safety glasses, and bowls on a table.
During the meeting:
Demonstrate how to use a screwdriver and which screwdriver is appropriate for each type of screw on the computer.
Identify a Cub Scout to remove the first screw and place the screw in a bowl.
Take turns allowing each Cub Scout the opportunity to take things off.
Lead a group discussion of each component of the computer.
Tip: Visit an electronics recycling store to find PCs and laptops.

requirements.text: Determine how to properly dispose of computer components.

activities.title: Do You Want To Build A Robot
activities.description: Cub Scouts will use old computer parts to build a robot.
supply_list: A variety of old computer parts including washers, bolts, and nuts (5-10 parts per Cub Scout)
School glue (1 bottle per 2 Cub Scouts)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Gather as many used computer parts as possible so Cub Scouts have enough materials to make their robot. Hint: Try asking in local buy nothing groups, check with thrift stores to see if they have any broken electronic items you could use.
Make a sample robot using 5-10 recycled computer parts. Use old bolts, washers, nuts, etc. to create arms, eyes and mouths (see photo in Additional Resources for ideas).
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and explain that while technology is helpful the waste ending up in the landfills is not good for the environment. It is important to recycle old electronics by returning them to stores, getting them to a recycling facility, or repurposing them. Tonight we will be repurposing them into models of robots.
Allow Cub Scouts time to explore the used parts that you have available. Instruct them to use the parts to construct their robots. Have the adults help with using a hot glue gun if needed.
After building their robots have Cub Scouts share their robots, their robot names, and what they do with each other.

activities.title: E-Waste Detectives
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn what happens to electronic waste.
supply_list: Recyclable items such as soda cans, paper, cardboard, etc.
Trash items such as empty food wrappers or broken plastic toys

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Label the 3 boxes/bins:
Regular Trash
Recycling Bin
E-Waste / Special recycling
Watch the
What Happens to Your Old Electronics
video
Research how your community handles electronic waste. Are there special drop-off events, will certain stores accept old electronics for recycling, etc.?
During the meeting:
Place all the items or printed images on a table with the labeled boxes/bins nearby.
Ask Cub Scouts, “What do you think happens to old computers, tablets, or phones when they stop working? Can we just throw them in the trash?”
Show Cub Scouts the
v
ideo.
Explain briefly: Computer parts have metals and plastics that can hurt the environment. They can also be recycled or reused if handled the right way.
Give each Cub Scout a turn to select an item (or image of an item) and place it into the correct bin.
Trash: food wrappers, broken plastic toys
Recycling: soda cans, cardboard, bottles
E-Waste: batteries, old phones, computer parts, printer ink
Share what your community does with e-waste (many towns have special drop-off events, or stores where you can drop off old electronics).

activities.title: Visit Electronics Recycling Center
activities.description: Visit an electronics recycling center and learn how they take apart items to recycle and reuse.
supply_list: Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record on each participant (youth and adult)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Identify an electronics recycling center.
Contact the recycling center and set up a time for a den visit.
Confirm the name and information of a contact of the person at the recycling center.
Ask the contact to be prepared to discuss how computers are properly disposed of at their facility.
Gather copies of the
Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record
on each participant (youth and adult)
Review Annual Health and Medical Records for any restrictions that may impact participation
During the meeting:
Bring copies of the
Visit the electronics recycling center.
Have contact give a tour and teach Cub Scouts how to dispose of computers properly. If possible, allow Cub Scouts to do a hands-on activity to help with the disposal of a computer.
Encourage Cub Scouts to politely listen and ask questions.
Thank the host.
After the meeting:
Send a thank you note to the recycling center.

requirements.text: Using a digital device application of your choice, create a story that you can share with others.

activities.title: Digital Story Building
activities.description: Use a computer-based program such as PowerPoint or Google Slides to create a digital story using pictures.
supply_list: Computer or smart device, preferably 1 for every 2 Cub Scouts

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Set up meeting space with room for the Cub Scouts to gather in buddy groups and set up the computers or smart devices.
During the meeting:
Ask the Cub Scouts to buddy up.
Give each buddy group 3 pieces of paper.
Each set of buddies is to create a story with pictures. They can draw the story out on paper.
With an adult assigned to each set of buddies, Cub Scouts are to build their story on a computer or smart device.
Have Cub Scouts share their story with the den.
Tip: There are several websites that provide help with building digital stories for free.

requirements.text: With your parent or legal guardian, set up a policy for safely using digital devices.

activities.title: Digital Safety Pledge
activities.description: Cub Scouts create digital usage contract with their parent or legal guardian .
supply_list: Digital Safety Pledge found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Digital Safety Pledge, one for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to sit down with their parent or legal guardian.
Hand out the Digital Safety Pledge to each Cub Scout.
Cub Scouts and adults review the Digital Safety Pledge together. The Cub Scouts initials each line.
Cub Scouts then work with their parent or legal guardian to create at least one rule for each of the following areas
What devices are you allowed to use?
What applications or programs are you allowed to use?
What times are you allowed to use them?
With whom are you allowed to communicate using your devices?
Both Cub Scout and adult sign.

requirements.text: Explore what it is to have a physical disability.

activities.title: Chair Ball
activities.description: Cub Scouts shoot baskets from a sitting position.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up the meeting space in a large open area.
If using a basketball hoop, set the hoop height to 6 to 7 feet. If using a basket, place on top of something that is approximately 6 to 7 feet in height.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a physical disability. Examples of physical disabilities are people in wheelchairs because their legs do not work. Because of the physical disability, doing simple
tasks may
be difficult.
Tell Cub Scouts they are going to try to shoot baskets from a chair to help them understand physical disabilities.
Explain to Cub Scouts that they’ll play a game of “CUBS” while sitting in a chair.
Line up Cub Scouts.
Set up a chair from which Cub Scouts will sit and shoot the ball into the basket.
If a Cub Scout makes the shot, they are awarded a letter in “CUBS.”
Each time a Cub Scout makes a shot, they are awarded a letter.
Once all Cub Scouts have had a chance from the first location, move the chair to another location and have all Cub Scouts shoot the ball into the basket from the new location.
Continue until someone has completed spelling CUBS.

activities.title: Draw a Picture
activities.description: Cub Scouts will use tongs to draw a picture of their family.
supply_list: Kitchen tongs for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a physical disability. Examples of physical disabilities are people in wheelchairs because their legs do not work, or someone may be missing an arm. Because of a physical disability, doing simple tasks may be difficult.
Tell Cub Scouts they are going to try to draw a picture of their family with tongs to help them understand physical disabilities.
Hand out tongs, crayons or markers, and paper to Cub Scouts.
Have Cub Scouts use the tongs to draw a picture of their family.
When Cub Scouts are finished, ask them the following questions:
Was it hard to draw a picture?
What other things would be hard if we couldn’t use our hands properly?

activities.title: Mitten Hands
activities.description: Cub Scouts wear oversized gloves to complete simple tasks.
supply_list: Large gloves or mittens, winter gloves, work gloves, or oven mitts, 1 pair per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Collect supplies.
Spread coins, crayons, paper, and paracord on a tabletop.
During the meeting:
Hand out gloves to Cub Scouts and ask them to put them on.
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a physical disability. Examples of physical disabilities are people in wheelchairs because their legs do not work, or someone may be missing an arm. Because of the physical disability, doing simple
tasks may
be difficult.
Tell Cub Scouts they are going to try to do some simple tasks while wearing gloves or mittens to help them understand physical disabilities.
Have Cub Scouts take turns doing the following activities with their gloves or mittens on:
Pick up coins
Color a picture with the crayons and paper
Tie a knot with the paracord
After Cub Scouts have finished, ask them how they felt while trying to pick up the coins, color a picture and tying a knot while wearing gloves.

requirements.text: Explore what it is to have a visual impairment.

activities.title: Masked Artist
activities.description: Cub Scouts draw a picture then try to draw it again with their eyes covered.
supply_list: Paper, two sheets for each Cub Scout
Eye covering, one set for each buddy group

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up the meeting table with an area for Cub Scouts to draw.
During the meeting:
Provide each Cub Scout with two sheets of paper and crayons.
Ask Cub Scouts to draw a picture of their home.
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a visual disability
;
they may have trouble seeing or may not be able to see at all. Ask Cub Scouts what they would do
if they were
drawing a picture and could not see what they were drawing.
How would they decide the color to use when drawing if they could not see the color?
How would they know how big to draw their home?
How would they know where to put the front door?
How would they know when they reached the edge of the paper?
How would they know if the shape they draw is the shape of their house?
Have Cub Scouts buddy up. Provide eye covering to each buddy group. Ask for one buddy to be first to cover their eyes.
Have Cub Scout with their eyes covered draw the same picture of their home. The buddy may provide advice or guidance when drawing when asked.
Once Cub Scout with their eyes covered is done, have Cub Scouts switch.
Ask the Cub Scouts to compare the 2 drawings.
How are the drawings the same?
How are the drawings different?
Which drawing was easier?
How did your buddy help you?

activities.title: Service Dog Visit
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about service dogs.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Find a local group of service dog handlers for the visually impaired.
Invite the handler and service dog to an upcoming den meeting.
Let the families know that a handler and service dog will be attending the meeting.
Ask Cub Scouts to come up with questions to ask the handler.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a visual disability, they may have trouble seeing or may not be able to see at all.
Tell Cub Scouts that some visually impaired people have service dogs to help them.
Ask handlers to share how service dogs help people that are visually impaired.
Encourage Cub Scouts to ask questions about service dogs.
After the meeting:
Write a thank you note to the service dog handler.

activities.title: Where is the ball?
activities.description: Cub Scouts toss a Nerf™ ball back and forth learning depth perception .
supply_list: Nerf™ ball, 1 for every 2 Cub Scouts
Eye patch for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up meeting space with enough room for Cub Scouts to toss the ball back and forth between buddies.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a visual disability
;
they may have trouble seeing or may not be able to see at all.
Have Cub Scouts line up and look into the distance at an object. Ask them to share what they see.
Have Cub Scouts cover their right eye. Did the object move or did it remain in the same place?
Do the same covering the left eye. Did the object move or did it remain in the same place?
Have Cub Scouts buddy up. Give each set of buddies a ball.
Have
Cub Scouts
toss the ball back and forth 10 times.
Hand out eye patches and ask Cub Scout to cover up their right eye.
Cub Scouts stand 5 feet apart and throw the
Nerf™
ball back and forth 10 times.
Stop and ask
,
“W
as it the same, easier, or harder to catch the
ball.
Repeat the exercise with the left eye covered. How was this different than when the right eye was covered?

requirements.text: Explore what it is to have a hearing loss.

activities.title: “Hello, my name is”
activities.description: Use American Sign Language to communicate a simple sentence that includes your name.
supply_list: American Sign Language Alphabet worksheet found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print one copy of American Sign Language Alphabet worksheet for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a hearing loss
;
they may have trouble hearing or may not be able to hear at all. Another method of communicating is by using sign language.
Have the Cub Scouts buddy up.
Give each Cub Scout a copy of the American Sign Language Alphabet worksheet.
Ask Cub Scouts to practice signing “Hello, my name is” and their name to their buddy.

activities.title: Scout Law
activities.description: Cub Scouts try to speak to their buddy with a mouthful of marshmallows.
supply_list: Scout Law cards found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print and cut out Scout Law cards.
Fold the cards and place them in a large bowl.
During the meeting:
Sit Cub Scouts in a circle.
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a hearing loss; they may have trouble hearing or may not be able to hear at all. It is difficult to speak clearly when you are unable to hear clearly. Ask Cub Scouts how they would learn to talk if they could not hear.
Give one Cub Scout enough marshmallows to fill their mouth, 4 to 6. Ask them to draw a card from the bowl.
Ask Cub Scout to put the marshmallows in their mouth and read the Scout Law on the card. (You may help those who have difficulty reading.)
The other Cub Scouts try to guess what is being said.
Repeat for each Cub Scout.
Ask Cub Scouts the following:
Did you understand what Cub Scouts were saying when they had marshmallows in their mouths?
How would you make the message clearer?
What would be another way to communicate?

activities.title: Tele-What?
activities.description: Cub Scouts play “telephone” while ears are covered.
supply_list: Ear coverings, one set per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a hearing loss
;
they may have trouble hearing or may not be able to hear at all. Ask Cub Scouts how they would talk on the phone if they could not hear.
Tell Cub Scouts they’re going to play the “telephone game.” The game is to whisper a message from one person to another, with the goal of seeing how much the message changes as it gets passed along.
Have Cub Scouts sit in a circle.
Ask Cub Scouts to put on their ear coverings.
Give the first Cub Scout a message. It’s most fun if it’s a bit quirky like “purple elephants dance on the moon.”
Have the first Cub Scout whisper it to the person on their right. Make sure it’s quiet enough so that others can’t hear. The message should only be whispered once.
Tell Cub Scout who received the message to whisper it to the person on their right, and this continues around the circle. Each person should only whisper the message they heard to the person next to them.
Tell Cub Scouts they should not repeat the message if asked, nor should they clarify or ask for repetitions if they didn’t hear it correctly. They must do their best to pass on the message as they understood it.
After the message has been whispered around the entire circle, the last Cub Scout in the group announces what they heard to the entire group.
Questions to ask:
Did the message change?
Was it hard to hear the message being whispered?
How would you make the message clearer?
What would be another way to communicate the message without speaking louder?

requirements.text: Explore barriers to getting around.

activities.title: Accessibility Walk Around
activities.description: Cub Scouts will take a walk around your meeting space to identify accommodations and lack of accommodations for people with disabilities.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a physical disability. Examples of physical disabilities are people in wheelchairs because their legs do not work. Because of a physical disability, it is difficult to get around. This is especially true if a building’s design isn’t accessible.
Take Cub Scouts on a walk around their meeting space to discuss disability accommodations. Start in the parking lot.
Ask Cub Scouts the following questions:
Are there specific handicap parking spots?
Can you find any doors that have automatic openers?
Do you think a wheelchair could get into the building? What would prevent this?
Are there stairs you need to walk up to get into the building? If so, are there ramps or elevators that would help?
Are the doorways wide enough to accommodate a wheelchair?
What do the thresholds look like? Are they raised? Can a wheelchair roll over them easily?
Are the bathroom doors wide enough to accommodate a wheelchair? Are there handicap accessible stalls that are big enough for a wheelchair?
Are there other things about your meeting space that would make it difficult for someone in a wheelchair to get around?

activities.title: Obstacle Course
activities.description: Cub Scouts will have to traverse an obstacle course using crutches.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Find a park that contains sidewalks, ramps, and open green areas.
Communicate the location to the guardians and when the meeting starts.
Gather materials needed.
Create an obstacle course using sidewalks, ramps, cones, and towels for Cub Scouts to traverse using the crutches. The course shouldn’t be longer than 25 feet.
During the meeting:
Explain the goal of the meeting.
Show Cub Scouts how to properly adjust and use the crutches.
Explain to Cub Scouts they will be using the crutches to traverse the obstacle course. Cub Scouts are to keep at least one foot off the ground during the entire time when they are in the obstacle course.
Allow each Cub Scout to try the obstacle course at least once.
Once all Cub Scouts have completed the obstacle course ask the following questions:
What was the hardest part of moving through the obstacle course with crutches?
(Did anything surprise you about how difficult it was?)
How was using crutches different from walking or running the way you normally do?
What obstacles in the course would be extra challenging for someone who uses crutches every day?
What could we change about the obstacle course to make it easier or safer for someone using crutches?
How can we be helpful or kind to someone at school or on the playground who uses crutches or has a mobility challenge?
After the meeting:
Pick up materials and Leave No Trace.

activities.title: Out of Reach
activities.description: Cub Scouts sit on chairs to explore barriers to getting around.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Place the scissors on one side of a table. Put two or three chairs on the opposite side of the table.
Place the pencils on the floor near a wall where they won’t be stepped on. Put a chair next to them.
Place the Wolf handbook on a wall shelf. Put a chair below and facing the shelf.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that some people have a physical disability. Examples of physical disabilities are people in wheelchairs because their legs do not work. Because of the physical disability, it is difficult to get around and to retrieve items they may need.
Explain to Cub Scouts that they are going to sit in a chair and try to reach various objects they may need.
Have Cub Scouts take turns sitting in one of the chairs at the table. Ask them to pick up a pair of scissors without standing or rising up out of the chair.
Next, have Cub Scouts take turns sitting in the chair by the pencils. Ask them to pick up a pencil off the floor without moving off the chair.
Have Cub Scouts take turns sitting in the chair by the shelf. Ask them to retrieve the Wolf handbook off the shelf without standing or raising up out of the chair.
When Cub Scouts have tried all the tasks, have them sit in chairs and then ask the following questions:
Was it hard to reach the items sitting down?
Look around the room. What other things would be hard to retrieve if you must stay seated?
What can we do to make it easier to reach the things we need?

requirements.text: Play a dinosaur game that shows what you know about them.

activities.title: Dino Detective
activities.description: Play a dinosaur identification game.
supply_list: Dino Cards found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print and cut out 1 set of Dino Cards on cardstock. Put the picture and the fun facts together in the deck. The picture will be used to the Cub Scouts. The fun facts are for you.
Review the cards and become familiar with the different types of dinosaurs.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts with their Wolf handbooks and let them know for this activity they can use their handbook and the Digging in the Past Adventure chapter.
Explain to Cub Scouts that they are going to guess the names of dinosaurs based on a picture and some clues.
Show pictures of the dinosaurs and ask Cub Scouts to guess the name of the dinosaur.
If Cub Scouts have trouble guessing based on the picture, provide clues, based on the fun facts, about the dinosaurs without revealing the name.

activities.title: Dino Match
activities.description: Play a dinosaur matching game.
supply_list: Dino Cards found in Additional Resources
Each Cub Scout will need their Cub Scout Wolf handbook

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print and cut out 1 set of Dino Cards on cardstock.
Review the cards and become familiar with the different types of dinosaurs.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts with their Wolf handbooks and let them know for this activity they can use their handbook and the Digging in the Past Adventure chapter.
Divide the Cub Scouts into two groups.
Give one group the cards with dinosaur photos.
Provide the other group with the dinosaur cards with the fun facts.
Tell Cub Scouts to work together and match the photos with the fun facts.

activities.title: Dino Trivia
activities.description: Play a dinosaur trivia game.
supply_list: Dino Cards found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print and cut out 1 set of Dino Cards on cardstock.
Separate the photos from the fun facts. Review the cards and become familiar with the different types of dinosaurs.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts with their Wolf handbooks and let them know for this activity they can use their handbook and the Digging in the Past Adventure chapter.
Lay out pictures of three different dinosaurs.
Select one of the dinosaurs and read the fun facts. Have Cub Scouts guess which dinosaur you are describing. Replace the dinosaur photo that matches the fun facts with another photo.
Continue until all the fun facts cards have been used.
Tip: Use plastic dinosaurs instead of the cards.

requirements.text: Create an imaginary dinosaur. Share with your den or family its name, what it eats, its size, and where it lives.

activities.title: Dino Clay Creations
activities.description: Make a dinosaur out of clay.
supply_list: Sculpting tools such as a craft knife, toothpick, and clay shaping tools a set for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Prepare your workspace. Cover your work surface with a plastic tablecloth or parchment paper to prevent the clay from sticking.
During the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to sculpt a basic dinosaur shape by shaping the clay into the rough outline of a dinosaur.
Ask Cub Scouts to create a basic body shape and then add limbs, head, tail, and other details as needed.
Encourage Cub Scouts to use sculpting tools to add details like scales, facial features, claws, and teeth. They can reference images to get a sense of the dinosaur’s anatomy.
Suggest that Cub Scouts use tools to smooth out the surface and refine the shape. They can also use a damp cloth or sponge to achieve a smoother texture.
Ask Cub Scouts to share their dinosaurs with the den. Encourage Cub Scouts to name their dinosaur and tell where it lived and what it ate.

activities.title: Dino Imagination
activities.description: Create custom dinosaurs by assembling cutout body parts.
supply_list: Dino Imagination worksheet found in Additional Resources
Scissors, one pair for each Cub Scout
Glue or glue stick for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Dino Imagination on cardstock, one for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to cut the dinosaur images into different body parts, such as heads, tails, bodies, legs, and arms along their outlines.
Ask Cub Scouts to select body parts and assemble them on the background sheet to create their unique dinosaur designs. Cub Scouts can mix and match different parts to come up with imaginative combinations.
Encourage Cub Scouts to use markers, colored pencils, or crayons to add details and personalize their dinosaurs. They can draw scales, patterns, or features on their creations.
Ask Cub Scouts to share their dinosaur creations with the group. This is an opportunity for them to explain their designs and discuss what makes their dinosaurs unique.

activities.title: Recycled Reptiles
activities.description: Create an imaginary dinosaur out of recycled materials.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to collect recycled materials that they could use to build a dinosaur to bring to the meeting.
Set up a workspace on a table. Cover the table with a plastic tablecloth.
During the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to use their imagination and the supplies on the workspace to build a dinosaur.
Have Cub Scouts build their dinosaur using recycled materials.
Encourage Cub Scouts to share their dinosaurs with the den. Ask Cub Scouts to name their dinosaur and tell where it lived and what it ate.

requirements.text: Be a paleontologist and dig through a dinosaur dig.

activities.title: Dino Dig
activities.description: Make a dinosaur dig.
supply_list: 3 cups corn starch for each Cub Scout
1 ½ cups water for each Cub Scout plus ½ cup additional water to correct texture if needed
1 mixing bowl for each Cub Scout
Dinosaur toys or fossil skeletons, several for each Cub Scout
1 container such as a deep-dish style pie plate for each Cub Scout
Digging equipment such as a toothbrush, paintbrush, toothpick, and a lightweight hammer for each Cub Scout
Safety glasses for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
This Activity will take two meetings to complete.
Before the meeting:
Gather all materials and lay out items on a newspaper-covered work surface.
During the first meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to combine the 3 cups cornstarch and 1 ½ cups water together in a big bowl to make oobleck. If the mixture is too watery, add more cornstarch. The consistency should feel like quicksand, when you apply force, it becomes thicker.
Have Cub Scouts pour the mixture into the container. Tell them to bury the dinosaurs in the mixture so that you can’t see them. The bones may not want to stay buried, so they may have to push them back down into the mixture. It’s OK if a couple of them are poking out of the mixture, but have Cub Scouts make sure that most of them are totally submerged in the oobleck.
Set the containers aside to dry in a place where they can stay until the next den meeting.
During the second meeting:
Cover your workspace with newspaper.
Bring containers and put them down on top of the newspaper. This is going to get messy. Corn starch dust will be everywhere.
For safety, Cub Scouts must wear safety glasses while working in case any pieces or dust go flying.
Ask Cub Scouts to carefully turn the container upside down onto the work surface. Remove the container, and the dig should slide right out.
The dig may crumble a bit. If it doesn’t, Cub Scouts can use the hammer and very gently tap on it to start breaking it up.
Tell Cub Scouts to brush and dig their way through the dinosaur dig. When they see a bone, they should gently excavate around it, removing the cornstarch debris with a brush. Soon, they’ll find their dinosaur bones!
Tip: Consider holding the second meeting outside so that cleanup will be easier.

activities.title: Dino Egg Dig
activities.description: Cub Scouts will make dinosaur eggs.
supply_list: Mixing bowl for each Cub Scout

Assorted fossils such as shark teeth, sea clam fossil, trilobite, ichthyodont, ammolite, copal amber, graptolite, rhynchonellida, conchostracan, tower corals, spirifer. These can be found for purchase online.
1 cup used coffee grounds per egg for each Cub Scout
1 cup flour per egg for each Cub Scout
1/2 cup salt per egg for each Cub Scout
1/4 cup sand per egg for each Cub Scout
3/4 cup water per egg for each Cub Scout
Digging equipment such a toothbrush, paintbrush, toothpick, and a lightweight hammer for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Gather all materials and lay out items on a newspaper-covered work surface for each Cub Scout
Preheat oven to 150*
During the meeting:
Tell Cub Scouts to mix coffee grounds, flour, salt, and sand together, and add 1/4 cup water at a time.
Once mixed, have Cub Scouts flatten a chunk of dough out in their hand and place fossils inside to later dig out and find. Have them roll the rest of the dough over the toy to form an egg or rock.
Bake in the oven at 150*F for about 20-30 minutes. Allow the eggs to cool before handling.
Place newspaper down for each Cub Scout. This is going to get messy.
The egg may crumble a bit. If it doesn’t, have Cub Scouts use the hammer and very gently tap on it to start breaking it up.
Encourage Cub Scouts to dig their way to the dinosaur toys.
TIP: While the dino egg is baking complete other requirements for this or other Adventures.

activities.title: Fossil Expedition
activities.description: Visit a location where fossils can be found.
supply_list: Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record on each participant (youth and adult)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Choose a fossil site. Research and choose a location where fossils are known to be found such as national or state parks, nature reserves, or museums with fossil exhibits. This may include a beach that has seashells. Ensure the site is safe and suitable for Cub Scouts.
Obtain permissions. Contact the site authorities or landowners to obtain any necessary permissions for your visit. This is especially important if you plan to disturb the fossils in any way.
If possible, arrange for a guided tour or a local expert to explain the geological history of the site and provide insights into the fossils found there.
Gather copies of the
Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record
on each participant (youth and adult)
Review Annual Health and Medical Records for any restrictions that may impact participation
During the meeting:
Bring copies of the
Brief Cub Scouts on safety rules, including staying with the group, wearing appropriate clothing and footwear, and watching out for hazards like steep cliffs or slippery rocks.
Have Cub Scouts explore and search for fossils. Encourage Cub Scouts to handle fossils gently and respect the site. Tell Cub Scouts that they should leave the fossil instead of taking it home.
Encourage Cub Scouts to document their findings. This can be through sketches, photographs, or written descriptions in their journals. It’s a great way to create lasting memories.
At the end of the visit, gather the Cub Scouts for a discussion. Have Cub Scouts share their favorite discoveries and what they learned. Discuss the importance of preserving such sites.

requirements.text: Build a fossil layer.

activities.title: Dig in and Devour
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about fossil layers by making edible fossil layers.
supply_list: 8 to 10 oz. clear plastic cup for each Cub Scout
3.25 oz. of prepared flavored gelatin one for every two Cub Scouts
4 animal crackers for each Cub Scout
3.25 oz. of prepared pudding for each Cub Scout
1 graham cracker for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Gather all ingredients.
Place 1.625 ounces of prepared flavored gelatin into each of the clear plastic cups.
Place 2 animal crackers in the flavored gelatin so the animal crackers will be soft by the end of the activity.
Become familiar with how fossils are formed.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and share with them that this activity is to demonstrate how fossils are formed. When something like animal bones is covered, they can turn into fossils but not all the time. Sometimes an object gets wet and starts to dissolve but when this happens it will not turn into a fossil. Sometimes rock or other hard things will form around it and keep it dry and over time it may turn into a fossil.
Tell Cub Scouts to scoop crushed graham crackers onto the flavored gelatin layer.
Have Cub Scouts place an animal cracker on the layer.
Ask Cub Scouts to scoop more graham crackers on top, making sure to cover the animal cracker.
Tell Cub Scouts to scoop pudding onto the graham crackers.
Ask Cub Scouts to scoop more pudding.
Encourage Cub Scouts to eat their fossil layer dessert. Ask them if they notice that some of the crackers stay crunchy and some are soft. Tell them that this is because some of the crackers will absorb moisture from their surroundings layers and some will not. Each of the materials surrounding the animal crackers affects them in a different way.

activities.title: Dino Canvas
activities.description: Draw fossil layers and add in dinosaurs.
supply_list: Drawing paper for each Cub Scout
Colored pencils for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up meeting space for Cub Scouts to draw.
Become familiar with fossil layers and
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts draw three different layers of the ground where fossils are found, drawing horizontal layers to represent different geological strata.
Encourage Cub Scouts to color each layer using colored pencils. Darker for the deeper parts and lighter for the top layer with a thin layer of green at the top.
Suggest Cub Scouts create texture for each layer by adding lines or small shapes to represent different types of sediment or rocks.
Tell Cub Scouts that this first layer, darkest, is the oldest fossil layer. The oldest fossils are fossils that were formed from things that lived in the sea. To represent this have them draw seashells in this layer.
Next tell the Cub Scouts the second layer is where we will find dinosaurs. To represent this have them draw a dinosaur in this layer.
Next tell the Cub Scouts that the next layer, the lightest color, will have things that are not as old, and this is where we will find fossils or artifacts from humans. To represent this have them draw an arrowhead in this layer.
Inform Cub Scouts that paleontologists use fossil layers to help determine how old a fossil may be and to help them know how far they must dig to find fossils.
Ask Cub Scouts to share their drawings with the den.

activities.title: Fossil Dough Discovery
activities.description: Cub Scouts build fossil layers with play dough.
supply_list: 2 ounces of Three different colors of play dough for a total of 6 oz. for each Cub Scout
Small rolling pin for each Cub Scout
Small arrowhead (plastic or real) at least one per Cub Scout
Small plastic dinosaurs at least one per Cub Scout
Small shell at least one per Cub Scout
Piece of paper for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up the meeting space and cover the table or workspace with a plastic tablecloth.
Set out all the supplies.
During the meeting:
Tell Cub Scouts that they’re going to make layers of the earth where fossils are found using play dough.
Instruct Cub Scouts to collect their supplies.
Have Cub Scouts take one color of playdough and roll it out flat into a rectangle.
Tell Cub Scouts that this first layer will be the oldest fossil layer. The oldest fossils are fossils that were formed from things that lived in the sea. To represent this place the seashells in this layer.
Next tell the Cub Scouts the second layer is where we will find dinosaurs. To represent this have them place the dinosaurs in this layer.
Next tell the Cub Scouts that the next layer will have things that are not as old, and this is where we will find fossils or artifacts from humans. To represent this have them place the arrowhead in this layer.
Inform Cub Scouts that paleontologists use fossil layers to help determine how old a fossil may be and to help them know how far they must dig to find fossils they are looking for.

requirements.text: Using a map, locate where you live.

activities.title: Google Maps Adventure
activities.description: Cub Scouts use Google Maps to show where they live.
supply_list: Computer or tablet with internet access.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Contact Cub Scouts’ parents or legal guardians and ask that they write down their address for their Cub Scout to bring to the next meeting or use Scoutbook to identify each Cub Scouts address.
During the meeting:
Tell the Cub Scouts that we use maps to help us find where we are, where we need to go, and how to get there. The first step is knowing where you are. Today we are going to identify on a map where you live.
Navigate to
Google Maps
on the computer or tablet.
Have Cub Scouts gather around the computer or tablet.
Ask each Cub Scout in turn to type their address into the Google Maps search bar.
Ask questions:
What do you see on the map near your home?
Does anything look like it does not belong on a map?
Can you find your school?

activities.title: Home Sweet Map
activities.description: Cub Scouts find and show their town on a map.
supply_list: A map of your community centered on your den meeting location, one copy for each Cub Scout
Pencil or pen for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Using an app with mapping capabilities use your meeting location as a starting point.
Zoom out of the map to encompass your community and capture the neighborhoods that the members of your den live in.
Use Scoutbook to identify where the members of your den live.
Print a copy for each Cub Scout of the map.
During the meeting:
Tell the Cub Scouts that we use maps to help us find where we are, where we need to go, and how to get there. The first step is knowing where you are. Today we are going to identify on a map where you live.
Pass out the maps and pencils or pens to each Cub Scout.
Have Cub Scouts look at the map and ask if anyone can identify a street, building, or other landmark on the map. Work to guide Cub Scouts to identify common landmarks and major intersections. Guide Cub Scouts to help them find their neighborhood and then their house.
Ask Cub Scouts to locate where they live and circle it.
Work with the Cub Scouts to locate where they go to school and circle it.
Work with the Cub Scouts to locate where the pack meetings are held.

requirements.text: Draw a map for a friend to locate your home or school. Create a key for the map.

activities.title: Let’s Go Home
activities.description: Cub Scouts draw a map to their house.
supply_list: 8 ½”x11” paper, at least one sheet for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts buddy up.
Explain to Cub Scouts that they are going to draw a map to get from their house to their school .
Have each Cub Scout create a symbol for their house and a symbol for their school. This is the legend. Put the symbol in a box in the lower right corner of the paper.
Have them think about the buildings they might see on their way to their school. Think about grocery stores and libraries. Create a symbol for each building and put it in the legend.
Each Cub Scout should then draw a map from their house to their school using the symbols (keys) in their legend to mark buildings and other landmarks.
Tip: This activity can be combined with Requirement 3 Make a Compass Rose activity.

requirements.text: Find the directions north, east, south, and west and the compass rose on a map.

activities.title: Make a Compass Rose
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about directions by making a paper plate compass rose.
supply_list: Make a Compass Rose found in Additional Resources
One 9” paper plate for each Cub Scout
One glue stick for every two Cub Scouts
One pair of scissors for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Make a Compass Rose, one for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Explain to the Cub Scouts that when we look at a map, we need to have a way to tell what direction the top of the map is pointing to. Is the map pointing north, south, east, or west? Maps traditionally are drawn with the top of the map pointing to north. Maps use what is called a compass rose to confirm what direction north is on the map.
Knowing what direction north is on a map allows us to position the map in real life in that direction, this is called orienting the map. Today most digital maps will do this as an option, we can either have the map stay pointing north or the have the map stay oriented to the direction that you are moving.
Pass out compass rose printable and paper plate to each Cub Scout.
Have Cub Scouts color the parts of the compass rose and cut them out.
Ask Cub Scouts to glue the parts to their paper plate.
Tell Cub Scouts to use their Wolf handbook as a reference and write the directions on the compass rose.

Tell the Cub Scouts to use the compass rose on the bottom of the question sheet and the campsite map to answer the questions.

activities.title: Create a Sundial
activities.description: Cub Scouts make a sundial.
supply_list: Paper plate for each Cub Scout
Bendy straw for each Cub Scout
Sharpened pencil for each Cub Scout
​ ​ ​ Compass, used both at the meeting and at home to finish project

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts’ parent or legal guardian to bring a compass to the meeting if they have one.
During the meeting:
Tell Cub Scouts that they’ll be making a sundial.
Pass out supplies.
Ask Cub Scouts to carefully poke a hole through the center of the plate using the pencil.
Instruct Cub Scouts to push the straw through the hole and tape the short end underneath to hold it in place.
Explain to Cub Scouts that they’ll need to do part of this activity over a day’s time at home, but that they’ll be practicing what to do.
Tell Cub Scouts to place their sundial on the floor. Explain that when they’re home, they’ll put their sundial in a sunny area. They may need to find rocks to hold their sundial down.
Ask Cub Scouts to use their compass to find north. Next, they need to tilt the straw slightly north. Explain that when they do this at home, the tilted straw will cast a slightly longer shadow.
When Cub Scouts are at home, they will mark the shadow with the time.
Every hour, Cub Scouts will check their sundial and will mark the shadow with the time.
Tip: This is a good activity to do during a pack campout.

activities.title: Simon Says Never Eat Soggy Waffles
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn directions by playing a Simon Says using a compass.
supply_list: Four pieces of paper, labeled North, South, East, and West

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Make signs for north, south, east, and west.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that they’re going to play Simon Says Never Eat Soggy Waffles.
Stand in the center of the room with the compass and ask Cub Scouts to gather around.
Demonstrate how to use the compass. Discuss which wall is north, south, east, and west. Have a Cub Scout take each of the signs and tape it to the appropriate wall.
Ask Cub Scouts to line up, side by side.
Tell Cub Scouts that when they hear “Simon Says” and a direction, they are to turn and face that wall. For example, after “Simon Says East,” Cub Scouts should turn and face the east wall.
Proceed with calling out directions with and without “Simon Says.”
Cub Scouts who don’t face the correct wall at the correct time are out.
Continue playing until there is only one player left.

activities.description: Cub Scouts practice using a map and compass while taking a walk in their neighborhood.

If you choose to do this activity away from your regular meeting location you will need a Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record on each participant (youth and adult)
Compasses, enough for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Decide on a route for a short walk in a local neighborhood.
Mark several points on the map where Cub Scouts can safely stop to orient themselves.
Ensure the walk has all four directions for the Cub Scouts to walk: north, south, east, and west.
Make copies of the map with the marks.
Notify Cub Scouts’ parents or legal guardians about the walk location and where to meet.
If this activity is done away from your regular meeting location:
Gather copies of the
Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record
on each participant (youth and adult)
Review Annual Health and Medical Records for any restrictions that may impact participation
During the meeting:
If this activity is away from your regular meeting location, bring copies of the
Tell Cub Scouts that the den is going on a walk using a map and a compass. Explain that you will be “north.”
Tell Cub Scouts that whenever they get to a point that is marked on their map, everyone will stop, and you will be facing a point north.
Explain that Cub Scouts will orient themselves using their compass. They can do this by standing still and turning their compass until the north point is facing the same direction as the leader.
Tell Cub Scouts to call out the direction they’re facing. Ask the other adults on the walk to confirm that their answer is correct.
