activities.description: Cub Scouts build a bat house.
supply_list: Bat House instructions found in Additional Resources
Power drill. Power drills may only be used by adults
Drill bits ½-inch drill bit for vent holes 3/32-inch drill bit for screw pilot holes
One quart of exterior water-based primer
Two quarts of exterior black or gray water-based paint
½-by-30-by-36-inch sheet of exterior plywood (not pressure treated)
½-by-26-by-36-inch sheet of exterior plywood (not pressure treated)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print Bat House instructions, one for each Cub Scout.
Purchase or gather necessary tools and materials based on the list from requirement 4. This may include contacting families to bring tools.
Cut the boards to size and sand the edges smooth.
Pre-drill pilot holes for nails or screws.
Set up meeting space for each Cub Scout to have a designated work area with plenty of room to move about and a safe distance away from one another.
During the meeting:
Review appropriate tool safety with Cub Scouts.
Distribute Bat House instructions.
To build the bat house:
Cut out all the bat house boards.
Use your pocketknife to scribe shallow grooves (less than 1⁄16 inch deep) across the inside of the back sheet of plywood, about ¼- to ½-inch apart. The grooves help bats grip the plywood.
Run a bead of caulk onto the contact surfaces of the interior frame and spacer blocks, and then screw them in place on the back of the front panel. All surfaces that are in contact with each other should be caulked before screwing them together. Caulking acts as a gasket, sealing out water.
Drill ½-inch vent holes in the front panel. In cold climates, you need only three or four vent holes.
Stain the interior of the bat house, including the plywood, frame, and spacer blocks. Allow the stain to dry.
Caulk and screw the back panel to the frame and spacer blocks. Be sure to drill pilot holes to avoid splitting.
Caulk and screw on the roof. A drop of caulking in each screw pilot hole will help waterproof the bat house and keep the inside dry.
. Paint the exterior with primer, then apply two coats of paint. Use black paint for colder climates and gray paint for warmer climates. Attach the bat house to a building or other structure. Face it south or east, about 10- to 12-feet off the ground.
After the meeting:
Find a place to hang the bat house.

activities.description: Cub Scouts build a candy dispenser.

Dowel or peg about ¼ inch in diameter, 4 inches long
Dowel or peg about ¼ inch in diameter, 2 inches long
A clean quart or pint canning jar with metal ring

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:

To build the candy dispenser:
Cut all the boards to size and sand smooth.
Glue and screw the base onto the sides.
Pencil an X from corner to corner on the top board.
Drill a ⅞-inch hole through the center of the top board.
Glue and screw the top board onto the sides and base. Sand the slide until it moves smoothly in the square hole in the center of the dispenser.
Drill a hole ¾ inch from the front of the slide. This is for the 4-inch peg or dowel. Drill a hole ½ inch from the back of the slide. This is for the 2-inch peg or dowel. Glue the 4-inch peg or dowel in the front hole on the slide.
Push the slide into place until it stops at the 4-inch peg. Draw a circle through the ⅞ -inch hole on the top board onto the slide.
Drill a ⅞ -inch hole ⅜ inch deep into the slide as shown.
Bevel the ⅞ -inch slide hole with the pocketknife and sand smooth.
Drill and nail the jar ring onto the top board.
Push the slide into place. When the slide is pushed in all the way, the hole in the top and the hole in the slide should line up. Glue the 2-inch peg or dowel onto the back of the slide.
Fill the jar with candy, screw it onto the ring and your dispenser is complete.

activities.title: Paddling Safely Rule Game
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn the safety rules to follow when using a paddle craft.
supply_list: Paddling Safely Rules Game found in Additional Resources
Access to Paddling Safely Rules Key found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Review safety rules when using a paddle craft.
Personal Health Review
—Completing the Scouting America Annual Health and Medical Record will be needed. Are there any restrictions on the part of the participant?
Swimming Ability
—Complete an annual swim test. Do you know what that is?
Life Jackets
—Properly fitted U.S. Coast Guard–approved life jackets are worn by everyone engaged in boating activities.
Buddy System
—Make sure each member is accounted for, especially when in the water.
Skill Proficiency
—Everyone in an activity afloat must have sufficient knowledge and skill to participate safely.
Planning
—Check for weather and contingencies as needed prior to your activity.
Equipment
—All craft must be suitable for the activity, be seaworthy, and be capable of floating if capsized.
Discipline
—Remember that rules are only effective when they are followed.
Print a single copy of the Paddling Safely Rules Game cards. Cut into 16 individual cards, 8 topic cards and 8 rule cards.
Mix up the topic cards and lay flat on a tabletop, print side down. Mix up the rule cards and lay flat on a tabletop in a separate layout.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts the safety rules to follow when safely using a paddle craft.
Explain to Cub Scouts that they will be playing a matching type game. In turn, they will each select two cards. One from the topic pile and one from the rule pile. The object is to match the rule topic with the rule.
One Cub Scout will go first. They select one card from each pile. Ask them to read the rule aloud and decide if the rule matches the topic.
If the topic matches the rule, and they got the right answer, they are done, and it is the next Cub Scout’s turn.
If they are incorrect, they place they return the cards and try again.
If the topic does not match the rule and they got the right answer, they replace the cards and try again.

supply_list: United State Coast Guard approved life jackets in assorted sizes, one for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:

During the meeting:
Tell Cub Scouts that they must wear a properly fitted life jacket for all boating activities.
Explain that the only life jackets Cub Scouts should use are the ones that have been approved by the United States Coast Guard. Show Cub Scouts that a life jacket that has been approved by the Coast Guard has the approval information printed on the inside of the jacket.
Share with Cub Scouts the performance list of Coast Guard-approved life jackets. It is required that everyone, Cub Scouts and adults, wear a level 70 life jacket or above during paddle- craft activities.
Level 50 Buoyancy Aid: Not recommended for weak or nonswimmers. No self-turning ability.
Level 70 Buoyancy Aid: Equivalent to the Type III life jackets. They are the most common life jackets worn by recreational boaters. No self-turning ability.
Level 100 Life Jacket: High flotation life jacket. Some self-turning ability.
Level 150 Life Jacket: High flotation life jacket. Offshore waters, self-turning ability.
Demonstrate with Cub Scouts how to wear a life jacket.
Check the label to see if it’s designed for your size and weight.
Put the jacket on, buckle it, and tighten the straps.
Hold your arms over your head. Have a friend pull up on the tops of the arm openings. If the jacket rides up over your chin or face, it’s too loose.
Ask Cub Scouts to find a buddy. Have Cub Scouts try on the life jackets. Tell them to take turns pulling up on the tops of the arm openings to see if their jacket fits properly.

requirements.text: Show how to properly wear a bicycle helmet.

activities.title: Biking Expert
activities.description: A biking expert will help Cub Scouts learn how to properly adjust their bike helmets.
supply_list: Bike helmet, one per Cub Scout
Helmet Safety Checklist found in Additional Resources

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Invite a biking expert to your meeting. It could be a biking club member or someone from a bike shop with knowledge of fitting bike helmets. Share with your expert the requirements of the adventure.
Remind parents and legal guardians that Cub Scouts will need to bring their bike helmet to the den meeting.
Print a copy of the Helmet Safety Checklist for each Cub Scout.
Become familiar with the proper fitting of a bike helmet by reviewing the Helmet Safety Checklist found in additional resources.
The day before the meeting, remind everyone in the den of the date, time, and location, and to bring their helmets and to wear what they would wear on a bike ride.
If anyone is going to borrow a helmet, disinfect the helmet with an over-the-counter disinfectant spray.
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and introduce your expert.
Have the expert inform them that when we ride bikes, wearing a helmet is one of the most important safety gear we have. A bicycle crash can happen at any time. A properly fitted bicycle helmet reduces the risk of head injury. More children aged 5 to 14 go to hospital emergency rooms for injuries associated with bicycles than with any other sport. Many of these injuries involve the head. Just like any safety gear, you have to wear it properly so that it to work properly.
Have the expert demonstrate how to know that your bike helmet is fitted properly and how to adjust it if it doesn’t.
Your helmet should fit snuggly. While it is sitting flat on top of your head, make sure the helmet doesn’t rock side to side. Sizing pads come with new helmets; use the pads to securely fit to your head. Mix or match the sizing pads for the greatest comfort. In your child’s helmet, remove the padding when your child’s head grows. If the helmet has a universal fit ring instead of sizing pads, adjust the ring size to fit the head.
The helmet should sit level on your head and low on your forehead—one or two finger-widths above your eyebrow.
Center the left buckle under the chin. On most helmets, the straps can be pulled from the back of the helmet to lengthen or shorten the chin straps. This task is easier if you take the helmet off to make these adjustments.
Adjust the slider on both straps to form a “V” shape under, and slightly in front of, the ears. Lock the slider if possible.
Buckle your chin strap. Tighten the strap until it is snug, so that no more than one or two fingers fit under the strap.
Does your helmet fit right? Open your mouth wide…big yawn! The helmet should pull down on the head. If not, refer back to and tighten the chin strap.
Does your helmet rock back more than two fingers above the eyebrows? If so, unbuckle, shorten the front strap by moving the slider forward. Buckle, retighten the chin strap, and test again.
Does your helmet rock forward into your eyes? If so, unbuckle, tighten the back strap by moving the slider back toward the ear. Buckle, retighten the chin strap, and test again.
Roll the rubber band down to the buckle. All four straps must go through the rubber band and be close to the buckle to prevent the buckle from slipping.
Invite Cub Scouts to put on their helmets and have the biking expert check the fit of each helmet.

Adjust the slider on both straps to form a “V” shape under, and slightly in front of, the ears. Lock the slider if possible.
Buckle your chin strap. Tighten the strap until it is snug, so that no more than one or two fingers fit under the strap.
A. Does your helmet fit right? Open your mouth wide…big yawn! The helmet should pull down on the head. If not, refer back to step 5 and tighten the chin strap. B. Does your helmet rock back more than two fingers above the eyebrows? If so, unbuckle, shorten the front strap by moving the slider forward. Buckle, retighten the chin strap, and test again. C. Does your helmet rock forward into your eyes? If so, unbuckle, tighten the back strap by moving the slider back toward the ear. Buckle, retighten the chin strap, and test again. D. Roll the rubber band down to the buckle. All four straps must go through the rubber band and be close to the buckle to prevent the buckle from slipping.
Separate Cub Scouts into two teams. Assign an adult to each team.
Have Cub Scouts form two separate lines.
Adults stand about 5 yards away with the helmets of the Cub Scouts on their team.
When you say go, one player from each team runs run to their helmet, puts it on and checks to make sure it is on correctly.
Using the checklist, the adult checks the fit. Once the helmet fits properly, the Cub Scout runs back to their team, with their helmet on, and tags the next player.
Continue until all Cub Scouts have finished.
The team that gets their helmets on properly and is sitting first wins.

requirements.text: Decide what you should wear when riding a bike.

activities.title: Dress the Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions

Before the meeting:
Collect and gather needed supplies.

Draw a stick figure of a Cub Scout on the sidewalk or driveway.
During the meeting:

requirements.text: Demonstrate proper hand signals.

activities.title: Bear Says
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn and demonstrate proper biking hand signals by playing “Bear Says.”

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up meeting space for Cub Scouts to have room to move about freely.
Understand the rules for playing Simon Says.
The adult leading the activity is “Bear.” The Cub Scouts gather around Bear, who gives instructions by saying, “Bear says…” telling the Cub Scouts to perform a physical action. For this activity, it will be the different hand signals for cycling. For example, “Bear says left turn,” “Bear says stop.” Each Cub Scout must perform the action. If Bear leaves out “Bear says” before giving instruction, anyone who performed the action or gave the wrong signal is out!
Become familiar with the hand signals for cycling.
To signal a left turn, fully extend your left arm out to your side. Make this signal approximately 100 feet before you turn to alert others so that you can get your hands back onto your bike as you turn.
There are two ways to signal a right turn. The first, and most frequently used, is to simply extend your right arm out to your side – just as you would for a left turn, on the opposite side. Another option to signal a right turn, is to extend your left arm out to the side and turn your arm up at a 90-degree angle. Whichever method you use, be sure to make the signal about 100 feet before turning, and leave your arm extended for about 3 seconds.
To indicate that you are stopping or slowing down, simply extend your left arm out, and bend your arm down at a 90-degree angle, with your hand open.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that when riding a bicycle, it is important for those around to know which way they will be going when turning and when they are stopping.
Demonstrate the hand signals for left turn, right turn (both options), and stop.
To practice the signs, they will be playing “Bear Says” which is like Simon Says but only using Bear.
Have Cub Scouts stand up. Practice the following signs calling out “Bear Says” or just the sign.:
Left Turn
Right Turn
Stopping
Alternate Right Turn
Do this for a few rounds until you feel confident Cub Scouts know the hand signals.

activities.title: Hand Signals Worksheet

Have Cub Scouts complete the worksheet and compare answers. Correct if needed.

activities.title: Left Turn, Right Turn
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn and practice bike hand signals.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Using orange safety cones, set up meeting space with a start and finish line 10 yards in length.
Become familiar with the hand signals for cycling.
To signal a left turn, fully extend your left arm out to your side. Make this signal approximately 100 feet before you turn to alert others so that you can get your hands back onto your bike as you turn.
There are two ways to signal a right turn. The first, and most frequently used, is to simply extend your right arm out to your side – just as you would for a left turn, on the opposite side. Another option to signal a right turn, is to extend your left arm out to the side and turn your arm up at a 90-degree angle. Whichever method you use, be sure to make the signal about 100 feet before turning, and leave your arm extended for about 3 seconds.
To indicate that you are stopping or slowing down, simply extend your left arm out, and bend your arm down at a 90-degree angle, with your hand open.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that when riding a bicycle, it is important for those around to know which way they will be going when turning and when they are stopping.
Demonstrate the hand signals for left turn, right turn (both options), and stop.
Explain to Cub Scouts that they will be walking from the starting line to the finish line. As they walk, you will be calling out bicycle hand signals. They are to do the hand signal and complete the action. Have Cub Scouts gather at the starting line.
Have Cub Scouts start walking toward you.
Call out the hand signals at various intervals.
”Left turn”, Cub Scouts are to stick out their left arm, do a counter-clockwise turn and keep walking.
”Right turn,” Cub Scouts are to stick out their right arm, do a clockwise turn, and keep walking.
”Stop,” Cub Scouts are to bend their arm in the stop position and stop walking
Any Cub Scout who does not stop, has to go back to the starting line.
Cub Scout who reaches the end first wins.

requirements.text: Demonstrate how to adjust saddle height.

activities.title: Saddle Up
activities.description: Cub Scouts demonstrate how to adjust a bike seat.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up meeting space with a bicycle with an adjustable seat.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts surround the bike as you demonstrate how to adjust the seat.
Explain to the Cub Scouts that you know your bike seat is at the right height if you can keep your hips stable on the bike instead of rocking them back and forth to reach the bottom of the pedal stroke. When your foot is at the lowest point while pedaling, you want your knee to be slightly bent, not locked out completely straight or curved.
Using the EDGE method do the following:
E: Explain how to adjust the seat: “You pull the lever under the seat away from the bar, and it should loosen.”
D: Demonstrate how to adjust the seat, while you are explaining how to do it.
G: Guide each Cub Scout by giving them the ability to try to do it on their own and assisting them if they need it.
E: Enable them to take a turn adjusting their own seat.
Have each Cub Scout adjust the seat of the bike so that is proper for them.

requirements.text: Demonstrate how to operate brakes.

activities.title: Brake Test
activities.description: Cub Scouts demonstrate how to operate their bicycle brakes.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Find a safe are free of obstacles to conduct the activity.
Mark off area with orange safety cones.
A day prior to the meeting remind Cub Scouts, parents, and legal guardians to bring their bikes, bike helmets, and other safety gear to the meeting.
Draw a start and stop line on the parking lot in chalk.
During the meeting:
Review bicycle helmet safety and have Cub Scouts put on their helmets.
Have Cub Scouts line up along the start line. They will complete this activity one at a time.
Tell Cub Scout that when you say “GO!” they will begin pedaling toward the finish line. When you say “STOP!” they are to use their brakes and stop. Explain that they will start and stop several times on their way to the finish line. Remind them that they should use their “stop” hand signal.
Say “GO!” so that Cub Scout will start pedaling. After they’ve pedaled for a bit, say “STOP!”
Repeat until everyone is across the finish line.

requirements.text: Learn how to use a pump to inflate your tires. Discuss why riding with low-pressure or flat tires is unsafe and can cause damage to your bike.

activities.title: Pump It Up
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn how to pump up their tires safely.
supply_list: Tire pressure gauge, if bike pump does not have one

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up meeting space with a bicycle.
Become familiar with how to use the bike pump you will be using by reading the instruction manual for that bike pump.
Identify on the tire where the proper PSI (Pounds Per Square Inch) for the tire.
Make sure the tire needs air by releasing air out of the tire so it is below the recommended PSI.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts surround the bike as you demonstrate how to pump the tires.
Show Cub Scouts that on every bike tire there is a place that indicates how much air should be in the tire. Explain that air in bike tires expands and contracts with weather conditions. Air expands when it is hot and contracts when it is cold so you always should check your tire pressure before riding.
Show Cub Scouts on the tire where the PSI is. Explain to Cub Scouts that tire pressure is measured in PSI which stands for pounds per square inch. For example, if it says 60 PSI that means that the pressure pushing out on the tire is equal to 60 pounds for every 1 inch by 1 inch square on the tire. That would be like 7 gallons of milk stacked on top of each other placed on your toe.
Demonstrate how to check the tire pressure and compare it to what the pressure should be.
Demonstrate how to pump the tire up to the proper pressure.
Release the pressure in the tire and allow each Cub Scout to check the pressure and pump air into the tire to reach the proper pressure.

The day before the meeting remind Cub Scouts, parents, and legal guardians of the date, time, and location of the meeting and that everyone will need to bring their bike, safety gear, and Cub Scout Six Essentials.

requirements.text: Discover natural resources.

activities.title: Build A World
supply_list: Construction paper in blue, green and brown 1 sheet of each color per Cub Scout
1 pair of scissors per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print 1 Build A World Worksheet per Cub Scout found in additional resources.
Gather the supplies for the meeting
During the meeting:
Explain that each Cub Scout is going to become a
world planner
. They will design a community where people need places to live, food to eat, water to drink, and resources to make the things they need.
Gather Cub Scouts and say:
“Today you get to create your own world! Imagine that people are moving into a brand-new place. You are in charge of deciding where they will live, where their food will come from, how they will get water, and what resources they can use to make the things they need.”
Ask a few quick questions to get them thinking:
Where will people get
water
?
Where will they get
food
What will they use to
build homes
Where will people
live and work
What natural resources will your world have?
How will people travel from one place to another?
Explain that there aren’t necessarily right or wrong designs. The challenge is to make choices and be able to explain why they made them.
Give each Cub Scout a
Build a World Worksheet
.
Before anyone begins cutting and gluing, have them use the worksheet to plan their world.
Ask them to decide:
Water:
Will their world have a river, lake, ocean, pond, or another source of water?
Food:
How will people get food? They might include farms, gardens, orchards, fishing areas, or places for animals.
Natural Resources:
What resources can people use? Examples might include trees, sunlight, water, rocks, soil, or open land.
Buildings:
Where will people live? What other buildings might the community need?
Transportation:
How will people move around? They might create roads, sidewalks, bike paths, bridges, or trails.
Encourage Cub Scouts to think about where things should go. For example, a farm may need to be near water, while a bridge would need to cross a river or stream.
Give Cub Scouts construction paper, scissors, glue, and drawing supplies.
Have them begin with the
natural features
of their world.
They can cut or draw:
Rivers, lakes, ponds, or oceans
Trees and forests
Grasslands or farmland
Mountains or hills
Next, add places that help provide
food and resources
, such as:
Farms
Gardens
Orchards
Fishing areas
Trees for wood
Fields for animals
Then add the
community
, including things such as:
Houses
Stores
Schools
Parks
Roads
Bridges
Trails
Other buildings they think their community needs
Cub Scouts can draw directly on their base paper or cut shapes from construction paper and glue them into place.
As they work, the den leader can walk around and ask questions such as:
“Where does your drinking water come from?”
“How do the people in your world get food?”
“What resources do you have that could be used to build houses?”
“What would happen if you didn’t have enough water?”
“How do people get from their homes to the places they need to go?”
The goal is not to have Cub Scouts create a perfect community. The questions encourage them to think about how
resources and people’s needs are connected
Before declaring their world finished, ask each Cub Scout to check that they have included:
A source of
A way to produce or obtain
Places for people to
live
At least one
natural resource
A way for people to
travel
Something that makes their world special
If something is missing, they can add it before the tour begins.
When everyone is finished, gather the group for a
World Tour.
One at a time, Cub Scouts become the tour guide for the world they created.
Encourage them to point to different parts of their creation while explaining them.
For example:
“Welcome to my town! Our river gives us water. We grow vegetables on this farm because it is close to the river. We use some of the trees for wood to build houses, and we plant new trees to replace them. We have a bridge so people can cross the river.”
Ask each Cub Scout to explain at least:
Where people get water
Where people get food
One natural resource people use
Something they built using their resources
After each tour, allow the other Cub Scouts to ask the world planner one or two questions.
Questions might include:
“Where does your food come from?”
“What happens if your river dries up?”
“Why did you put your houses there?”
“How do people cross the river?”
“What do you use your trees for?”
“How do people travel around your world?”
Finish by asking:
“Did every world look the same?”
Point out that communities can look very different because they have different resources and different ways of meeting people’s needs.
Ask:
“What were some things almost every world needed?”
Guide Cub Scouts toward recognizing common needs such as
food, water, shelter, resources, and ways to move people and supplies
End with:
“When we build communities, we have to think about what people need, what resources are available, and how we can use those resources wisely.”

requirements.text: Discover what happens to the wastewater in your community.

activities.title: Water Conservation Charades
activities.description: Cub Scouts will learn ways of conserving water by playing charades.
supply_list: Conservation Charades clues found in Additional Resources
Pen and paper for keeping score

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Investigate how wastewater is managed in your community: physical water treatment, biological water treatment, chemical treatment, or sludge treatment.
Where does wastewater go to be cleaned?
How is it returned to the water cycle?
Print the Conservation Charades clues .Cut the clues into strips.
Fold each strip and place in a small bowl.
Set up meeting space so Cub Scouts have plenty of room to move around.
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and share what you learned about what happens to wastewater in your community.
Explain to the Cub Scouts that something everyone can do to help the environment is to conserve water and today you will play a game of charades about how to conserve water.
Divide Cub Scouts into two teams.
Have one person from team one pull a water conservation clue from the bowl. Give Cub Scout one minute to act out their clue while the rest of their team tries to guess what the person is doing.
If the team guesses correctly, they get one point.
Continue this process giving each team a turn to guess. Have a different Cub Scout do the acting each time.
The team with the most points at the end wins.

Gather Cub Scouts outside the water management facility.

How does the water get to my house?

requirements.text: Investigate soil.

activities.title: Aqua Pollution Adventure
activities.description: Cub Scouts demonstrate how pollution can enter our groundwater.
supply_list: Clear glass loaf pan or baking pan, 9”x13”, 1 per two Cub Scouts
Powdered drink mix, red or purple in color
Book or small block of wood

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up workspace for Cub Scouts.
During the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts to make a small pile of powdered drink mix in one end of the clear glass pan.
Have them sprinkle sand over the rest of the pan.
Place the end of the pan with the powdered drink mix on top of the book or wood block so the pan is tilted.
Using the spray bottle of water have Cub Scouts wet the sand. Make sure it’s really wet. Let it sit for a few minutes, and then wet it again.
Carefully lift up the pan and look underneath it. What is happening
?
As you can see, the water is carrying the powdered drink mix through the pan. Pollutants spread through our sources of water the same way. They can travel a long distance and can damage drinking water miles from where the pollution starts!

activities.title: DIY Composter
activities.description: Cub Scouts will build their own composter.
supply_list: One empty two-liter soda bottle for each Cub Scout
Dirt (not potting soil, use dirt from outside)
Compost materials: grass clippings, vegetable scraps, coffee grounds
Flat plastic dish to hold composter for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Rinse all the two-liter soda bottles and peel off labels.
Using the sharp knife, cut off the top of the bottle, approximately 1-2″ inches below the neck of the bottle. Cub Scouts will need both pieces of the bottle.
Set up meeting space for Cub Scouts to have room to move around. Cover any tabletops.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts investigate the types of soil found in their handbooks. Discuss with them the differences in soil and what things each type can do. Talk about what compost can do well.
Set out the shredded newspaper, dirt, compost materials, and dead leaves.
Give each Cub Scout a bottle, a nail, and a flat dish.
Ask Cub Scouts to carefully use a nail to punch 8 to 10 small air and drainage holes along the sides and bottom of the bottle.
Tell Cub Scouts to put their bottle on their flat dish. Have them put some dirt, shredded newspaper, and old leaves inside the composter as their compost starter.
Have Cub Scouts use the spray bottle to wet the compost starter.
Tell Cub Scouts to add compost materials to their compost. Next, have them turn the bottle top upside down and place it in the open top of the bottle.
Explain that Cub Scouts will take their composter home. They should place it in a spot where sunlight can reach it and should cover the top with a kitchen towel when not in use.
Tell Cub Scouts to check the composter each day to see what it looks like. Every few days, Cub Scouts should stir the compost and make sure to keep the contents damp. As their compost breaks down, they can add more kitchen scraps or plant litter, as well as some more soil from outside to mix in.

sections.content:

What color is the soil?
What does the soil feel like? Does it feel gritty or smooth?
Is the soil crumbly or clumpy?
Does the soil have rocks? How about leaves or sticks?

How are the soil samples different from each other?

requirements.text: Investigate air pollution.

activities.title: Acid Rain Investigation
activities.description: Cub Scouts conduct an acid rain experiment.
supply_list: Three jars or other containers for each Cub Scout
Three flowers with stems of equal lengths for each Cub Scout
Three pieces of masking tape for each Cub Scout
Small box or other container for taking flowers home

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Set up the meeting room with tables to provide enough space for the activity.
Lay out the supplies for the activity for each Cub Scout.
During the meeting:
Have Cub Scouts write “water,” “slightly acidic,” and “acidic” on the pieces of masking tape.
Have Cub Scouts add water to the three jars. Have them completely fill the first container, fill the second one ½ full, and the third one ¼ full.
Ask Cub Scouts to add enough vinegar to the second and third containers to fill them completely. Tell them to put the pieces of masking tape on the appropriate container.
Tell Cub Scouts to put a flower into each jar.

activities.title: Air Pollution Investigation

supply_list: Four index cards for each Cub Scout
Hole punches for every two or three Cub Scouts
String or yarn, four pieces approximately 24” long for each Cub Scout
One Q-Tip for each Cub Scout
One piece of paper for each Cub Scout
Pen or pencil for each Cub Scout
Ziploc bag for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
During the meeting:

Have Cub Scouts use the Q-Tips to smear Vaseline inside the square.
Tell Cub Scouts to put their index cards into their Ziploc bag and take them home.
Instruct Cub Scouts to hang the Index cards in different locations outside their home. Have them write down the number and location of each card.
Ask Cub Scouts to collect their Index cards after a few days and to examine the results.
Tell Cub Scouts to use a magnifying glass to count the number of particles stuck in each of the Index cards. Have them write down their observations on the paper.
At the next meeting, ask Cub Scouts to share where they hung the index cards and how many particles were stuck to each one.

activities.title: Human Air Pollution Detectors
activities.description: In this activity, Cub Scouts will be “indoor pollution detectors” to investigate air pollution.
supply_list: One onion cut up in a tightly sealed plastic bag

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Cut up the onion, and tightly seal it in a plastic bag.
During the meeting:
Space individual Cub Scouts evenly around the room. Tell them that they will be “indoor air pollution monitoring instruments.”
Place a fan in the front of the room and turn it on. Show Cub Scouts the bag with the onion in it.
Ask the “monitoring instruments” to close their eyes tightly and use only their sense of smell for this activity. They need to keep their eyes closed until you tell them to open them.
Tell Cub Scouts to raise their hands as soon as they detect onion smell “pollution” and to leave their hands up as long as they continue to smell it.
In front of the fan, open the bag with the cut onion.
Use a stopwatch or watch with a second hand to time how long it takes for all of the “monitoring instruments” to detect the “pollution.”
Allow the fan to continue to run. Record how long it took for indoor air pollution to spread through the room.
Close and seal the bag as soon as each child has detected the “pollution”. Place the bag in a drawer or outside.
If possible, open a window and place the fan so that it is blowing in fresh air from outside.
Restart the stopwatch.
Ask the “monitoring instruments” to lower their hands when they can no longer smell the onion “pollution”.
Record how long it takes for fresh air to sweep the “pollution” from the room.
Have the children open their eyes.
Discuss how long it took for everyone to detect the “pollution,” and how it took for it to go away.

requirements.text: Pick a kitchen appliance that uses technology to complete the following requirements.

activities.title: Now we are Cooking with Air
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about air frying.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Review the owner’s manual for the air fryer you will demonstrate.
Learn how air fryers work by watching the YouTube video “
How an air fryer works.
” (duration 56 seconds)
Set up the meeting so Cub Scouts can easily see the air fryer. Lay out the different pieces of the air fryer.
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and inform them that for this Adventure they are going to use an air fryer.
Explain what an air fryer is and how it works. An air fryer uses hot air to cook food. This is like an oven, but the big difference is that an air fryer moves the air around the food at a much higher speed than an oven, which reduces cooking time.
Explain the difference between frying with oil and using an air fryer. When you fry with oil the oil can cook food fast because it can get really hot. The problem that some have is that when frying in oil, some of the oil is absorbed into the food and for some that can be a problem for their health or other dietary concerns.
Tell the Cub Scouts to always have an adult supervise them when using an air fryer.
Point out the different parts of the air fryer and explain what they do.

activities.title: Pick a Pot
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about pressure cooking.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Review the owner’s manual for the pressure cooker you will demonstrate.
Learn how pressure cookers work by watching the YouTube video “
The Science Behind Pressure Cookers.
” (duration 1 minutes 49 seconds)
Set up the meeting so Cub Scouts can easily see the pressure cooker. Lay out the different pieces of the pressure cooker.
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and inform them that for this Adventure they are going to use a pressure cooker.
Explain what a pressure cooker is and how it works. A pressure cooker is a pot that has a lid with a special seal that locks the lid in place. When the pot heats up the water or moisture that is inside can get hotter than boiling water using a regular pot. This way the water gets hotter before turning into steam. This higher temperature cooks food faster and the moisture in the pressure cooker keeps it from drying out compared to cooking in an oven.
Explain that with this extra hot water and steam, the pressure inside the pot can be dangerous. Point out the safety valve on the pressure cooker and explain that there is a safety measure to keep from opening the lid if the pressure has not been released.
Tell the Cub Scouts to always have an adult supervise them when using a pressure cooker.
Point out the different parts of the pressure cooker and what they do.

activities.title: The Science Oven
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about microwave ovens.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Review the owner’s manual for the microwave oven you will demonstrate.
Learn how a microwave oven works by watching the YouTube video “
How a Microwave Oven Works.
” (duration 5 minutes 11 seconds)
Set up the meeting so Cub Scouts can easily see the microwave oven.
During the meeting:
Gather the Cub Scouts and inform them that for this Adventure they will use a microwave oven.
Explain what a microwave oven is and how it works. Early microwave ovens in the 1950’s was called science ovens and used only commercially. Residential microwaves were introduced in 1967. A microwave oven uses small waves of energy to make water molecules move. When water molecules move, they create energy which generates heat. Unlike other methods of cooking where heat is applied from the outside to cook the food to its inside, a microwave oven will cause the water molecules to heat all parts of the food at the same time.
The more moisture a food has the quicker and more effective the microwave oven will cook the food. This also means that when the water molecules heat up, they can turn into steam causing moisture to leave the food that can cause it to become dried out when cooking.
Tell the Cub Scouts to always have an adult supervise them when using a microwave.

requirements.text: Explore the term “forensics” and how it is used to help solve crimes.

activities.title: Scene Forensics Worksheet
activities.description: Cub Scouts look at a crime scene and fill out a worksheet

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print 1 copy of the Forensics Worksheet per Cub Scout.
Set up the meeting space by:
Knocking over a cup with a little water spilled
Placing a napkin on the floor
Tipping a chair
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and tell them that today they will be learning about forensics.
Share with them the vocabulary
Evidence: Clues that help us understand what happened
Observation: What we see (no guessing!)
Inference: A smart guess based on evidence
Give each Cub Scout a copy of the Forensics Worksheet and ask them to walk around the room and write down what they see (they may not touch anything).
Have them complete the worksheet and share their answers with each other.
Ask them, did everyone think the same thing happened? Explain that is why the evidence is so important.

activities.title: Solve the Mystery
activities.description: Cub Scouts become investigators by observing and analyzing the scene to determine who ate the cookie.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Decide which leader or den chief ate the cookie.
Gather supplies.
Find an adult volunteer or den chief to be the “cookie eater.”
Set up the crime scene.
Use an ink pad to transfer the “cookie eater’s” fingerprint to the cup of milk.
Use chalk to transfer the “cookie eater’s” shoe print near the scene.
Leave a plate with cookie crumbs on the scene.
Leave bit of sugar and baking soda near the plate.
Rope off the area with rope or crime scene tape.
During the meeting:
Tell Cub Scouts they are going to be investigators by figuring out who ate the cookie.
Have Cub Scouts share their observations about the scene.
What do they see?
What is missing?
Give Cub Scouts a set of gloves to wear.
Have Cub Scouts collect fingerprints from one another, adults, and den chief (see requirement 2 “Fingerprint Fun.”)
Have Cub Scouts collect shoe imprints from one another, adults, and den chief (see requirement 3 “Gumshoe.”)
Allow Cub Scouts to compare the collected fingerprints and shoe imprints they have collected to the fingerprints and shoe imprints left at the crime scene.
Once Cub Scouts have discovered “the eater,” congratulate them and let them eat a cookie.
If they ask about the sugar and baking soda, have the “cookie eater” share that they were trying to make cookies of their own, but then decided eating already made cookies would be easier.

requirements.text: Analyze your fingerprints.

activities.title: Are You There?
activities.description: Cub Scouts discover that even if they can’t see their fingerprint with their naked eye, they are still there.
supply_list: 8 ½” x 11” piece of white paper, one for each Cub Scout
Magnifying glass, one for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Become familiar with using magnetic powder to find fingerprints by watching this video on YouTube, “
Developing Latent Fingerprints with Magnetic Powder
(2 minutes 46 seconds.)
Gather the supplies.
Set up meeting space so Cub Scouts have an area to do their fingerprinting.
During the meeting:
Let Cub Scouts know that fingerprints are skin patterns on the ends of your fingers and thumbs. Their fingerprints are different from those of everyone else on earth. Even identical twins have different fingerprints! When we touch things, we always leave fingerprints even if we cannot see them! That’s because our skin produces sweat and oil.
Explain that because everyone has unique fingerprints, law enforcement officers can use them to figure out who was at a crime scene. Using the Fingerprint Pattern worksheet, show Cub Scouts the fingerprint patterns and point out differences.
Tell Cub Scouts that now they will get to investigate their own fingerprints.
Give each Cub Scout a blank piece of paper and ask them what they see. Can they see any fingerprints on the piece of paper?
Explain that when we touch things, we always leave fingerprints even if we cannot see them! That’s because our skin produces sweat and oil.
Demonstrate how to use magnetic powder. Remind the Cub Scouts that it doesn’t need to touch the paper.
Hand each Cub Scout a magnifying glass to examine their fingerprints. Ask what they see? How is their fingerprint different than another Cub Scout’s fingerprints?

activities.title: Fingerprint Fun
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn the different patterns in fingerprints and analyze their own fingerprints.
supply_list: Fingerprint Card found in Additional Resources
Fingerprint Patterns found in Additional Resources
2 pads of dark ink, black, blue or red work best
Magnifying glass, one for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Print one Fingerprint Card on white cardstock for each Cub Scout.
Print a single copy of Fingerprint Patterns.
Gather the supplies.
Set up meeting space so Cub Scouts have an area to do their fingerprinting.
During the meeting:
Let Cub Scouts know that fingerprints are skin patterns on the ends of your fingers and thumbs. Their fingerprints are different from those of everyone else on earth. Even identical twins have different fingerprints! When we touch things, we always leave fingerprints even if we cannot see them! That’s because our skin produces sweat and oil.
Explain that because everyone has unique fingerprints, law enforcement officers can use them to figure out who was at a crime scene. Using the Fingerprint Pattern worksheet, show Cub Scouts the fingerprint patterns and point out differences.
Tell Cub Scouts that now they will get to investigate their own fingerprints.
Make sure Cub Scouts’ hands are clean and dry so ink can stick to fingers.
Demonstrate how to take a fingerprint.
Extend one finger at a time while tucking under the other four fingers.
Roll the finger on the ink pad so the entire fingerprint pattern area is evenly covered with ink. The ink should cover from one edge of the nail to the other and from the crease of the first joint to the tip of the finger. Try not to push too firmly on the pad, you don’t want the finger to have too much ink.
Roll each finger from nail to nail in the appropriate space on fingerprint card. Make sure to lift each finger up straight up after rolling to avoid smearing and smudging.
Have each Cub Scout decide which hand they want fingerprinted.
Have each Cub Scout practice fingerprinting a finger or two on a piece of scratch paper until they feel they have the technique down.
Give each Cub Scout a fingerprint card to take their “real” fingerprints.
Once each finger is printed give Cub Scout a baby wipe to clean the ink off.
Give each Cub Scout a magnifying glass and a fingerprints patterns sample.
Have each Cub Scout share with a buddy what patterns they see in their fingerprints. Are they the same as their buddy?
Tip: Combine this activity with requirement 1 “Solve the Mystery.”

activities.title: Whose Fingerprint Is It
activities.description: Cub Scouts look at fingerprints and try to match them.
supply_list: 10 pieces of paper (2″ × 2″) per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Cut the paper into 2″ × 2″ squares, enough for 10 per person
During the meeting:
Gather Cub Scouts and explain that everyone’s fingerprints are unique.
Give each Cub Scout 10 pieces of paper.
Instruct Cub Scouts to place a finger on the ink pad, then put their fingerprint on 2 pieces of paper. They should write their name on 1 paper and then continue with the rest of the fingers on that hand.
Have Cub Scouts wipe and wash their hands.
Collect the papers with their names on them in 1 pile and without their names in another pile.
Have Cub Scouts spread out the fingerprints with names on the table.
Give each Cub Scout 5 pieces of paper at random and ask them to match the fingerprints.
Ask Cub Scouts what the hardest part of matching the fingerprints was.

requirements.text: Make a shoe imprint.

activities.title: Gumshoe
activities.description: Cub Scout investigate how their shoe can leave a print.
supply_list: 9” x 12” black construction paper, one sheet for each Cub Scout
1 light colored sidewalk chalk for each Cub Scout
Baby wipes or a wet rag

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Using the information below, make a sample of a shoe impression.
Gather supplies.
Set up meeting space so Cub Scouts have an area to do their shoe print.
During the meeting:
Ask the Cub Scouts if they have ever walked outside in the snow and looked behind them? What did they see? Explain to Cub Scouts that just like our fingers have prints our shoes have prints. Law enforcement officers will look for shoe prints and will then make an impression. They can find the brand and size of the shoe. They can tell how tall the person is by measuring the length of the shoe. Today they will be looking more closely at their shoe impression. Show them your example.
Have each Cub Scout sit in a chair and place a piece of construction paper on the ground in front of them.
Give each Cub Scout a piece of chalk and have them liberally apply the chalk to the bottom of their shoe.
Have the Cub Scout stand on top of the piece of paper in front of them.
Have the Cub Scout sit back down and clean off their shoe with a baby wipe or damp cloth.
Let each Cub Scout look at their impression. Ask what do you notice? Do you see a shoe size? Is there a pattern? Is the bottom of your shoe the same as mine?
Tip: Combine this activity with requirement 1 “Solve the Mystery.”

activities.title: Heavy Shoes
activities.description: Cub Scout make a shoe impression.
supply_list: Shoe boxes, one for each Cub Scout
One pound of Plaster of Paris in a strong plastic bag for each Cub Scout
2 cups of water in a plastic bottle for each Cub Scout
Wood craft sticks, one for each Cub Scout
Toothpicks, one for each Cub Scout
A small trowel or spade for each Cub Scout
Soft paint brush for each Cub Scout
Soft toothbrush for each Cub Scout
Bubble wrap or a cardboard box (optional)

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
This activity will take two meetings to complete.
Before the meeting:
Become familiar with shoe impressions by watching this YouTube video, “
Casting Footwear Impressions.
” (duration 6 minutes and 10 seconds.)
Collect enough larger shoes boxes for your Cub Scouts.
Locate soil and fill shoe boxes half full.
Gather remaining supplies.
Set up meeting space so Cub Scouts have an area to do their shoe print.
During the first meeting:
Ask the Cub Scouts if they have ever walked outside in the snow and looked behind them. What did they see? Explain to Cub Scouts that just like our fingers have prints our shoes have prints. Law enforcement officers will look for shoe prints and will then make an impression. They can find the brand and size of the shoe. They can tell how tall the person is by measuring the length of the shoe. Today they will be looking more closely at their shoe impression.
Demonstrate how to make a good shoe impression in the shoe box of dirt. Press your foot down firmly and lift straight up to avoid distortion.
Have each Cub Scout make their own impression in their shoebox full of dirt. Hint: Spray the impression with hairspray to help hold the soil in place and secure the impression.
Have the Cub Scouts help mix their Plaster of Paris mixture by following the directions on the bag. When mixed there should be no lumps and should be the consistency of pancake batter.
Either cut a hole in the corner of the bag or open the bag a little at the top.
Begin pouring the Plaster of Paris on the top or bottom of the impression. Slowly pour toward the other end of the shoe. Avoid distorting the impression by not pouring in the middle.
Once all the Plaster of Paris is used, give each Cub Scout a wood craft stick to gently smooth out the surface.
Have each Cub Scout gently write their names or initials in the Plaster of Paris with a toothpick.
Let the impressions set for 30 minutes.
Use a spade or trowel to lift the cast from the shoe box. Dig into the soil a few inches away from the cast. Avoid hitting the cast with the spade to prevent breakages.
Set impression aside to finish setting. Finish cleaning and investigating at the next den meeting.
During the second meeting:
Have Cub Scouts carefully remove the soil using a soft paint brush or a soft toothbrush.
Once most of the soil has been removed, help the Cub Scouts put the cast under a running tap and use the paint brush to gently brush the cast to remove any remaining soil.
Let the impression dry again once it has been cleaned. Then, spray with hairspray (or lacquer) to strengthen the cast and prevent it from crumbling during handling.
Have the Cub Scouts observe the impression. Ask what they notice about this impression? Is there a difference in how deep their impression is versus yours? Do they notice patterns or cracks?
If the Cub Scout wishes to keep the cast, wrap it in bubble wrap or put it in a cardboard box to protect it from breaking.

activities.title: Muddy Shoe
activities.description: Cub Scout investigate how their shoe can leave a print in the dirt.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Determine the best place near your meeting location to make a shoe impression. Avoid rocky or hard surfaces.
Clear the area of extra rocks and debris. Smooth it out as much as possible.
Let parents and legal guardians know to have their Cub Scout wear a pair of shoes they don’t mind getting a little muddy.
During the meeting:
Ask Cub Scouts if they have ever walked outside in the snow and looked behind them? What did they see? Explain to Cub Scouts that just like our fingers have prints our shoes have prints. Law enforcement officers will look for shoe prints and will then make an impression. They can tell how much a person weighs by how deep the impression is in the mud or soft ground. They can find the brand and size of the shoe. They can tell how tall the person is by measuring the length of the shoe. Today they will be looking more closely at their shoe impression.
Bring Cub Scouts to the pre-determined spot and demonstrate how to make a shoe impression by firmly pressing your foot into the ground and the lifting straight up to avoid distorting your impression. Be careful not to slide or fall.
Have Cub Scouts make their shoe impressions.
Have Cub Scouts observe their impression. Ask what they notice about this impression? Is there a difference in how deep their impression is versus yours? Do they notice patterns or cracks?
Have the Cub Scouts measure their shoe. Compare the size of their shoe to the impression. Is the size the same?

requirements.text: Do an analysis of four different substances: salt, sugar, baking soda and cornstarch.

activities.title: In the Kitchen
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn how to test for various substances.
supply_list: Substance Observations worksheet found in Additional Resources
Pen or pencil, one for each Cub Scout
½ sheet black laminated paper split into 4 quadrants for each Cub Scout
Magnifying glass, one for each Cub Scout
Eye dropper/pipettes, one for each Cub Scout
Toothpicks, one for each Cub Scout
1/4 teaspoon of salt for each Cub Scout
1/4 teaspoon of sugar for each Cub Scout
1/4 teaspoon of baking soda for each Cub Scout
1/4 teaspoon of cornstarch for each Cub Scout
Cup of water, enough to share
Cup of vinegar, enough to share

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Make laminated black quadrant papers for each Cub Scout. The lamination keeps the paper from soaking through and makes for easier clean-up. If you can’t laminate, use a sheet protector folded in half.
Print Substance Observations worksheet, one for each Cub Scout.
Gather supplies.
Set up meeting space to conduct experiment.
During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that forensic chemists do tests to identify unknown substances. For example, they might add a chemical to the substance to see how it changes. They will now get to going to analyze some white substances that look a lot alike to see how we can tell them apart like a forensic chemist.
Give each Cub Scout a black quadrant paper, Substance Observations worksheet, and a pencil.
Tell Cub Scouts that you will be putting a little bit of white powder on their black paper. Have them begin looking at the substances with their naked eye. Ask what difference do you see? What similarities do you see? Have them write down observations.
Give each Cub Scout a magnifying glass. Have them look at the substances again. Ask what difference do you see? What similarities do you see? Have them write down observations.
Have each Cub Scout feel each substance between their fingers. Ask what it feels like. What differences do you feel?
Have each Cub Scout smell each substance. Caution them not to get too close. Ask what does it smell like?
Give each Cub Scout a toothpick. Tell them to split each substance in half using the toothpick.
Give each Cub Scout an eyedropper/pipette.
Let each Cub Scout put a drop or two of water on each of their substances. Ask what happened? Did the appearance change? Was there a chemical reaction?
Let each Cub Scout put a drop or two of vinegar on each of their substances. Ask what happened? Did the appearance change? Was there a chemical reaction?
Have them make their best guess in identifying each of the four substances.

requirements.text: Learn about chromatography and how it is used in solving crimes.

activities.title: Fall Leaf Chromatography
activities.description: Cub Scouts discover pigments found in fall leaves using chromatography
supply_list: 1 –2 fresh fall leaves that have started to change colors and are not dry or crispy per Cub Scout
12 oz. clear plastic cups, one per Cub Scout
Regular-sized white coffee filters, one for every four Cub Scouts
Plastic wrap, enough to cover each plastic cup

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting
This experiment must sit for 24 hours.
Review the experiment and conduct it yourselfat least
two days before the meeting
.
Read page 215 of the Bear handbook to become familiar with what chromatography is, so you can explain it to the Cub Scouts during the meeting.
Cut the coffee filters to create four equal rectangular (oblong) strips.
24 hours before the meeting, gather fall leaves from the same species and place them in a plastic cup.
With the back end of a spoon, smash up the leaves as small as possible.
Add three tablespoons of rubbing alcohol into the cup with the leaves.
Cover the cup with plastic wrap to keep the alcohol from evaporating.
The next day, remove the plastic wrap from the cup.
Take a coffee filter strip and fold it so it hangs over the cup and the end inside of the cup just touches the rubbing alcohol.
It will take 20 to 30 minutes to see the effect of the separation of pigments on the coffee filter strip.
Let the strip dry.
Repeat steps 4-7, using different species of leaves and labeling each cup to identify what tree the leaves came from.
During the Meeting
Gather Cub Scouts and explain what chromatography is. Tell them that you will conduct an experiment to see what pigments are in fall leaves.
Have Cub Scouts take the fall leaves from the same tree or species and place them in a plastic cup.
With the back end of a spoon, ask them to smash up the leaves as small as possible.
Next, have them measure and add three tablespoons of rubbing alcohol into the cup with the leaves.
Have Cub Scouts cover the cup with plastic wrap to keep the alcohol from evaporating. Set the cups aside.
Give each Cub Scout one of the cups of leaves you prepared 24 hours ago. Explain that because the experiment needs to sit for 24 hours, you prepared some in advance so that they can continue the experiment.
Have the Cub Scouts discuss what they see and any differences between species of trees.
Tip from the experts:
Match this activity along with the MMmm Chromatography activity while they are waiting for the 20 to 30 minutes for the leaf pigments to separate.

activities.title: MMmm Chromatography
activities.description: Cub Scouts dissolve the candy coating to discover the colors used
supply_list: 5 – 7 oz. clear plastic cups per Cub Scout
1 Regular-sized white coffee filters, per Cub Scout
7” non-paper plates, one per Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the Meeting
Review the experiment and conduct it yourself.
Read page 215 of the Bear handbook to become familiar with what chromatography is, so you can explain it to Cub Scouts during the meeting.
Cut the coffee filters to create four equal rectangular (oblong) strips
Place 4 M&M’s® on the plate separate them from each other.
Using the water pipette, have them fill their pipette and place several drops of water on each M&M’s®.
Wait several minutes as the candy coating starts to melt away.
Have Cub Scouts fold their coffee filter strips in half and then fold it back again to create a crease.
Using an empty water pipette, have Cub Scouts soak up one of the puddles of water that now has the candy coating color in it and place several drops ¼ of the way on the coffee filter. This part does not need to be rushed, and it is okay if the colored drops dry on the coffee filter.
Repeat the last step for the other 3 colors
Next, have Cub Scouts hang the coffee filter strip over the side of the clear plastic cup with the colors inside the cup. Do this for each colored strip.
Instruct Cub Scouts to fill each cup with just enough water so that it touches the bottom of the coffee filter strip. This is similar to the experiment in the Bear Handbook on pages 215-216, with the difference being that instead of black ink, the strip has the candy coloring on it.
After several minutes as the water will climb up the coffee filter strip and hit the candy coloring, and the pigments will start to separate. Note that some colors will have several pigments, as others may only have one or two.
During the Meeting
Gather Cub Scouts and explain what chromatography is. Tell them that they will conduct an experiment to see what pigments are used to make different colored candies.
Give each Cub Scout a 7” plate, five plastic cups, 4 water pipettes, and four strips of coffee filters.
Have Cub Scouts fill one of their cups halfway with water.
Give each Cub Scout four different colored M&M’s®. Tell Cub Scouts not to eat them.

activities.title: What Color Is It?
activities.description: Cub Scout learn that not all chemicals are what they appear to be.
supply_list: Assortment of nonpermanent felt-tip markers of different brands such as Flair and Color Scents.
Glass of water for each Cub Scout
Paper plates, one for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Test out each of the markers to ensure that they will work for the experiment. Not all markers will separate.
Cut the coffee filter into 1” strips.
Gather supplies.
Set up meeting space to conduct experiment.
During the meeting:
Explain that chromatography is the process forensics scientists use to separate different parts of a mixture. By separating the parts, they can identify drugs, DNA, and poisons. Most chromatography is done in laboratories with expensive equipment, but today they will get to do a simple chromatography investigation using felt tips marker, coffee filters, and water.
Give each Cub Scout a strip of pre-cut coffee filter.
Have each Cub Scout choose a marker.
Ask Cub Scouts to label one end of the coffee filter with the color and brand of marker. Fold the labeled end so that it fits over the glass.
Have each Cub Scout draw a horizontal line with their marker across the middle of their coffee filter strip.
Put the strip in the glass of water, making sure the line the Cub Scout drew with the marker is above the water.
Now watch what happens. The coffee filter will slowly absorb water, which will rise toward the top of the strip. As the water rises, it will carry along components of the ink. Lighter components will travel the longest distance; heavier components will not travel as far.
When the water nearly reaches the top of the strip (or when you don’t see any more changes happening), take the strip out of the water and set it on a paper plate to dry.
Repeat the experiment with several different types of markers. Compare the results to see how similar or different the inks you used are.

requirements.text: Review the buddy system and how it works in the outdoors.

activities.title: Bear Buddies Rule
activities.description: Cub Scouts review what to do while using the buddy system.
supply_list: Cub Scouts will need their Bear handbook

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Become familiar with the Buddy System by watching this video “
The Buddy System.
”
During the meeting:
Review the Buddy System section in the ​​Bear handbook with Cub Scouts​​.
Separate Cub Scouts into buddy groups, by counting off 1-2. If an odd number of Cub Scouts are present, a group of three Cub Scouts can be created.
Tell Cub Scouts to be with their buddy during the entire meeting. Reinforce the fact that they should have a buddy with them at all times especially if they need to use the bathroom.
Conduct the meeting as you had planned.
At two or three random times during the meeting, yell “Buddy Check”.
Identify which buddies are together and which buddies are not. If buddies are not together, encourage Cub Scouts to find their buddy. Once they have their buddy, ask Cub Scouts to hold hands and raise them above their heads.
At the end of the meeting, discuss:
Why is it important to remember our buddy when we are outside?
Why is it important to have a buddy when you have to leave the group?

activities.title: Standing Bear Buddies
activities.description: Cub Scouts learn about the buddy system by playing a game.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Become familiar with the Buddy System by watching this video “
The Buddy System.
”
During the meeting:
Review the Buddy System section in the ​​Bear handbook with Cub Scouts​​.
Divide Cub Scouts into buddy pairs by counting off.
After Cubs Scouts paired up, have them space out across the room to ensure they have enough room to play the game.
Have Cub Scout buddy pairs sit down, with their backs together and touching. Have Cub Scouts interlock their arms.

requirements.text: Make a marble bag.

activities.title: Make a Marble Bag
activities.description: Create a personal drawstring bag to hold your marbles.
supply_list: For each Cub Scout: Piece of fabric about 5 inches by 9 inches Needle and thread Safety pin Shoestring or piece of cord about 3 feet long Scissors
Beads, press on stickers or patches, felt/fabric markers, etc.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Collect supplies.
Make a marble bag to use as an example.
Ask that parents and legal guardians be available to assist as needed.
Organize supplies into a set for each Cub Scout.
Set up meeting space with room for Cub Scouts to work on their marble bag.
During the meeting:
Tell Cub Scouts that they will be making a marble bag to hold their marbles using the supplies on the table.
Have Cub Scouts fold the long ends of the cloth over about 1 inch and make a crease. Sew along the cut edges of the fabric to form two pockets.
Fold the fabric in half so the printed side is on the inside. Sew along both edges — but not over the pockets you formed in the previous step.
Attach the safety pin to one end of the shoestring or cord. Put the safety pin at the end of one of the pockets and push it through to the other end.
Next, put the pin in the closest end of the other pocket, and push it through to the other end. Remove the safety pin and tie the ends of the shoestring or cord in an overhand knot.
Turn the bag right side out. Fill the bag with marbles. To close it, scrunch the fabric at the top together and tie another overhand knot where the shoestring or cord comes out.
Decorate if desired.
Put marbles into the bag.

activities.title: No Sew Marble Bag
activities.description: Make a personal drawstring bag to hold your marbles without sewing.
supply_list: For each per Cub Scout: 10-inch square scrap of felt, fleece, or other non-fray material 24-inch-long shoestring, paracord, yarn, or other sturdy corded material 9-inch paper plate Pencil Ruler Scissors to cut fabric
Beads, press on stickers or patches, felt/fabric markers, etc.

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Make a sample marble bag. Collect supplies.
Ask additional parents to be available to assist as needed.
Organize supplies into a set for each Cub Scout.
Set up meeting space with room for Cub Scouts to work on their marble bag.
During the meeting:
Tell Cub Scouts that they will be making a marble bag to hold their marbles using the supplies on the table.
Lay the fabric square out flat on the table.
Place the paper plate on top of the fabric face down. Note: Check to make sure no part of the plate is off the fabric.
Use the pencil to trace around the outer edge of the plate to create a circle pattern on the fabric.
Use scissors to cut out the circle.
Using the ruler and pencil, at the top of the fabric, measure one inch away from the edge of the fabric.
Mark a ½ inch line. Mark a second ½ inch line ½ inch to the right.
Repeat the markings every 45 degrees. When complete, there should be eight sets of marks around the fabric.
Cut each mark to create a space to weave the thread through.
Tie an overhand knot towards the end of each end of the cord.
Note: If beads or other decorations are available to add to the cord, they should be available to begin adding now.
Weave the cord through the holes of the fabric.
Pull the loose ends tight until bag is closed and tie into a bow or other desired knot.

requirements.text: Play three different marble games.

activities.title: Ringer, Plums, and Dropsies
activities.description: Learn and play Ringer, Plums, and Dropsies.
supply_list: 2 shooter marbles, 1/2” – 3/4” in size for each Cub Scout
10 or more target marbles, 1/2” in size for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Collect all supplies
Set up an area for each game in the meeting space allowing room for Cub Scouts to freely move about.
Set up individual game areas:
RINGER Use the masking tape (or painter’s tape) to create a ring on the ground 10 feet in diameter
PLUMS In another area, create two separate parallel lines each approximately 6 feet long (may be longer depending on the number of Cub Scouts) and approximately 4-8 feet apart. One is the shooting (taw) line, one is the target line.
DROPSIES In a third area, create a 2-foot square for every 4 players.
During the meeting:
Share with Cub Scouts that they will be playing three different marble games round robin style. They will start at one game, play for a period of time, and then move onto the next game.
Assign an adult to help at each of the game areas.
Allow 15 minutes for each game by using the timer.
Play each of the following games.
RINGER This marble game needs at least two players.
Put 13 marbles in the middle of the ring arranged in an X shape. They should be about 3 inches apart.
The first player kneels outside the ring and uses their shooter to try to shoot a marble out of the ring. If it misses, the player’s turn is over, and they pick up the shooter. If the shooter hits and stays in the ring, the player can shoot again from where the shooter stopped. If the shot hits and the shooter goes out of the ring, the player’s turn is over. The player keeps any marbles that go out of the ring.
When the first player’s turn is over, the second player takes a turn, etc.
Keep playing until time is up or most of the marbles have been knocked out. The player with the most marbles is the winner.
PLUMS This game is for an even number of players.
Draw two parallel lines about 6 feet apart.
Each player puts the same number of marbles (called “plums” in this game) on one line a few inches apart. The players stand behind the second line.
Players take turns shooting at the plums from behind the second line. They keep any plums they knock off the line.
Keep playing until time is up, if a time limit has been set, or until all the plums have been picked. The player with the most marbles is the winner.
DROPSIES This game is good for two, three, or four players.
Each player places five marbles inside the square.
The first player stands on one side of the square with their feet outside the line. That player drops a shooter from above waist height onto one of the other players’ marbles to try to knock it out of the square. If that happens and the shooter stays in the square, the player keeps the marble that rolled out, and they get another turn. If a marble is knocked out, but the shooter also rolls out, the player keeps the marble that rolled out and their turn ends.
After playing all the game, ask Cub Scouts which they liked the best and why.

requirements.text: Build a marble racetrack with at least two lanes.

activities.title: Marble Racetrack
activities.description: Create a marble racetrack from recycled materials.
supply_list: Five to ten paper towel tubes
Five to ten toilet paper tubes
Ten paper plates of various sizes
PVC pipes, at least ¼” larger diameter than the marble size

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
Before the meeting:
Familiarize yourself with the possibilities by watching the following videos:
Make an Easy DIY Marble Race Track
Marble Run Challenge
How to make a recycled marble run
Gather supplies.
Set up meeting space with room for Cub Scouts to build a marble racetrack together.
During the meeting:
Share with Cub Scouts that they will be building a racetrack together for marbles that has at least two lanes using the materials in the meeting space.
Talk about the different ways the supplies could be used to create a marble racetrack.
Tubes can be used as tunnels, cut in half length wise to create channels which could also be taped together to create different lanes, cut multiple times along the width and then reassembled to fame a curve, and used as support towers to create varying heights to the track.
Paper plates can be cut and tilted to make spirals, cork screws, and funnels. Different sized plates will allow for wider or tighter curves.
Egg cartons can be used as a trap at the end of the course to collect the marbles, and an obstacle for the marble to navigate through during the race.
Pipe cleaners can be used to create different lanes for the marbles on the track
Paper or plastic cubs can be used as traps at the end of the race, and tubes or funnels during the race
Cardboard boxes can be used as a frame for the racetrack, additional supplies for parts of the racetrack, or simply inclined with tape for lanes.
Talk about gravity and friction.
Gravity: The track needs inclines to allow the marbles to race under their own power. The track should start at a high point and end at a low point.
Friction: Different materials will affect the speed at which the marbles can race.
Let the Cub Scouts discuss what they would like their racetrack to look like. Remind them the more complex the design, the more time it will take to build the track before racing.
Play! Allow the Cub Scouts to race their marbles.

activities.description: Create a maze for marbles.
supply_list: Shallow cardboard box, cardboard box lid, or sheet cake pan, one for each Cub Scout

sections.content:

During the meeting:
Explain to Cub Scouts that a maze is a game with a defined starting point and end point. The goal is to get from the starting point to the end point by navigating the various twists and turns.
Mazes can be varying levels of complexity. The more corners, turns, and dead ends the mazer has, the more challenging it will be.
The marble is navigated through the maze by the player holding the maze and twisting and turning the maze to control the direction of the marble through the maze.
Share your marble maze design. Point out what you did and how you could make it different.

activities.description: Den or pack provides a build day for Cub Scouts.
supply_list: Safety goggles, for anyone working with or near power tools
Ear protection, for anyone working with or near power tools
Band saw, only adults may use
Scroll saw, only adults may use
Pinewood Derby® Car Kit , one for each Cub Scout and a couple of spare kits (Scout Shop SKU: 17006)
Pinewood Derby® flat weights , one for each Cub Scout (Scout Shop SKU: 7602)
Small Phillips head screwdrivers, enough to share
Small flathead screwdrivers, enough to share
Paint, high gloss acrylic, various colors
Small paint brushes, one for each Cub Scout

sections.heading: Directions
sections.content:
A build day is longer than a typical meeting. Cutting out cars, painting them, allowing them to dry, and assembling them will take hours based on the number of power tools available and the number of Cub Scouts in the den or pack.
Before the meeting:
Visit the
Pinewood Derby® website
and share with members of the den to get familiar with the race and ideas for designs.
Confirm meeting location.
Confirm that equipment is in good working order.
Three days before the meeting remind Cub Scouts, parents, and legal guardians of the meeting date, time, and location of the build day.
Prepare the meeting location to give everyone enough room to work on their cars.
During the meeting:
Draw a design for your car.
Take the block of wood in the Pinewood Derby® car kit and place it on its side. Draw an outline of the wood on paper. Now draw the profile (side view) of the car.
Cut out your car from the block of wood.
Cub Scouts may use a handsaw, or an adult may use a power tool to cut out the car.
Sand the car.
Sanding will remove any sharp corners and will allow paint or any other decoration to be added to the car stick better.
Paint and decorate your car.
Pinewood Derby® cars are made of soft wood. When painted, it may take a couple of layers or coats of paint. Paint the car once. When the paint is dry, use sandpaper to lightly sand it. Clean off any dust from sanding and paint it again. This can be repeated until you get the desired look is achieved.
Assemble your car.
Using the nails that came with the kit, attach the wheels that came in the kit to the car in the pre-cut areas on the bottom of the car.
Check the weight.
Do this step last as everything else will either add or subtract weight from the car. The car should weigh exactly 5 ounces. If it weighs less, additional weight may be added.
Tip: Make sure the axles are square, at a 90-degree angle. This will keep the car straight when going down the track. If the axles are not square, the car may want to turn and rub up against the track causing it to slow down. Test the car by simply pushing it across the floor to see if it goes straight.
